`ART-04` asked whether a 512 px atlas cell should mean a bigger sprite on screen, or the same size at twice the resolution. Bigger is a whole-game layout change — every screen-space calculation, the measured pivot, the accessibility baselines all move. Higher resolution is far cheaper in code, a draw-time scale, and is the option that would have won on looks alone. **It is rejected on performance**: the sixteen-yaw library already measures 157.3 MB of uncompressed atlas VRAM, and quadrupling the area per cell takes that to roughly 630 MB on GL Compatibility — not a number to spend with no complaint driving it, and decision 056 already recorded the opposite call, accepting detail loss at distance on purpose. `ART-01`'s sixteen-yaw heads bought the real fidelity win already, a turret that tracks instead of snapping, for 157 MB and 30 percent under the ceiling the PRD's own risk register warns about. This is the rare case where quality-first and no point the same way. Reopen only on a reported legibility complaint at zoom 1.0, never on a feeling that sharper would be nicer.
067 — a check that cannot fail

`PRESSURE_FLOOR` in `sim/run.py` asserts the player is pressed against reactor capacity. It has now been measured dead **twice**: 0 of 72 anchor-by-difficulty cells fail it, including under the four new capped-core policies, and including restricted to winning builds only — which was the original backlog item's own proposed repair. A check that cannot fail is worse than no check at all, because it implies coverage that isn't there. Raising the floor until it discriminates was the alternative on the table, and it is rejected too: a threshold picked to make today's data fail is fitted to that data, not derived from anything. The design property behind it is real and worth keeping — it's the one genuinely good idea the whole game rests on — but peak load ratio is simply the wrong instrument for it. What replaces the constant is a question with its own evidence to gather (`LF-164`), not another number chosen to make a graph turn red. All 24 anchors still grade clean with the check gone.
068 — the branch that argued back

19 of 20 `.gd` files were already indented in tabs, `.editorconfig` already pinned it, and the editor was settling the question by attrition anyway. `main.gd` is reindented as a standalone whitespace-only commit with a blame-ignore entry, so it doesn't poison `git blame` on every line it touches. The more interesting move is what got **deleted**: a 6,000-line worktree branch carrying the opposite choice, all 19 files reindented to four spaces. It was never going to be merged once tabs had 19-to-1 and a config file already saying so — keeping it alive was how this question stayed open for sessions. A branch is diligence when it represents work still being weighed. This one represented a vote that had already lost, still sitting in the tree as if the question were unsettled.
069 — closed, not merely unscheduled

Line of sight (`TER-12`) and a per-node power grid (`WAR-11`) were reserved for the owner since the PRD was written, and the PRD's own text already recommended against both. Both close outright rather than sit open in a way that reads as "coming eventually." Line of sight is the largest single work item in the programme and **invalidates all 24 anchor grades** on its own — a cost that matters more now than when the PRD was written, since the previous entry in this journal showed the grades are still moving under abilities the grader now models honestly. Stacking a rule that changes what every emplacement can reach on top of a grading model that doesn't yet track ability charge would compound two unsettled things instead of settling one. The regional grid fares no better on cost: relay nodes already deliver the interesting half of the idea, supply as ground you take and defend, for a fraction of what a full per-region rewrite of both rule engines would cost.

What ties the four together is not the subject matter, it's the shape of the delay. Three of these had been measured to death before this commit ever existed: the `PRESSURE_FLOOR` emptiness was measured twice, the atlas VRAM number had been sitting in the library since `ART-01` landed, and tabs had already won 19-to-1 with a config file saying so in writing. The evidence was complete in every one of the three; what was missing was somebody saying the word. And the honest failure worth naming is that a **branch** was being used to keep a rejected indentation scheme alive, and a **backlog item** was being used to keep a check already shown twice to catch nothing alive — both of them ways of not deciding that look, from outside, exactly like diligence. Open work still under consideration. Neither was still being considered. Both were only costing sessions.
Also filed: the wrap is running the wrong check in the wrong place

The same commit files `PRC-20` (`#93`), refined from the owner's own `#90` with a fourth cause they hadn't named: the session wrap runs the full gate unconditionally, and now that every commit on `main` arrives through a gated pull request, that gate is largely re-proving what the PR flow already proved. The number behind it: tier 4 on the run that motivated the issue came to **1,755,759 ms — 29 minutes**, of which `rules parity` alone was roughly 13 across 1,440 runs, and roughly 20 of more than 32 total wrap minutes had already passed with the commit and this journal still outstanding. `PRC-05` already built the fix — a content-hash cache that skips parity entirely when nothing that affects it changed — and it simply isn't wired into the wrap's own path. Filed as the highest-priority item in the programme, ahead of any feature work, because what it's billing is the owner's own attention, not compute.

entries.title: Silent and wrong: a guard built to stop that, doing exactly that
entries.summary: scripts/main.gd's reindent to tabs closes the mechanical half of decision 068, verified whitespace-only rather than assumed. The real story is what landing the previous entry ran into on the way past: the guard rail built to stop one agent's git stash sweeping five workstreams together made a brand-new file uncommittable by the documented workflow, and the failure mode was not a refusal — it was a published site with a dead link and nothing red anywhere.

commits.subject: style(gdscript): reindent main.gd to tabs — whitespace only
chore: teach git blame to look through the reindent, and file two tooling traps

body.text: `scripts/main.gd` was the last of twenty `.gd` files still holding four-space indentation. Decision 068 had already settled that indentation is tabs, and the other nineteen files were already there with `.editorconfig` pinning it — the editor was going to keep re-settling this by attrition either way. The transform is mechanical: n leading spaces become `n//4` tabs plus `n%4` spaces, preserving nesting exactly, 721 lines changed. Worth two sentences mostly for the verification shape — whitespace-only was **proved, not asserted**: `git diff -w --stat` printed nothing against the same commit that plain `git diff --stat` reports as 721 insertions and 721 deletions, and `godot boots` was run on top of `gdscript parses`, because `main.gd` is the main scene's script and a parse check alone would not have caught a broken boot. Decision 068 also called for deleting the 6,000-line all-spaces branch that had been keeping the rejected option alive; it doesn't exist on origin and isn't local, so there was nothing left to delete — the branch that had been arguing back was already gone.

The same pair of commits teaches `git blame` to look through the reindent: `.git-blame-ignore-revs` now lists `698d3d8`, so a blame on any reindented line skips past the whitespace-only commit to whoever last touched the content. GitHub honours the file automatically; locally it needs one `git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs`. The file states its own bar for admission, because a commit listed there is invisible to blame and a real change smuggled inside one would be unattributable.
The real story is what landing the previous entry ran into

While the previous entry in this journal — the four owner-gated decisions, published in `048dcfd` — was being committed, the documented coordinator workflow silently published a broken chronicle page. `git commit --only docs/chronicle` committed the regenerated `chronicle.json` and `index.html`, and silently dropped the new entry page both of them link to, because `--only` commits tracked modifications and the new file was untracked. No error; the commit reported three files changed and looked complete. Naming the file directly then failed outright — `pathspec ... did not match any file(s) known to git` — and `tools/hooks/guard.py`'s git-safety rule denies `git add` with no escape hatch, unlike `rule_background` (`LF_ALLOW_BACKGROUND=1`) and `rule_raw_engine` (`LF_ALLOW_RAW_ENGINE=1`), which both ship documented opt-ins. The retry loop failed five times running before anyone stepped back and asked why.

So a rail built to stop one agent's `git stash` sweeping eleven files across five workstreams had, as a side effect, made it impossible to commit a single new file — and the failure mode was not a refusal, it was a GitHub Pages publish with a dead link and nothing red anywhere. The guard exists precisely because silent-and-wrong is worse than loud-and-blocked; here, it produced silent-and-wrong. The way through was `git update-index --add <path>` — plumbing rather than `git add`, one named path, which cannot do the thing the guard actually defends against. That is the tell that the rule is too broad: the documented harm is a wide add sweeping other agents' files, and a single explicit pathspec cannot cause it. Filed as `LF-166`, with the fix left open between two shapes — give the rule the same `LF_ALLOW_*` opt-in the other two already have, or narrow it to deny only the wide forms and let an explicit single pathspec through.

Filed the same way in the same pass, by hitting it rather than by reading code first: `LF-165`, 584 tracked render PNGs, 224 tracked `.import` sidecars, and 360 more sitting untracked in every agent's `git status` before it reaches that agent's own edits. The game never loads a loose render — `sprites.gd` reads only `sprites.json` and the packed atlas pages — so the sidecars are build output of an editor import, not content. Left open rather than fixed here, because `git rm --cached` is an index operation and the index is shared across whatever else is running in the tree at the time.

entries.title: Measuring the fifth non-negotiable, for the first time
entries.summary: CLAUDE.md's fifth non-negotiable — loudness-match audio, never peak-normalize — had never been measured by anything in the gate. The only audio check, check_sfx_reproducible, verifies determinism, not loudness; a synthesis change that reproduces byte-identical but drifts the whole bank's perceived level would have passed every check the project has ever run. PRC-18's testing audit found the gap. tools/audio/loudness.py closes it with a real ITU-R BS.1770-4 / EBU R128 gated integrated LUFS implementation, validated three independent ways and proved red on real assets before being trusted — and it ships with its own blind spot named rather than hidden.

commits.subject: feat(audio): measure loudness, the non-negotiable nothing was measuring

body.text: CLAUDE.md states five non-negotiables for this project. The fifth reads: "Loudness-match audio, never peak-normalize — peak normalization is why programmer audio sounds flat." It has sat in that file since early in the project. Nothing in the gate ever checked it. The only audio check that exists, `check_sfx_reproducible`, verifies exactly one thing — that re-synthesizing `ui_confirm.wav` reproduces the committed bytes — which is a **determinism** check, not a loudness one. A synthesis change that is perfectly deterministic but drifts the whole bank's perceived loudness, the precise failure the non-negotiable names, would have passed every check this project has ever run, for the project's entire life. `PRC-18`'s testing audit is what found the gap, rather than anyone noticing it was missing.
A real implementation, not a proxy

`tools/audio/loudness.py` is a real ITU-R BS.1770-4 / EBU R128 gated integrated LUFS measurement — K-weighting (a high shelf plus a high-pass), 400 ms blocks at 75% overlap, the −70 LUFS absolute gate, the −10 LU relative gate. Two details worth recording because they are the kind of thing that is easy to get quietly wrong: the K-weighting filter coefficients are derived from **each file's own sample rate**, not the standard's published 48 kHz table, because the SFX bank is 44.1 kHz and the music is 48 kHz — resampling to reuse the published numbers would have been exactly the kind of precision the measurement doesn't have. And a first pass took minutes to run, because raw `rfft` on prime-length audio files is pathological; padding to the next power of two fixed it. SFX now measures in about 2 seconds across 86 files; music takes about 85 seconds across 14, because full-length stereo FFTs over several-minute tracks dominate the cost — which is also why the tool is not one check but two, split by tier.
Validated three ways before being trusted

An unvalidated LUFS number that looks authoritative is worse than an honest peak/RMS proxy, so this was checked three independent ways rather than assumed correct because the formula was copied faithfully. First, calibration: a 0 dBFS 997 Hz sine measures −3.052 LUFS at both 44.1 and 48 kHz, against −3.01 LUFS, which is a BS.1770 fact independent of any implementation. Second, gain linearity: shifting that same signal by ±6.02 dB moves the measurement by ±6.02 LUFS to within 1e-4. Third, and the one that matters most because it is the only one checked against a second, independently-written implementation: `assets/audio/music_manifest.json`'s `target_lufs` field is what ffmpeg's `loudnorm` filter — already in this repo, driving `tools/audio/ingest_music.py` — two-pass-normalized every one of the 14 shipped music tracks to. Measuring the shipped files with this tool and comparing against that target is a cross-check between two separately-written BS.1770 implementations, not a self-check. The result: median delta −0.03 LU, mean −0.00 LU, worst 0.58 LU, across all 14 tracks. Two independent implementations of the same standard, agreeing to within a rounding error.
Bands anchored to the bank, not to a broadcast target

The pass/fail band for each category is mean ± 3 sample-stdev of the *current accepted bank*, measured at commit `048dcfd` — never a broadcast target like −14 or −23 LUFS. Decision 011 already records what happens on this project when a metric gets tuned against itself; anchoring to a fixed external number would have meant either picking one that happened to already fit, or immediately failing the whole bank. SFX and music are banded separately, because a UI hover tick and a three-minute music bed are not comparable material and gating them together produces a check that is either useless or permanently red: SFX bands to (−34.05, −10.87) LUFS, mean −22.46, σ 3.86, n=86; music bands to (−26.45, −11.69) LUFS, mean −19.07, σ 2.46, n=14.
Proved red before being trusted green

A check that has never failed has not been proven to work — it has only been proven not to have failed yet. So before this was trusted, it was run against real committed assets, copied to scratch and deliberately shifted: `shield_break.wav` at +6 dB measured −8.89 LUFS, FAIL. `threshold_idle.wav` at −6 dB measured −36.77 LUFS, FAIL. `A1-FIN_eleven_years_of_nothing.ogg` at +6 dB measured −11.03 LUFS, FAIL. `SYS-DBF_debrief.ogg` at −6 dB measured −30.02 LUFS, FAIL. Run against the untouched, unmodified bank: 100 of 100 files pass, exit 0.
The honest half: what a band anchored to a bank's own spread cannot see

The SFX band is 23.2 LU wide, and that width is not slack in the measurement — it is because the cues in this bank are **deliberately** not loudness-matched to each other. A hover tick and a heavy footfall are not supposed to be equally loud; that is mix balance, not drift. The consequence was measured rather than left as a theoretical caveat: **`ui_confirm.wav` at +6 dB still passes.** A mid-band cue can drift a full six decibels and this check will not notice, because six decibels does not carry it outside the bank's own historical spread.

Underneath that sits a structural limit that no band width can fix: a per-file band anchored to a bank's own mean and spread can never catch a **uniform** bank-wide drift. Shift every cue in the bank by the same N dB and the mean moves, the standard deviation moves, and the band — computed from that same shifted data — moves with it. The check would stay green through the exact failure the fifth non-negotiable exists to prevent: a whole bank drifting hot or flat together. This is filed as `LF-168`, and the instruction recorded there is deliberately not "narrow the band" — narrowing it would start failing cues the sound design intends to be quiet, repeating the mistake decision 011 already warns against. What it needs instead is a second signal: the bank's mean LUFS tracked against a frozen historical baseline that does not move when the bank does.

So the honest summary is two-sided. A stated non-negotiable went from zero measurement, for the entire life of this project, to a validated implementation that catches real per-file drift at the edges of what the sound design allows — that is a genuine gain. And the same tool ships with a named, proven blind spot at its center and a structural one underneath that no amount of tightening fixes. Both halves belong in the record; a journal that kept only the first would be exactly the kind of quiet overstatement this tool was built to stop happening to loudness.
Not wired in yet, and that is deliberate

`tools/check.py` is not touched by this change. That file was owned by another workstream in flight the same session this landed, so wiring the two checks in was left for that workstream to pick up rather than risked as a collision. The registration is recorded in the commit body rather than left to be re-derived: `Check("sfx loudness", 2, check_sfx_loudness)` and `Check("music loudness", 4, check_music_loudness)`, split across tiers because the SFX half costs about 2 seconds and the music half alone, at roughly 85 seconds, would exceed tier 3's entire current budget on its own.

entries.title: The wrap decides its tier before it spends anything
entries.summary: The owner's own complaint opened this one: the last session wrap took over thirty-two minutes and was still not finished, with roughly twenty of those minutes gone before the commit and journal had even started. Tier 4 on that run measured 1,755,759 ms — 29 minutes, ~13 of it rules parity. Only one of the three faults found was a slow check; the wrap now decides its tier before spending anything, and the escalation it added fired for real, twice, for reasons nobody staged.

commits.subject: feat(process): the wrap decides its tier before it spends anything

body.text: The complaint was the owner's own: the previous session wrap took over thirty-two minutes and was still not finished. Roughly 20 of those >32 minutes had gone by with the final commit and the journal entry still outstanding. `PRC-20` (`#93`) measured what actually happened on that run — tier 4 of `check.py`, unconditional, total **1,755,759 ms — 29 minutes**, of which `rules parity` alone cost roughly **13 minutes**.

The issue spec named three faults, and it is worth being precise that only one of them was a slow check. First, the wrap ran the full gate unconditionally, and that is simply the wrong **place** to do it: work now lands through pull requests, each already gated before it opens, so by the time a wrap starts, everything on `main` has already been verified once — the wrap's full gate was largely re-proving what the PR flow just proved. Second, the fix for the slow part already existed and was not being used on this path — a content-hash cache makes `rules parity` skip entirely when nothing that can affect it changed, and a wrap invoking the gate with no flags paid full price regardless. Third, everything was serialised behind the slowest check — the backlog groom, the STATE rewrite, the journal entry and the commit itself do not depend on the gate's result until the very last step, and were pure wall-clock spent waiting on it.

The cost was also growing, and growing **because of good work**: `rules parity` was 864 runs at roughly 9 minutes in the morning of the same day and 1,440 runs by the evening, because `BAL-02` added four capped-core grading policies and `BAL-01` four scheduled ones. Every policy that makes grading more truthful multiplies the parity matrix — the tension is real and this journal has no tidy resolution for it beyond `#85`, which is what actually right-sizes the matrix rather than just hiding its cost from the wrap.
What landed

A new tool decides the tier **before** anything expensive starts. Tier 2 by default — and the choice is justified in the skill itself, not just made: the wrap is verifying **the wrap's own edits**, `docs/STATE.md`, `docs/BACKLOG.md`, `docs/DECISIONS.md` and everything under `docs/chronicle/`, none of which touch rules or assets. Tier 4 runs on `--release`, or automatically on either of two self-explaining triggers: the session's own diff touching `scripts/anchor_sim.gd` or anything under `sim/`, `data/` or `assets/`, or a parity digest cache miss for any other reason. The second trigger is deliberate and covers the case with **no repo diff at all** — the digest folds in the Godot binary's own version string, so an engine upgrade invalidates the cache and must force the full check.

The skill itself is reordered around that decision: reap, decide the tier, launch the gate **in the background**, do the backlog groom, decisions, STATE narrative and journal entry while it runs, **end the turn** — the owner-blocking boundary — then join on the completion notification, regenerate STATE's AUTO block from the gate's own saved JSON, commit, reap again. Backgrounding goes through the harness's own tracking under an explicit opt-in, never a raw shell `&` or `nohup`: the project's launch guard denies those outright, for the reason `CLAUDE.md` already states — an untracked background process is precisely the thing that re-invokes the model and bills a session everyone believed was over.
The parity harness now prints its content-hash digest on **every** full run, cached or not — previously there was no way to tell a cached skip from a slow run without watching it happen.
The numbers, against the issue's own targets

rows: 24.9 s under 92%-CPU parity load · 26.4 s idle
bounded by the turn-end, so under 1 min
clean at every checkpoint, including after two ~13-min parity runs

body.text: Proved both ways, and the real half was not staged

The escalation logic was not merely asserted to work — it fired for real, twice, on the actual shared working tree, for two reasons nobody arranged: untracked sprite-render `.import` litter left behind by a different workstream, and mid-session uncommitted edits to two sim files from a concurrent agent, which also produced a genuine digest cache miss on their own. And it correctly did **not** fire on a docs-only diff — `tier 2, reasons []`. A shared tree with several agents in it is a harder environment than any test would have staged, and this is what it actually did to the tooling: proved the escalation both ways in the course of one ordinary session, not as a planned demonstration of it.
The honest half

Tier 2's own 25-second budget is now genuinely tight — 24.9 to 26.4 seconds measured, against a 25 s budget the wrap does not itself assert. And it sits close to that line with a timer that cannot be fully trusted: `LF-170`, filed this session, records the gate timing its checks with a wall-clock call rather than a monotonic one, observed once reporting a **negative 796 ms** elapsed under heavy concurrent load. One data point, not reproduced on demand — but a timer that can move backwards under load is the wrong instrument to be sitting this close to a threshold with.

`LF-169`, filed the same session: the asset-path escalation trigger fires on editor-generated import sidecars that carry no gameplay content at all, so a shared tree can escalate the wrap for reasons unrelated to the session's own work — exactly the mechanism that fired above. It interacts directly with `LF-165`, filed the session before, which already found hundreds of those sidecars sitting untracked in every agent's working tree.

Two items closed on the way past rather than opened new. `LF-134` turned out to already be fixed — the parity harness's own subprocess had carried a timeout since an earlier commit, and the backlog item had simply never been marked done. Worth recording as its own small lesson: an argument for closing an item at the commit that fixes it, not at the next wrap that happens to notice. And `LF-115` was a latent trap rather than a live bug — the STATE regeneration tool never forwarded its tier flag to the gate, which cost nothing only because the default was the full gate regardless of what was asked for. This change is exactly what would have made that silent default dangerous, so it was fixed in the same commit that created the hazard, not left for the next session to rediscover.

entries.title: The headline did not survive its own follow-up
entries.summary: ‘largest-hole-closes’ published Threshold Surge flipping 9 of 72 anchor-by-difficulty cells from loss to win, with its own caveat attached: charge accrual was unmodelled, and the next regrade could not start until it was. LF-163 modelled it. The claim does not reproduce — zero cells flip — and the reason is not that boards fail to earn charge. This is that correction, appended rather than edited in, the way the rule says it has to be.

body.text: This entry corrects ‘The largest hole in the project closes: a grade that presses buttons’ (`largest-hole-closes`, commit `4daeb7c`, #89), published earlier the same day. That entry is not edited — nothing in it is wrong about what it measured, and the chronicle does not rewrite a past entry when a later one overturns it. It gets a new one, linked back, the same way `docs/DECISIONS.md` never edits a settled decision. This is that entry.

The published finding was precise: Threshold Surge, fired on a deterministic schedule with no charge, cooldown or cost modelled, flipped 9 of 72 anchor-by-difficulty cells from loss to win — sweeping all three difficulties on both anchor-12 and anchor-13 — and was 0 worse across all 72. The entry declined to read that as mispricing. It named the gap plainly — charge accrual did not exist in `sim/engine.py` at all — and it named the follow-up: `LF-163`, model charge, re-run those nine cells, and block `BAL-04`'s regrade on it. `LF-163` is now closed.
The first finding reframes the task

The gap was never in the rules. `scripts/abilities.gd`'s `AbilityState` already tracked Surge's charge in full — `charge_max`, `charge_per_leak_cost`, `ready()`, `began()` — and `scripts/anchor_view.gd`'s `_charge_surge()` was already wired to `AnchorSim`'s `unit_killed` signal, live, on every kill. That code sits deliberately outside `anchor_sim.gd` itself, on the same precedent decision 033 already set for `sell()`. What was unmodelled was `sim/engine.py`'s and `scripts/test/parity.gd`'s own scheduled-dispatch layer — the machinery `BAL-01` built to press buttons on a fixed clock. Both files carried the same admission in their own words: Surge "has no charge/cooldown model in this file at all." The rule itself was never in question. `scripts/anchor_sim.gd` has a zero diff.

The port is the existing rule, not a new one: `charge += leak_cost * charge_per_leak_cost` on every kill from either `_damage()` or Surge's own `_fire_surge()`, clamped at `charge_max`, ready at `>= charge_max`, reset to zero on an actual cast. A scheduled cast whose time arrives before a full charge has accrued is still consumed off the schedule but does nothing — mirroring `anchor_view.gd`'s `activate_ability()` returning nothing and playing a deny cue on a press that isn't ready yet.
Proved red before it was trusted

A gate that silently no-oped would have reproduced the original 9-of-72 result exactly and looked like confirmation rather than correction. It did not: anchor-12, brutal, `surge-on-peak` — 12 scheduled attempts, 3 actually fired, 9 denied for insufficient charge, with charge reaching the full 100 only at t=135s, 295s and 415s of the run.
All 72 cells were then regraded charge-gated against ungated, run twice — byte-identical both times — and cross-checked against the `sim.run` CLI with 0 mismatches. **Zero cells flip.**
Why zero, and the real finding underneath it

Not because boards fail to earn charge — they don't. Anchor-12 at brutal difficulty earns three full charges from ordinary combat across a roughly 470-second run, which is exactly what the original entry's own design note predicted when it estimated the wins needed five to fourteen casts rather than one. The actual reason is that **`surge-on-peak` is not the sole winner on any of the 72 cells under today's ruleset, gated or not.** Gating drops it out of 7 cells' winner lists — anchor-11 standard, and anchor-12 and anchor-13 at all three difficulties, exactly where the original entry flagged its own concern, so the location of the worry was real — but every one of those 7 cells is already won independently by a conventional build with no ability involved at all: `mortar-core`, `burst`, `flak-screen` or `intel-first`, depending on the anchor. The loss-without-Surge premise the whole “flips 9” headline rested on is gone. “0 worse across all 72” still holds.
Two loose ends, on the record rather than buried in a backlog item

Nobody knows why the winner lists moved between the two measurements. The obvious explanation is ruled out: `BAL-01`'s own report says the four capped-core policies — `mortar-core` among them — were already in its 16-policy baseline when it ran, so their arrival is not what changed. Candidates not yet investigated: the balance fixes `LF-098`, `LF-129`, `LF-130` and `LF-136` landed in between, or a content edit to anchor-12 or anchor-13 itself. Unresolved, filed as part of `LF-172`.

And three of the nine cells were never written down. `BAL-01` said nine. Only six are named anywhere — anchor-12 and anchor-13 at three difficulties each — across the issue spec, the original chronicle entry, `docs/DECISIONS.md` and the backlog. The other three cannot be checked, because nobody recorded which cells they were. That is a finding about how a measurement gets written down here, not just about Surge.
The angle

This is a good day for the method. A result was published with its own caveat attached and a named follow-up; the follow-up was done; the result did not survive; the correction is a new entry rather than a quiet edit to the old one. That loop working — catching its own headline rather than letting it stand uncontested — is the entire point of keeping the chronicle and the backlog this way. The uncomfortable half is just as real: a measurement can rot in a single day of otherwise good work, and this one did, and three of its nine data points were never recorded well enough to even check.

The practical upshot: `BAL-04` is unblocked. No grade in the current 72-cell table depends on Surge being available on demand. But it inherits no evidence either way about whether the 130-damage, 35%-falloff numbers are correctly tuned — nothing in this regrade exercised that question, because nothing in the current winner lists depends on the ability at all. “The grader has no evidence either way, because nothing depends on the ability” is what `BAL-04` actually gets handed. That is a different, and more useful, thing to hand it than either “trust it” or “don't.”

entries.title: The stronger test was the one nobody ran
entries.summary: PRC-18's testing audit grepped every tracked scripts/*.gd filename against every tools/*.py, scripts/test/*.gd and data/scenarios/*.json file. Sixteen scripts came back with zero references, and gamepad input had no test in any form anywhere in the project — while two scenario files already on disk pinned real numbers to four decimal places and had simply never been wired into the gate. This entry closes gamepad, save/load, the recovery draft and audio loudness, and records the session's most expensive mistake along the way: a save-isolation flag that does not exist on this Godot build, silently ignored rather than rejected, that ran a tool twice against the real shared Linux dev save before an unchanged-mtime check caught it.

body.text: PRC-18 started from a blunt, mechanical audit: grep every tracked `scripts/*.gd` filename against every `tools/*.py`, `scripts/test/*.gd` and `data/scenarios/*.json` file, as a proxy for whether anything in the verification surface ever touches that script's behaviour. Sixteen came back with zero hits — `recoveries.gd` and `draft.gd` (the between-anchor recovery draft, already flagged fragile twice by LF-065 and LF-070), `progress.gd` (save/load), `pause_menu.gd`, `audio_director.gd`, `ui_theme.gd`, `abilities.gd`, `dialog_view.gd`, `cli_args.gd` among them. Gamepad input was worse than zero references — it was zero anything: grepping Godot's own `Joypad`, `JoyButton` and `JoyMotion` identifiers across the whole project returned no hits at all, in any file, while `CLAUDE.md`'s invariant table and the PRD both state full keyboard, mouse and gamepad control as a shipped non-negotiable.

The sharper part of the finding was not the empty column, it was the full one nobody read. `check_scenarios_pass` hardcoded a single path, `smoke.json`, confirmed by reading the function body. Sitting next to it on disk, unreferenced by anything: `abilities.json`, which pins `dealt = 130 * lerp(0.35, 1.0, dist/path_length) = 47.1782638888889` to four decimal places, plus `a11y-worst.json` and `lf161_edge_scroll_contained.json`. `smoke.json` says in its own note field that it is not a claim about anchor-01's balance. The stronger test was the one nobody ran.
The failure — a silent flag, a real save, twice

`--user-data-dir` is not a flag this project's Godot build recognises. Confirmed against `--help` directly, not assumed. It is also not rejected — Godot does not error on an argument shaped like a flag it does not have; it is simply never read. The first version of `tools/save_roundtrip.py` believed that flag isolated its scratch save, and it did not: the tool ran twice against the real, shared Linux dev/test save at `~/.local/share/godot/app_userdata/Latticefall/progress.json` before an unchanged-mtime check on the default location caught it. State was reconstructed as far as it could be, but some ambiguity remains, because several agents were active on the machine at the time. The owner's Windows save was checked directly and is clear — that directory has no `progress.json` at all, and only its logs folder carries a recent mtime, from the unrelated Windows parity leg of the gate.

The mechanism that actually works is `XDG_DATA_HOME` set in the child process's environment, which Godot's Linux backend does honour — and, just as important, asserting the default save location's mtime is unchanged after every run, rather than trusting the isolation flag to have worked. That second half is the real lesson: the failure mode is silent and destructive, so isolation has to be checked, not assumed. Filed as LF-175, and it belongs next to `CLAUDE.md`'s existing `.godot/` cache warning — same class of mistake, same shared machine, same tree the owner plays out of. It is also the third time in this session that a silent failure has been the expensive one, after LF-166's dropped file publishing a dead link and `wrap_gate.py` escalating on every invocation making a whole feature inert without ever going red.
What landed

items: Loudness measurement wired into the gate at last: `sfx loudness` at tier 2 (measured 1.9–2.0 s), `music loudness` at tier 4 (85.1 s) — the module itself, a real BS.1770 integrated-LUFS implementation, landed separately and is described in the previous entry; this is the check registration that actually runs it.

One check per scenario file instead of one hardcoded path: `smoke.json` (30.7 s), `abilities.json` (15.9 s), `a11y-worst.json` (8.9 s), `lf161_edge_scroll_contained.json` (12.7 s) and the new `gamepad_build.json` (18.7 s). Split rather than looped deliberately — a loop's failure names whichever file happened to run first that iteration and buries the rest in detail text; a red run should name one thing.

Gamepad injection proved to work: `Input.parse_input_event()` with a real `InputEventJoypadButton` or `InputEventJoypadMotion` on device 0 — not the `InputEventAction`-shaped `press` verb LF-139 already proved — is matched by the InputMap and reaches `_unhandled_input()` one frame later, exactly like the keyboard path. `Input.get_connected_joypads()` stays empty throughout, so none of this needed a physical pad. A new `gamepad` scenario verb and `data/scenarios/gamepad_build.json` drive cursor, build and select entirely through synthetic device-0 events.

A real collision surfaced building that scenario, previously invisible: `lf_build` and `lf_confirm` share the same device-0 button-0 binding, and `dialog_view.gd` deliberately swallows it while the boot brief is on screen, so the button that advances a dialog line does not also place an emplacement. The scenario now pages through the dialog by gamepad first, matching what a real player on a controller actually has to do before reaching the board.

Save/load round trip, `tools/save_roundtrip.py`, driving `draft.gd` through two separate Godot processes sharing an isolated save location — proving persistence across process death, not merely in-memory state. Tier 3, ~9.6–10.8 s. Closes the verification half of LF-065.

Every one of the above was proved red before it was trusted: a broken assertion planted in `abilities.json`, `a11y-worst.json`, `lf161_edge_scroll_contained.json` and the gamepad scenario each failed naming the exact expression and file; the loudness checks failed against ±20 dB and +12 dB gain-shifted scratch copies; the save round trip failed, naming the exact field mismatch, when the second launch was pointed at a different scratch directory than the first.

body.text: The honest cost

Tier 3 grew from a claimed ~66 s to a measured ~182 s — roughly three minutes. That is the real price of running scenarios that already existed on disk. It stayed at tier 3 rather than moving to tier 4 on purpose: there is no tier in between, and pushing it to nightly would hide a PR-time coverage regression until then, which is the exact class of gap this issue exists to close.

Tier 2's budget moved 25,000 → 28,000 ms. `sfx loudness` cost only about 2 seconds, but a real tier-2 run measured 27.8 s afterward — over the old budget. That is marginal creep, not the doubling `--budget` exists to catch, but raising a threshold to fit a measurement is exactly the move this project is normally suspicious of, so it is worth saying plainly rather than letting it pass unremarked. It sits alongside LF-170, which found `check.py`'s own timing checks using `time.time()` and reporting a negative 796 ms elapsed under load.

Twelve of the sixteen originally-named zero-coverage scripts are still uncovered: `pause_menu.gd`, `audio_director.gd`, `ui_theme.gd` and `cli_args.gd` entirely; `dialog_view.gd` and `abilities.gd` only partially, as a side effect of this PR's own scenarios. Filed as LF-174 rather than left to quietly stay at zero with no record anyone looked.

entries.title: The cost was never the retry
entries.summary: The sequel to `silent-and-wrong`: the guard rail built to stop one agent's `git stash` sweeping five workstreams was denying commands for mentioning a guarded thing, not for doing it. Four false positives in one session, all worked around rather than blocked, and a fifth that caught its own repairer mid-verification.

commits.subject: fix(hooks): the guard denied commands for mentioning a thing, not for doing it

body.text: This is the sequel to `silent-and-wrong`, filed earlier the same day. That entry left `LF-166` open with two candidate fixes, and one live wound: a coordinator's `git commit --only docs/chronicle` had silently dropped a new entry page because the guard denies `git add` with no escape hatch at all, and the published site carried a dead link with nothing red anywhere. `tools/hooks/guard.py` exists for a real reason — an agent's `git stash` once swept eleven files across five workstreams and left every other agent silently reading `HEAD` instead of its own edits, a harm that never raises an error, it just makes any measurement taken in that window describe code nobody wrote. The guard is a good idea. What this commit fixes is that it was denying commands for **mentioning** a guarded thing, not for **doing** it.
Four false positives, one session, three rules

items: `ps -eo pid,etime,pcpu,args | grep -E "test_parity|sim.run|godot"` — a process listing that launches nothing, denied anyway.
`git commit -m "<message>"` — denied because the commit **message text** named the engine's import-cache directory, in a message explaining why a sidecar file cannot affect the rules.
`gh pr comment --body "<text>"` — denied because the pasted body quoted `tools/test_parity.py`'s own success output, which names the Windows binary by its versioned filename.
`git add` — denied outright, with no escape hatch at all, unlike two sibling rules (`LF_ALLOW_BACKGROUND=1`, `LF_ALLOW_RAW_ENGINE=1`) that both ship one.

body.text: A fifth occurrence happened while verifying the fix: a coordinator probe written as an inline `python -c` was itself denied, because the probe's own text contained the trigger strings it was testing for. The probe now lives in a file instead. Worth keeping in the record — the bug was still catching people during its own repair.
The point worth making: the cost was never the retry

Every one of the four was worked around, not blocked. Occurrence 2 was defeated by `git commit -F <file>`, which the rule never inspected at all — the guard prevented nothing and only forced a reroute. A guard that is routinely worked around stops guarding, and it teaches the reflex of reaching for the escape hatch on commands that never needed one.

Occurrence 4 was worse than an annoyance. Combined with `git commit --only <newfile>` failing outright and `git commit --only <dir>` silently dropping untracked files — the exact mechanism `silent-and-wrong` recorded — it made a new file uncommittable by the documented coordinator workflow, and it is what shipped that earlier entry's `index.html` and `chronicle.json` without the page they both link to. A dead link on the published site, nothing red anywhere.
The fix: argv structure, not shell text

Root cause fixed rather than patched: every rule reasoned about shell text rather than argv structure — `_segments()` said as much in its own docstring. It now tokenises with `shlex`, so a pipe inside a quoted grep pattern or a `-m` message no longer splits the command in two. `_is_inspector_segment()` skips a segment entirely, before any pattern runs, when its `argv0` is a read-only inspector — `ps`, `grep`, `rg`, `awk`, `sed -n`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `git log`/`show`/`diff`/`status`, `gh pr`/`issue comment`, `echo`. `_scrub_payload_values()` blanks the value that follows `-m`/`--message`/`-F`/`--file`/`--body`/`--body-file`, so a path named only in a commit message or PR body is never read as something the command does.

`rule_git_safety` took the narrow-pathspec route rather than a new escape hatch, and the reasoning is the interesting part. Widening the hatches is how everyone learns to prefix `LF_ALLOW_RAW_ENGINE=1` onto a `ps` invocation, which is the failure mode and not the fix. `git add <one-explicit-path>` is now allowed; `-A`, `.`, `-u`, `--all`, bare `git add`, multiple paths, wildcards and magic pathspecs all still deny. The documented harm is a broad add sweeping other agents' files, and a single named path cannot do that.
A regression caught before shipping

Inspector-skip was initially applied to `rule_godot_write` too, which would have let a `cat` redirect write straight through — the redirect is the real write, `cat` merely reads. It was pulled back out of that rule, which only needed payload scrubbing rather than inspector-skip, and a new selftest case now proves the redirect still denies. A fix to a safety rail that quietly opened a hole in the same rail is exactly the outcome the verification bar exists to catch, and it caught it before this shipped.
Verified twice

rows: 45 passed, 0 failed (31 original, 1 flipped deny → allow for `git add`, 13 new)

body.text: The probe held the line on what must still deny — `git stash`, `git stash push -m`, `git reset --hard`, `git checkout -- <path>`, `git checkout .`, every wide `git add` form, `rm -rf` and `mv` on the import cache, a redirect write into it, a raw versioned engine binary, a bare `blender` — while confirming the five false positives now allow: `git add <one path>`, the `ps | grep`, the `git commit -m`, the `gh pr comment`, and `git commit -F`. `tools/check.py` needed no change of its own: its `hooks configured` check parses the pass/total straight out of the selftest output rather than hardcoding 31, so it now reports 45/45 with no edit at all.

entries.title: Counted, not argued
entries.summary: PRC-16 was filed because the gate's own documentation had drifted from the gate, and STATE.md's tier block had been wrong on the same day it was generated. In one session the gate went from 29 checks to 38 and tier 3 from a documented ~66s to a measured 187s. Check counts are now asserted against the live registry; wall-clock costs were deleted from the prose rather than kept honest, because nothing here can assert a number that only exists at runtime.

commits.subject: docs(gate): assert the gate's own counts, and delete the costs that rotted

body.text: PRC-16 (#82) was filed on a simple premise: the gate's documentation had drifted from the gate, and `docs/STATE.md`'s tier block had been wrong on the same day it was generated. This session made the premise far worse and, for once, far easier to see. In one session the gate went from 29 checks to 38, and tier 3 from a documented ~66s to a measured ~187s. Every number in `CLAUDE.md`'s command block was wrong — not stale by a little, wrong by more than double.
Counts are now asserted

A new tier-1 check, `tier counts`, parses `tools/check.py`'s own docstring for its "tier N (...), C checks" bullets and asserts each against the live `CHECKS` registry. A stale number is now a red run instead of a slow discovery. It found real drift immediately: the tier-1 bullet said 14 and did not mention `chronicle current` at all.

Proved red three separate times, which is the standard here. First by perturbing only the docstring's stated count, which produced `tier 1: docstring says 15 checks, CHECKS has 16 at tier <= 1`. Second by adding a throwaway `Check()` with no matching docstring edit, which turned all four tiers red at once: `tier 1: 16 vs 17; tier 2: 26 vs 27; tier 3: 35 vs 36; tier 4: 38 vs 39`. Third, independently, by the coordinator — who restored `tools/check.py` byte-identical afterward and verified it stayed that way.
A clever general doc-parser would just be a second thing to get wrong. It is a tripwire, not a documentation engine.

The check names its own limits in that docstring rather than pretending to more coverage than it has: it reads only that one phrasing, and it asserts counts only, so a re-tier that moves a check between tiers without changing any total is an accepted, named gap — not a hole nobody noticed.
Costs are deleted, not maintained

The part worth dwelling on is what got deleted rather than fixed. Wall-clock numbers cannot be asserted against any registry — they exist only at runtime and are machine- and load-dependent. `LF-178` is the proof: the same tier-2 gate measured 27,852ms and 28,751ms on two runs both fairly called clean. A generator that kept a docstring's timings honest would need its own caching subsystem just to answer a question the docstring did not need to ask. So every hardcoded cost is gone from the prose, replaced by pointers to `--list` and `--tier N --json`. Three fewer numbers that are all true beats a generator nobody maintains.

The same instinct closed decision 017 — the isometric camera angle that was wrong for six sessions because it was derived from memory rather than measured — and decision 067, which deleted `PRESSURE_FLOOR` rather than raised it. Precision that rots is a liability, not an asset.
Where generation was cheap, it was taken

Not everything hand-typed was deleted — some of it was generated instead. The `--tier` and `--budget` argparse help text used to hand-type the same figures as the docstring and was independently wrong: `--budget` claimed tier 2 was 25s when `TIER_BUDGET_MS` already said 28,000. Both are now built from `CHECKS` and `TIER_BUDGET_MS` at parser-construction time, so they cannot drift from the registry they describe.
The measured table
The honest half

Tier 2's budget was not raised, even though it is sitting right on it. `LF-178` records that the answer is to move a check out of tier 2, not to move the number again — it was already raised once earlier this session, from 25,000, and raising it a second time in the same session would have made the budget decorative rather than a contract.

Two traps from elsewhere in the session were folded into `CLAUDE.md` by the coordinator in the same commit, worth recording here because neither is about the gate at all. `LF-180`: `git commit --only` is for modifications to already-tracked files — it cannot add and cannot remove, and it fails silently at both. `LF-175`: `--user-data-dir` is silently ignored by this Godot build, so a tool that believes it isolated the save is quietly writing to the real one; the fix is `XDG_DATA_HOME`, asserted against the default location afterward.

entries.title: Behind infrastructure that did not exist
entries.summary: `rules parity` — in the gate's own words the one thing making a balance claim in this project falsifiable — had never run in CI, not once. PRC-17 (#83) replaces the unreachable self-hosted `nightly.yml` with a container gate on every pull request — whose first real run went red, for the first genuine reason in this project's CI history rather than its own onboarding breakage, because the local verification behind it had quietly been measured against an already-imported tree.

commits.subject: docs: decision 071 — CI runs the real gate in a container, self-hosted declined
ci: run the real gate on every PR, and parity in CI for the first time ever
fix(ci): the container job never imported, and the local repro could not see it

body.text: The owner named this the highest-value open work in the project, and the reason PRC-17 (#83) gives is stark rather than abstract: `nightly.yml` targeted `runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, latticefall]`, and zero runners with those labels — or any labels — were registered against this repository. `docs/STATE.md` had described the workflow as "inert behind a repo variable" for sessions, which reads like a one-flag fix. It was not one. Flipping `LF_NIGHTLY_ENABLED` would not have made the workflow run; it would have queued a job forever with nothing able to claim it. The workflow was not behind a flag, it was behind infrastructure that did not exist.

The consequence was not abstract either. Every merge to `main` was gated on 14 of 29 checks — the tier-1 set. The other 15, including `rules parity` and `rules parity (windows)`, had run in CI zero times. And the ten runs `gate.yml` (tier 1 only) had produced were read back rather than trusted at face value: every failure in that history was CI's own onboarding breakage, never a caught regression.
What landed

items: `tools/ci/Dockerfile` — `ubuntu:24.04` plus Godot 4.7.1 linux, `xvfb`, Mesa, and the exact jsonschema/numpy/pillow/soundfile/PyYAML versions the local `.venv` runs.

A `gate-tier3` job in `gate.yml`, running `check.py --tier 3` inside that image on every pull request — `sprite atlas`, `godot boots`, `game renders`, `menu renders`, `accessibility`, `terrain parsers agree`, `sfx determinism`, and every scenario check, none of which had ever run on a PR before.
`parity-shard.yml` — `test_parity.py --shard I/4` split across four hosted jobs, daily and on any PR touching the rules or the data.
`tools/ci/freshness_check.py` plus `freshness.yml` — fails loud past 48 hours stale, because this project has now twice believed a workflow ran when it had not.

body.text: The first real run of it went red, and that is the good half

The pull request's first real run of `gate-tier3` was red: `tier 3 — 22 passed · 12 failed · 3 skipped`, 27 minutes. It failed on verbatim the two clean-checkout errors `gate.yml`'s own tier-1 header comment already documents — `Loadout` not declared, because a `class_name` global is invisible until the editor imports, and the LFS-tracked font failing to preload, which takes every script reading `Ui.SANS` down with it (`LF-162`). Everything else cascaded from there: five scenarios timing out at 120 seconds and three rendered checks at roughly 300 seconds, all waiting on a frame an unimported Godot can never produce. That cascade alone was about 1603 of the run's 1638 seconds — the 27 minutes was almost entirely timeouts, not work.

`hooks configured` failed too, and correctly. Its `post-lint-gd` selftest parses `scripts/hud.gd`, which reads consts off the same font-preloading `Ui` autoload — so on an unimported checkout that file genuinely does not parse, and the guard was reporting truth about a broken environment rather than a bug: 44 of 45 unimported, 45 of 45 imported, no change needed to `tools/hooks/guard.py`. Worth a line on its own, since it is the same guard an earlier entry spent a full session hardening.

This is the first time in this project's history that CI went red for a real reason rather than its own onboarding breakage — every prior red run, across the entire population this journal has recorded, was CI still being built rather than a caught bug. The very first thing the new job did was catch something, in a pull request, contained, never reaching `main`. That is the whole argument for the one-branch-one-PR flow, and it landed on the change that gave the flow its own teeth.
Why the local verification missed it

The container had already been reported "verified twice" before this pull request opened, at `34 passed · 0 failed`. Both of those runs used a scratch clone that still carried a `.godot/` import cache left behind by an earlier one-off `--import`. `.godot/` is gitignored, so a later `git checkout` to a newer commit never cleared it — both "clean" runs were therefore measured against an already-imported tree, which is not the path CI actually takes, and `gate-tier3` had no Import step at all. That gap was invisible to anyone whose local reproduction always happened to carry the cache. The lesson is not "check your work" — it is that a local reproduction which shares any state at all with the machine that built it is not a reproduction, and a gitignored cache directory surviving a `git checkout` is exactly the kind of state nobody thinks to look for.
Re-verified on the path CI actually takes
Fresh clone, `git lfs pull`, the import cache confirmed absent and the font confirmed as 200 KB of real TrueType rather than an LFS pointer, then the exact sequence the fixed workflow now runs:

The underlying claim holds: the container reproduces this machine's coverage and contrast thresholds exactly, not approximately. What was false was that it had been established on the path CI actually takes. It has been now, and the number was right both times — only the route to it was wrong the first two.
The decision, and what it does not cover

Self-hosted registration was declined — decision 071, amended in place with this red run rather than superseded, because the decision had not merged and nothing it claimed had been published yet. The issue reserved the self-hosted question as an owner call, and declining is the half that does not touch the owner's own machine, so it was taken rather than deferred: a scheduled nightly on the box the owner plays from would compete with captures that already take about 8 of 16 cores, and it would mean `reap.py --kill` running unattended on a shared tree where `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` cannot tell a sibling agent's live process from a stray. The hosted path delivers what `nightly.yml` existed for without either cost. It is reversible, and the reversal — register a runner, flip the variable — is written down in the same decision.
This is still not a clean win, and the record should not read as one.

items: `rules parity (windows)` still has no CI coverage at all, and cannot get it from a hosted Linux path — it needs a Windows Godot binary. That matters specifically because a prior finding (BAL-06) established that all parity checking had been comparing CPython against the Linux build while the owner plays Windows. The leg that closed the larger hole is the one this change still cannot watch.

Real hosted-runner wall time is still unmeasured. The fixed job runs about 90 seconds end to end on this machine; there is no structural reason to expect anything near the original 27 minutes now, but one real green run on a hosted runner is the confirmation, not that estimate.

The hosted parity-shard timing is a projection, not a measurement: 3m14s and 3m17s per shard measured on this 16-core machine, extrapolated to a 4-core hosted runner. The workflow's own comment says to trust a real run over that estimate once one exists.

The GHCR image push and pull only run for real on merge to `main`. This pull request is its own end-to-end test — if `gate-tier3` goes green here, the mechanism is proved; if not, the failure is in the PR, not on `main`.
Branch protection still has no required checks at all. Deliberately not fixed in the same change that introduces the jobs it would require.

body.text: One small thing worth recording as a genuine win rather than a caveat: the freshness check was proved red as well as green against the real repository before merge — `gate.yml` reported fresh at 0.1 hours and exited 0, and a workflow with no successful run exited 1. A project that has now twice believed a workflow ran when it had not, and once believed a local check was clean when it was not, has something that at least notices the first kind.

entries.title: It is the levels
entries.summary: The owner, playing: “the placement of most turrets are barely able to hit the enemies on the field.” Nothing in this project could see that — the sim only asks whether a build wins. `sim/coverage.py` (LF-176) is the instrument built to look, and it agrees with the owner: the median gun has a target in range about a third of the time, roughly one in five placed emplacements does essentially nothing, and the geometry says why — range values short relative to lane length on most anchors, slots simply too far from the lane on five Act 1 anchors. No range or slot was changed to get this answer.

commits.subject: feat(sim): measure what the owner could see and the grader could not

body.text: Game is slow at times. I think it's because the placement of most turrets are barely able to hit the enemies on the field. The pace is also very slow.

Nothing in this project could see that. `sim/run.py` only asks whether a build wins. `tools/density.py` reports what is on screen, not who can reach it. A board where every gun fires at the extreme edge of its range for a sliver of each pass grades identically, on both instruments, to a board sited well. Until today the owner's own eyes were the only instrument that existed for this.

`sim/coverage.py` (LF-176) is the missing measurement, built as two independent halves because the three candidate causes need different evidence. `lane_coverage()` is pure geometry — what fraction of the lane falls inside a tower's range from a given slot, by sampling the lane. No sim, no RNG, no build order. It is a ceiling: what the best possible siting of any available tower at that slot could achieve. `InstrumentedSim` drives the real, unmodified `sim.engine.Sim` and reconstructs per-emplacement telemetry from public state after each tick — whether a live targetable unit was in range, independent of cooldown, and how much damage each emplacement actually dealt. `sim/engine.py` is untouched: every class here is a subclass wrapping existing methods, so the parity digest never moved and no 1,440-run re-run was owed.
Proved at runtime, not argued

items: geometric hand-check: slot (2,3) r=3.2 -> 0.3368 (hand calc 0.335)
far-slot geometric check: slot (500, 500) -> 0.0
far-slot dynamic check: 0/1690 combat ticks in range, 0.0 damage, across a real 1-wave run
determinism: anchor-09/burst/hard identical across two runs (9 emplacements, 10712.0 total damage)
outcome parity: `InstrumentedSim` == `Sim` on every policy/difficulty across anchor-01, anchor-09, anchor-13, anchor-24

body.text: The last line is the one that matters: the instrument provably cannot change a grade. Two full 24-anchor runs came back byte-identical to each other on top of that.
What it found — the owner was right

The median gun has something in range about a third of the time. The long tail the owner predicted is real: roughly one in five placed emplacements in acts 1 and 2 does essentially nothing — 178 of 589 samples on anchor-10, 172 of 644 on anchor-13, 88 of 320 on anchor-02.
The geometric half separates the causes

Median lane-coverage ceiling — the best any tower could do from the best slot — is only about 40%. Double the ranges and it jumps to 97–100% on 17 of 24 anchors. That is verdict (b): the range values are short relative to lane length, not the slots.

Five Act 1 anchors are the other problem — verdict (a), geometry: anchor-01, 03, 04, 05 and 07 do not recover even at 2× range, so their slots are simply too far from the lane. anchor-02's p10 uptime is 0%. Only anchor-06 and anchor-20 come back sited adequately.

And it rules out the third candidate. LF-053 and LF-072 both record that the autobuild fills slots in priority order regardless of coverage, so the obvious suspicion was that what the owner watched play itself was never a sited board at all. The ceiling numbers rule that out as the main cause: if the best available slot can only cover 40% of the lane, no build policy can fix it. It is the levels.
The discipline worth naming

Not one range value was changed and not one slot was moved. Tuning before the instrument existed is exactly what decision 067 rejected when it deleted `PRESSURE_FLOOR` rather than raising it — a threshold fitted to today's data is not evidence. The instrument exists now, so the tuning can be done against it, and that is filed as LF-181 for BAL-04, which re-grades the whole campaign against the distribution, not the mean — the mean hides the tail, and the tail is the complaint.

Worth one honest line too: this entry is late. The measurement landed at 18:33 and then sat unreported and uncommitted-to-the-journal while the session moved on to other work — the journal read quiet at exactly the moment it had the most to say.
Filed, not started: LF-177

The owner also asked for a fast-forward — the pace is slow to play at 1× and there is no way to speed it up. Deferred by the owner's own framing, but the trap is worth recording with it: a speed multiplier implemented by scaling delta is a rules change, and `scripts/anchor_sim.gd` and `sim/engine.py` are compared across 1,440 runs on two platforms where float64 accumulation over a different number of differently-sized steps does not reproduce. The safe shape, if this is ever picked up, is the same fixed tick run more times per rendered frame — never a larger `dt`.

entries.title: Elevation is a blit offset, measured against the real camera
entries.summary: TER-01. E4's data foundation already existed — the anchor schema carries terrain regions and “terrain parsers agree” is a green gate check. What did not exist was the spatial half: a z on every drawable, so a tile at elevation actually draws higher than one at ground level. The constants come from the measured camera, not the nominal tile — 32.0 px per level, derived from k = s·cos(30°) and checked against two throwaway Blender renders to within 0.004%. Proved two independent ways on anchor-01's authored plateau: the engine's own reported positions, and the rendered pixels of the screenshot itself.

commits.subject: feat(terrain): elevation is a blit offset, measured against the real camera

body.text: E4's data foundation already existed before this change — the anchor schema carries terrain regions, and “terrain parsers agree” has been a green gate check comparing the Python and GDScript parsers against a fixture. What did not exist was the spatial half: nothing gave a tile at elevation a screen position any different from a tile at ground level. TER-06 picking, TER-09 the climbing lane and TER-10 bridges all need that to exist first.
The constants are derived from the measured camera, not the nominal tile

`LEVEL_PX` = 32.0 px per level and `LEVEL_H` = 0.401872 world units per level come from k = s·cos(ε): s = CELL/ortho_scale = 91.9463 px per world unit, ε = 30°, giving k = 79.6279 px of screen rise per world unit. Checked against two throwaway Blender renders: k/s = 0.865994 against cos 30° = 0.866025 — **0.004%** off.

Deriving it from “128 px” would have been wrong, and this is decision 017's trap in a new place: the rendered tile is geometrically 130.03 px, and the 128 is an alpha-threshold artefact that `calibrate()` bakes in. The camera angle in this project's own instructions was wrong for six sessions because it was derived from memory rather than measured. Same shape of mistake, avoided this time.
The elegant part: most of the draw path needed no change at all

Height is baked into the tile cache's position, so `combat_fx.gd` and `fx_additive.gd` needed no change — they call `view.to_screen(tile)` with one argument and inherit elevation for free. `_draw_contact_shadow` needed none either. And `_draw_range` samples per point, so a range ring climbs a ridge rather than floating flat across it.

`Iso.depth()` gained an optional third z argument defaulting to 0.0, so every existing two-argument call site returns the same float byte-for-byte. It sits unused for now — reserved for TER-10, where tx+ty alone cannot break a tie between a bridge deck and whatever is underneath it.
Proved two independent ways

From the engine's own values, via a new `--heights` hook: tile (9,0) at z=1 sits 32.0 px above its same-diagonal ground neighbour — exactly `LEVEL_PX`. Tile (10,0) at z=2 sits 64.0 px above — exactly 2×`LEVEL_PX`.

And from the rendered PNG, independent of the hook's own arithmetic: the topmost silhouette row of tile (10,0) lands at image row 255; predicted from the reported position and the known diamond half-height, scaled to the 1440×810 capture, gives 255.1 — within one pixel. Against the un-elevated baseline a few tiles over at roughly 302, that is a **47–48 px** rise, matching the predicted 2×32×0.75 = 48.

body.caption: anchor-01's authored plateau, standing above the ground plane for the first time — a z=1 plate with a z=2 corner, the fixture both proofs above were taken against. A real `tools/shot.py` capture, not a mockup: the same frame the --heights hook and the pixel measurement both describe.

body.text: The hook's own prefix ate its own output, live

The `--heights` hook's marker prefix was added in the same change — which is the trap this project's own instructions already name for two other verification hooks, and which caught this one live: the first capture produced zero HEIGHT lines, because `tools/shot.py` filters relayed markers by prefix and had silently swallowed them. Worth a line on its own — a verification hook that runs, prints, and is quietly eaten has been a recurring shape this session.
The honest half

items: The rules are untouched — no diff to sim/engine.py or scripts/anchor_sim.gd, range stays 2-D per TER-13, and Iso.height_offset() returns a Vector2 (float32), which the PRD bans from the rules, so it cannot leak into a grade even by accident.

Parity is deliberately not cited as evidence. A 1440-run pass was observed during the work, but a concurrent agent was mid-refactor of the rules files at the time, so that result is not attributable to this change in either direction. It does not need to be — this change touches no file in the parity digest. Refusing to claim a green number that cannot be attributed is the more interesting fact than the number itself.

TER-03 (writing level_px into the manifest) is deferred, with reasons rather than a shrug: it needs tools/check.py, which was out of scope, and verifying the manifest write means a real Blender invocation against the tracked assets/renders tree, which then forces mask_glow, pack_atlas and a Godot import to keep the shared atlas in sync. That is a shared-build-artifact change and not one to leave half-verified in a tree the owner plays out of.
LF-183 filed: the editor overlay's path preview does not apply the height offset yet. Cosmetic, editor-only.

entries.title: The redundant sort is the contract: 24× and 34× off O(emplacements × units)
entries.summary: WAR-02 and WAR-03 close the tick-cost gate that WAR-06's unit budget and the still-open board-size call in PRD §6 both depend on. _step() was O(emplacements × units) with an inner O(units) splash loop — 24,000 distance checks a tick at 60 emplacements and 400 units at 30 Hz. WAR-02 resolves every unit's position once a tick instead of once per pair; WAR-03 adds a uniform grid sized larger than any real range or splash radius. Together: 20.08 ms to 0.84 ms at 512 units / 60 towers / 24 segments (24.1×), 58.43 ms to 1.73 ms at 1000/80/32 (33.8×), both PRD bars met. Selection was tested directly rather than inferred — decision 058 is the reason why — and decision 072 records the one thing about a spatial index that is invisible in its own diff: a sort that looks redundant because every bucket is already sorted, kept anyway, because it is the entire reason the indexed and exhaustive paths never disagree.

commits.subject: perf(rules): hoist unit positions, then index them — 24x and 34x

body.text: _step() priced every tick as O(emplacements × units), with a splash loop inside that added another O(units) on top of it — 24,000 distance checks a tick at 60 emplacements and 400 units running at 30 Hz. That cost is the actual gate on scale: WAR-06's unit budget depends on it, and so does the board-size decision still open in PRD §6, because the honest input to that call is a measured frame cost at 400 units, not a guess at one. This entry is the two fixes that closed it, WAR-02 and WAR-03, both landed in the same working tree and both worth telling apart, because they were verified differently and failed differently.
WAR-02: resolve a position once a tick, not once per pair

Every tick, the old fire phase called the lane's point_at() three separate times per unit it looked at — once in the targeting scan, once again for the reveal check, once more in the splash loop — and it looked at units once per emplacement, so the same unit's position was recomputed as many times as there were guns in range of it. WAR-02 resolves every live unit's position exactly once per tick, after the movement loop has advanced its distance along the lane, into an index-parallel cache that the targeting scan and the splash loop both read instead of recomputing. The one deliberate exception is bus_load(): it runs before _step() in the tick order, against pre-movement positions, and sharing WAR-02's post-movement cache with it would silently change what decision 027 prices — so it keeps its own resolve, with a comment now saying why, rather than being “fixed” into a shared read.
WAR-03: a grid sized larger than anything that queries it

WAR-03 adds a uniform grid over that same per-tick position cache, rebuilt from scratch every tick rather than maintained incrementally — an incrementally-maintained index is a second place for the Python and GDScript engines to drift apart, and decision 072 rejects it for exactly that reason. CELL_W is 8.0 tiles in both engines, a constant and never per-anchor data, chosen larger than the longest range or splash radius in data/towers.json (mortar-emplacement: 6.5 tiles range, 1.5 tiles splash), so a query at any real emplacement only ever touches a small, fixed number of cells regardless of board size. The exhaustive scan was not deleted — it is reachable behind grid=None in Python and a null grid in GDScript — specifically so the two paths could be diffed against each other rather than trusted on faith.
Every PRD bar was met: ≤ 4.0 ms and ≤ 1.5 ms at 512/60/24, ≤ 3.0 ms at 1000/80/32 — the second cell landing under the first cell's own bar despite carrying almost twice the units and towers.
Why the measurement is the deliverable, not the diff

Decision 058 is the reason this could not be verified by parity alone: a previous idle-rescan fix in this exact codepath passed 864 runs of parity and changed nothing measurable, because a change that passes parity has only proved it did not change anything observable — which is precisely what a no-op also proves. So target selection was tested directly rather than inferred from an aggregate grade. Four independent modes, all reporting zero differing selections between the indexed and exhaustive paths: a synthetic 512-unit / 60-tower / 24-segment board over 300 ticks; 300 randomised boards over 1,500 ticks; an LF-055-shaped case built specifically to have several structurally identical units alive on the same tick in range of the same guns; and every one of the 24 anchors, at all 3 difficulties, at every standard policy, driven through the real Sim.run() rather than a synthetic rig.

One structural proof sits next to the statistical ones and is the nicer of the two: wrapping point_at() and running an identical board once at 10 towers and once at 100 towers gives 1,024 calls per tick in both cases — a count invariant to tower count, which is exactly the property WAR-02 claims about itself. Before the change, that same count scales with tower count directly.
Parity, and why the Windows leg matters specifically here

The Linux leg is confirmed green, freshly run rather than read from cache: digest 52d5a4e66195, 1,440 runs identical. The Windows leg was started as this entry was being written and its result is not confirmed here — a machine running someone else's parity pass is not a machine to also drive a screenshot or a second parity run against, so this entry says only what it can stand behind.

Windows matters more for this change than for most. BAL-06 established that every parity run before it had been comparing CPython against the Linux Godot build while the owner plays on Windows, and LF-105 then measured that Windows Godot's atan2, sin, cos, pow, log, exp and tan diverge from CPython — parity has held so far only because the rules use none of them. A spatial hash is exactly the kind of code where someone reaches for one of those. This one does not: it uses floor and fmod, both measured byte-identical across all three runtimes, and the gate's safe operations check is green. Worth naming as a near miss rather than passing over — the trap was real, and this implementation happened to route around it rather than being designed around it from the start.
LF-098: the general fix beat the special one

An emplacement with nothing in range used to rescan every unit on the board, every tick, forever — measured at 2.19× cost at 8 towers / 32 units, rising to 2.87× at 100 towers / 800 units. WAR-03 closes it as a side effect: an idle gun now only scans the cells within its own range, so --all-idle now measures 0.74× — faster than the baseline it used to run nearly three times slower than. No targeted fix was written for LF-098, and none needed to be — decision 058 already records that a targeted attempt at this exact problem had been tried once and done nothing. The general fix arrived for an unrelated reason and happened to be the answer.
The ordering contract — decision 072

The actual risk in a spatial index is invisible in the diff, and decision 072 is what names it. Both engines' grid queries sort their merged candidate list on every call, even though each individual bucket is already sorted by construction from insertion order — and that sort looks, on a skim, like dead weight to delete. It is not: iterating buckets in their own order would be free, but it would make a tie between two units in the same cell depend on which of them entered the grid first, which is spawn history and container internals leaking into which unit a gun picks. That is PRD risk #3 by name, with LF-055 as its precedent. The redundant sort is what makes the ordering ours instead of the container's, and it is why the indexed and exhaustive paths provably pick the same unit on every tie, not just the ones a test happened to cover. GDScript keys its grid with a packed int (cy times a fixed stride, plus cx) rather than a Vector2i for the same reason — Vector2i hashing order is a Godot engine internal, and this index does not get to depend on one.

sim/coverage.py — the siting instrument that landed earlier the same session — needed no changes at all to keep working against the refactored engine, because _veteran_rank, _damage and _tick_once kept identical signatures and call sites throughout. Its own --selftest is green. A refactor this large leaving a fresh, unrelated subclass completely untouched is a good sign about both pieces of work.

As written, this work is uncommitted on lf/war-perf-core — sim/engine.py, scripts/anchor_sim.gd and tools/bench_tick.py — with the Linux parity leg confirmed and the Windows leg run but not yet confirmed complete. No screenshot accompanies this entry; there is nothing for one to show that a frame-cost number does not already say more precisely.

entries.title: None of them was red
entries.summary: Four tools, one shape: each was quietly telling the session something untrue, and none of them was red. A gate budget blown on every measurement anyone had taken, about to be raised a third time — judged by a clock that had once counted negative 796 ms under load. A journal renderer publishing invalid HTML to the live site. A safety hook denying a command over prose sitting in a heredoc it structurally could not see. All four were found by someone looking, not by the apparatus — not four bugs fixed, one thing noticed four times.

commits.subject: fix(gate): tier 2 was over budget four times — move a check, not the number
fix(gate): time checks with a clock that cannot run backwards
fix(chronicle): code spans were re-scanned, so a glob crossed its own tags
fix(hooks): a heredoc body is stdin, not argv, and the guard was reading it as paths

body.text: Four unrelated tools, one shape. A gate budget that had been blown on every idle measurement anyone ever took, about to be raised for a third time, and judged the whole while by a clock that had once run backwards.
