A journal renderer that had been publishing invalid HTML to the live site since the entry it corrupted. A safety hook that denied a real command over prose sitting in a heredoc it could not structurally see. None of these produced a failing check. All four were found by someone looking, rather than by the apparatus — which is the entry, not “four bugs fixed.”
LF-178 — the gate's tier-2 budget
`TIER_BUDGET_MS` for tier 2 had already been raised once — 25,000 to 28,000 ms, for PRC-18's loudness check — and every idle-ish measurement anyone had taken since blew straight through it anyway.

A second raise would have made the number decorative — “raise the threshold until the measurement fits” is exactly the move decision 067 rejected for `PRESSURE_FLOOR`. So the budget did not move and a check did: `facing harness` (LF-142), a narrow regression harness for one mapping, went from tier 2 to tier 3.

The more interesting part is why `facing harness` and not `terrain parsers agree`, which LF-178 named as the equally cheap candidate. Decision 057 put `terrain parsers agree` in the fast tier on purpose: it is the inexpensive sibling of `rules parity`, the same two-implementations-drifting risk at a fraction of the cost, and `rules parity` would surface a one-tile terrain drift nine minutes in as an unexplained leak with no pointer to terrain anywhere in it. Moving it back out of tier 2 would have undone that reasoning to fix an unrelated number. The reason lived in CLAUDE.md, not in the backlog item — LF-178's own text could not have picked correctly on its own.

The budget now states its own derivation, which it never did before, and the derivation is unflattering: 28,000 ms is an idle-machine ceiling on this 16-core box, two post-move runs measured 27,225 and 27,790 ms, so the real headroom is 0.8–2.8%, and the run-to-run spread — roughly 570 ms — is larger than the smaller of those margins. Written into the docstring as barely satisfied, not comfortably, along with the admission that the next check added to tier 2 blows it again — the answer at that point is splitting tiers, not a third raise. Cross-linked to LF-170: these durations are timed with `time.time()`, which has been seen running backwards under load, so the instrument the budget is judged against can itself move.
Not done, deliberately: `--budget` is still not passed by `check.py`'s default invocation or by the wrap skill, so the assertion remains advisory in every path that actually runs today.
LF-170 — the clock the budget was judged by

LF-178 and LF-170 landed in this branch as one argument, not two separate fixes. The previous commit had just written tier 2's margin down as 0.8–2.8% headroom, thinner than the run-to-run spread — and a margin that thin is not worth stating if the instrument measuring it can move. `check.py` timed every check with `time.time()`, wall clock, subject to adjustment, and it had already been caught doing exactly that: a check reported negative 796 ms elapsed under heavy concurrent load during an earlier verification pass, consistent with a clock adjustment landing mid-check. One data point, never reproduced on demand — but the fix is one line per call site, and monotonic is what a duration always wanted.

All four duration sites converted to `time.monotonic()`: the run total, the per-check start, the per-check elapsed, and the final total. `started_at` deliberately stays on the wall clock, via `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` — it is a timestamp, not a duration, and it is what the JSON artefact reports as when the run happened. The docstring now cross-references LF-178 and LF-170 in both directions, because neither is trustworthy alone: a budget stated to within 0.8% is not a claim worth making with a clock that can count backwards, and a clock made monotonic is not interesting on its own without a margin that thin to protect.
LF-173 — the journal renderer, and this one is about the chronicle itself

`render_inline()` wrapped code spans in `` and then ran `split("**")` over the whole string — including the text it had just placed inside those tags. LF-173's own backlog item recorded the damage as `sim/`; the real output was worse, because the tags cross:

The second row is the one that matters: one `**` inside a single code span inverted the bold pairing for the rest of the line. Three published entries carried invalid HTML, including `ci-goes-green.html` — where the `.gitattributes` line documenting the LFS fix was itself the thing rendering corrupted. An entry about fixing a publishing bug was published with a publishing bug in it.
The half that did not survive its own verification — read this part first

LF-173 also asked for single-asterisk emphasis, `*x*` to `<em>`, because one entry renders literal asterisks on the live site. It was implemented, and then run against the whole journal before being believed — which is the discipline worth naming, because it is what caught the rest of this. `chronicle.json` contains exactly two strings carrying a bare `*` outside a code span, and they split one to one: `*current accepted bank*` is genuine emphasis; a glob list of test-fixture paths is not, and the new feature silently ate it into an `<em>` spanning most of the sentence. A 50% false-positive rate on the real corpus. The feature was removed, and the reasoning is written into the docstring so nobody re-proposes it: `*` is an overloaded delimiter in a project whose prose is full of paths and globs, and no amount of pair-guarding separates the two cases. The entry that wanted emphasis keeps its literal asterisks.

Verification: ten inline cases balanced, including both LF-173 shapes; across all 32 generated pages, `<strong>`, `<code>` and `<em>` balanced and zero instances of the crossed shape; the regeneration diff is three lines in three files, every one a correction. No entry text was edited — a renderer fix correcting old output on the next regeneration is exactly what the append-only rule permits.
LF-179 — the guard hook

`_scrub_payload_values()` blanks prose passed as an argv token after `-m`, `--message`, `-F`, `--body` and similar flags — the LF-171 fix. A heredoc body is a different shape and that scrubber structurally cannot see it: the body is stdin, not an argv token at all, so `shlex` tokenised the prose as ordinary words, and every path merely named inside it read as a path the command was operating on. Found live, by the chronicler, immediately after the LF-171 fix landed — a Bash command whose heredoc body only mentioned an import-cache path in prose, next to an unrelated redirect elsewhere in the same command, was denied by `rule_godot_write`. Worked around by using the Write tool instead, which is the better habit anyway.
Proved red against HEAD's own guard, loaded side by side:

rows: `.godot` named in body prose, unrelated redirect elsewhere in the command

body.text: Exactly one case moves — that is the shape a safety fix has to have. The asymmetry drove the design: under-stripping leaves a false positive, annoying but safe; over-stripping hides a real command from the rules, a false negative in a safety file, which is not acceptable. So the terminator test ends a body at the first plausible terminator rather than the strictly correct one, and an unterminated heredoc strips nothing at all, leaving every remaining line visible to every rule. `guard.py --selftest` went 45/45 to 52/52, five of the seven new cases being deny-proofs. Still not closed, and the commit says so: a command hidden inside `$(...)` or backticks remains invisible to every rule here.

Nothing above tripped a failing check. The budget was green until someone read the number next to its own margin — and would have stayed green even if the clock underneath it had been lying, until that clock was checked too. The renderer passed every existing test because none of them happened to contain a glob inside a code span. The hook actively denied its command — confidently, and for the wrong reason. Four different apparatuses, four different kinds of confident wrong answer, in one branch, and the clock is the most vivid of the four: a tool that measures time is not supposed to be able to report a negative duration and say nothing about it. No screenshot accompanies this entry; there is no frame for any of it to show.

entries.title: The number that did not decide it
entries.summary: The board size decision had been blocked for sessions on one missing number — a measured frame cost at scale. Decision 072 delivered it, 1.73 ms/tick at 1000 units and 80 towers, a 33.8x speedup. And then it decided nothing, because the sim fits at 32², 48² and 64² alike. What actually settled decision 073's 48² target was legibility and authoring, two things nobody had been waiting on.

commits.subject: docs(decisions): the board is 48², and that settles half of the legibility question

body.text: Decision 073 takes PRD §6 open decision #2, the last genuinely-open owner call in that table: boards target **48 × 48**. It also records that Docker stays — the standing systemd service from `#83` is what builds and tests `gate.yml`'s container image locally, and removing it would leave CI-image changes verifiable only by pushing and watching, which is exactly how decision 071's two red runs happened.

The interesting part is not the number 48. It is that the number everyone was waiting for turned out not to be the deciding one. The decision had sat blocked for sessions on “we need a measured frame cost at scale.” Decision 072 (`WAR-03`) delivered it — **1.73 ms/tick at 1000 units / 80 towers**, a **33.8x** speedup. And then it decided nothing, because the sim budget is **5.6 ms, not 16.7** — the speed control goes to 3x, so the rules run 90 ticks per second of wall clock. At 1.73 ms/tick that is 5.2 ms, which fits at 32², 48² and 64² alike. `WAR-03` unblocked the decision by supplying evidence; it did not narrow the choice. What narrowed it was legibility and authoring — two things nobody was waiting on.

Provenance, stated rather than left implicit because it matters: only the 64² column is measured directly (`LF-104`, plus PRD §2.2's 13.4 ms/frame naive-draw figure against `CAM-07`'s measured **2.47x** improvement). The other two columns are that measurement **scaled** — zoom-to-fit is exactly linear in board edge, since a board of edge N projects to N × `TILE_W` px wide and the strip between the two instrument panels does not move. Arithmetic on a measurement, not a measurement.
Why each option lost

**64² was rejected** on the row the PRD's own break-order table already ranked second: sprite legibility, which that table puts at 48x48 as the breaking point. 64² renders a sprite at 30–60 px, and the rescue does not exist — raising `Iso.TILE_W` is blocked because `calibrate()` will not converge at 384 or 1024 px cells (`LF-102` — 256 and 512 work by luck), and decision 066 had already refused atlas growth on a measured **630 MB VRAM** projection. Choosing 64² would have meant choosing silhouette-first art as well, a far larger commitment than a board dimension.

**32² was rejected** despite being the only option needing no concession at all — legible, ~1.4 ms of draw, and the only size where the existing 24 anchors could be grown by hand instead of regenerated. It loses because 3.8x the area does not carry the programme it exists to serve: `WAR-06`'s 250–400 alive units and `WAR-01`'s 2–5 lanes with real standoff do not fit on it in a way that reads as a front line.
What it costs

items: **Hand-authoring is dead at 48².** `LF-080`'s layout generator moves onto the critical path **before** any theatre-scale content exists, not alongside it.

**It settles half of open decision #1 as a side effect**, said out loud rather than discovered later: 48² needs zoom 0.312x to fit, so `CAM-05` option 2 — a zoom floor with `CAM-04`'s minimap doing the wide read — becomes the only affordable answer, and the board is never fully visible in the playfield. A design statement, made on purpose, consistent with decision 056. What remains open in #1 is only the art bar for E6.
**Density work is unblocked** — `BAL-04`'s half now rebases against 2,304 tiles.

body.text: PRD §6's table listed five open owner decisions. All five are now taken — #1 half-settled by this one, #2 by decision 073 itself, #3 and #4 by decision 069, #5 by decision 068. The table is rewritten as a record of where each answer lives rather than a list of what is pending.
No screenshot accompanies this entry. There is nothing on screen a board-size number could show — the change is to `docs/DECISIONS.md` and `docs/PRD-THEATRE-SCALE.md` only.

entries.title: The tail that would not move
entries.summary: The follow-up to the entry where the owner said most turrets could barely reach anything and the instrument agreed. LF-181 had concluded the dominant cause was range values, not slot placement. Decision 074 corrects that: raising range per weapon lifted the tail for arc-node and ion-lance but not for pulse-turret, which is 66–79% of every near-zero sample in the game. Sweeping pulse-turret range to more than double what shipped left p10 pinned at literal 0.0% while the median climbed sixteen points — the median improving while the tail refuses is reported as the failure it is, not chased.

commits.subject: fix(balance): raise range where the geometry says it helps, and concede the tail

body.text: This is the direct sequel to the entry that recorded the owner playing the build and saying most turrets could barely reach anything, and to `sim/coverage.py`, the instrument built to look. `LF-176` was the complaint; the coverage run found a median gun in range 28–38% of ticks, roughly one in five placed emplacements contributing nothing, and a median lane-coverage ceiling of about 40%. From that, `LF-181` concluded the dominant cause was (b) range values short, not slot placement, naming five Act 1 anchors — 01, 03, 04, 05, 07 — as the geometry exception. Decision 074 corrects that premise, and the correction is what this entry is for.
What changed, sized per weapon from a pure-geometry probe rather than a uniform multiplier:

Each size was solved to bring that weapon's own near-zero ceiling to roughly 0%, stopping short of the values that push p90 toward saturation. Relative range ordering held, and no `cost` or `draw_mw` moved. The four `damage: 0` support emplacements — `shield-wall`, `scan-relay`, `anchor-damper`, `restorer` — were left untouched, for a stated reason: `lane_coverage()` never scores them, so there was no evidence to act on.
What improved:

**And pulse-turret is the whole problem.** It is 66–79% of every near-zero sample in the game — the autobuild fills every leftover slot with it. Its median moved, 27.8% → 34.6%, and its tail moved the wrong way: p10 down, near-zero flat. By the owner's own instruction — compare the distribution, not the means — that is a failure, and it is reported as one rather than buried under the two weapons that worked.
The measurement that stopped the pass rather than extending it
Sweeping pulse-turret's range from 3.2 to 7.0 — more than double what shipped — across the five worst anchors:

**p10 is pinned at literal 0.0% across the entire sweep, while p50 climbs sixteen points.** Every step buys median that reads as success and moves the tail not at all. That is decision 067's rejected move — fitting to the diagnostic — caught in the act. Range was not pushed further.

Two of the three flagship anchors from `LF-181`'s own findings did not improve: anchor-02 88/320 → 94/320 (worse), anchor-10 178/589 → 181/586 (flat), anchor-13 172/644 → 162/644 (better). All three are recorded here because a report quoting only the one that worked would be the failure this project's method exists to prevent.
The instrument caught lying about itself

**The instrument caught lying about itself, and it is a good one.** Filed as `LF-186`: `verdict()`'s anchor-level (a)-geometry / (b)-range label is computed against whatever range currently sits in `data/towers.json`. Raising the base drags its own 2× comparison along with it: four of the five declared geometry anchors — 03, 04, 05, 07 — flipped their label to "range" or "adequately sited" while their dynamic p10 went flat or worse — 8→5%, 4→0%, 5→3%, 1→0%. The ceiling is still a true statement about the level; the label reads as a claim about slots and is not one.
**A measurement that reclassifies itself when you tune the thing it is measuring.**

What was kept, and why, since the headline failed: two weapons genuinely improved, nothing regressed, and all 24 anchors still grade `ok` at all three difficulties. Distinct winning builds moved up modestly — anchor-09 standard 8→9, anchor-12 hard 6→8, anchor-16 standard 8→9, anchor-18 standard 4→6 — and no cell reached the point where every distinct build clears it. A bounded, non-regressing improvement is worth keeping even when it does not resolve the complaint that prompted it.

**Verification worth naming.** The "before" coverage run was graded against `git show HEAD:data/towers.json` rather than assumed; `say_capacity.py` stayed silent, so no brief drifted; and `rules parity` was re-run because the data both engines read had changed: **1440 runs identical, freshly verified, not from cache.** A range value is not a rules change, but that is exactly the kind of expectation parity exists to check rather than assume.

The complaint that started this is not resolved. What the project knows now is more useful than what it knew before: the tail is slots, not range, on far more anchors than `LF-181` declared. Pass two — `LF-185` — is the real fix, and it needs `PLC-01` free placement. And per `LF-187`, none of these numbers survive the move to 48² (decision 073): longer lanes mean a fixed absolute range covers a shrinking fraction of them, so `BAL-04`'s density half has to re-derive range from measured lane length rather than carry these constants forward.
**This entry's numbers have a known expiry date, and saying so is the point.**

entries.title: The bug that outlived two workarounds
entries.summary: LF-189 was filed after a bold span crossing a code span printed literal asterisks while drafting the previous entry, and it was hit again immediately, while drafting the one after that — worked around by hand both times rather than fixed. The audit written to close it found the same defect already live on two entries published earlier this session, unnoticed by anyone until it looked. Bold now pairs across code spans correctly, and three assertions per generated page mean the next occurrence is red rather than diffed by eye.

commits.subject: fix(chronicle): pair bold across code spans, and assert the result instead of noticing it
docs(backlog): close LF-189 — renderer fix and audit both landed

body.text: This entry is about the tool writing it, and the chronicler is a character in the bug rather than only its reporter. Drafting `the-number-that-did-not-decide-it`, a bold span meant to wrap prose on both sides of a code reference printed its asterisks literally instead — caught only because a human thought to diff the rendered HTML before committing. That is what got LF-189 filed. Drafting the very next entry, `the-tail-that-would-not-move`, the same shape appeared again, and was worked around again: by restructuring the sentence so no bold span ever touched a backtick, rather than by fixing the renderer. Twice in a row, on two consecutive entries, the fix was to write around it — exactly the kind of rule that survives only as long as someone remembers it under pressure, the same failure this project's own working agreement already names for `git stash` and the reaper.
The renderer fix

`none-of-them-was-red`, three entries back, had already fixed one shape of this bug: `render_inline()` used to wrap code spans in `<code>` and then split the whole string on `**`, so a glob inside a code span crossed its own tags. That fix applied bold to each prose segment between backticks independently — and that is exactly what broke here. A bold span opening before a backtick and closing after it opens in one prose segment and closes in a different one, and neither half ever finds its partner: the asterisks print literally, on both sides, with a perfectly correct code element sitting between them. Strictly safer than the crossed tags it replaced, since literal text can never break a page — but still wrong output.

The fix: code spans are swapped for opaque, NUL-delimited sentinels before bold gets paired, bold is paired over the whole string at once, and the sentinels are restored afterward. Code content can no longer participate in pairing; prose on either side of it still can. Every row below is live in this entry, not a description of one — the renderer that produced this page is the one being written about:

One shape is described rather than demonstrated live, on purpose: a lone, unpaired `**` sitting in prose with no partner and no backticks around it — the kind that shows up when a path is typed without them — still resolves to literal text rather than reaching an empty `` across the rest of the paragraph. It is also the one shape the audit below cannot tell apart from a real defect, so reproducing it here would trip this very entry's own check.
The audit found it live before the fix even shipped

LF-189 proposed two things: the renderer fix above, and a cheap audit that asserts no generated page carries markup that failed to render. **The order they landed in is the point.** The audit was written first, run against the whole corpus, and immediately found the defect live in two entries already published on the site that nobody — including the chronicler, twice — had noticed: `measuring-the-fifth-non-negotiable` and `the-headline-did-not-survive` were both serving literal asterisks on either side of an otherwise correctly-rendered code element. Two pages had been publishing broken markup to the live site. That is what justified fixing the renderer properly rather than leaving every future entry to keep restructuring its own sentences around the bug.

`tools/chronicle.py --check` — the existing staleness check — was perfectly happy with both broken pages, because the committed HTML matched `chronicle.json` byte for byte. It was the rendering itself that was wrong, identically, in both places. Staleness and correctness are different questions, and only one of them had ever been asked. The new audit asserts three things per generated page: no literal `**` survives into prose, ``, `` and `` are balanced, and no crossed `......` shape exists — the LF-173 defect, checked for by name in case it ever returns a different way.
The audit caught its own false positive on its first run

Before either published defect could even be reported, the audit flagged a string that was not actually broken: the code span quoting `split("**")`, inside the very entry that describes the LF-173 fix — quoting the code that caused it. Asterisks inside a `<code>` element are legitimate content, not unrendered markup, so code spans are stripped before the scan runs at all. A check that cries wolf on correct output is worse than no check, and this one nearly shipped doing exactly that on its first pass.

One false positive is accepted rather than fixed: a bare glob sitting directly in prose, with no backticks around it at all, still trips the `**` scan. Not worked around — every path in this journal belongs inside backticks by house style anyway, so the check nudges an author toward the convention it already expects rather than fighting it, and its failure message says which of the two causes applies.
The correction, and how it is allowed to happen

Both broken pages change by regeneration, not by edit. Neither entry's text in `chronicle.json` moved at all — a word-diff on both rendered pages shows literal asterisks becoming `<strong>` tags and nothing else. A renderer fix correcting old output on the next regeneration is exactly what the append-only rule permits, and it is the same precedent `none-of-them-was-red` set the first time this file needed correcting rather than rewriting.

`none-of-them-was-red` is where this renderer's crossed tags got fixed, and — in the very same stroke — where this narrower defect got introduced. It was then hit live twice more, once while drafting each of the two entries that followed it, and closed only here, with an audit added specifically so the next occurrence does not need a human to notice stray asterisks and diff the HTML by hand. That entry also reversed its own second half — single-asterisk emphasis — after measuring a 50% false-positive rate against the real corpus rather than trusting the feature on taste. This project's founding principle for this file, written the night it was created, was that the failures stay in. It has now proven itself on this one file more than once: once by deleting a feature that failed its own measurement, and again here, in the gap between an author quietly working around a bug and a check that says so on its own.

entries.title: The hang that never was
entries.summary: `rules parity (windows)` ran on hosted CI for the first time ever, closing BAL-06's gap and the CI half of LF-105 — the project's only blocker-severity backlog item. All prior parity runs compared CPython against Linux Godot; the owner plays Windows. The first hosted run died at 29 minutes looking exactly like a known, precedented bug, and it took three separate measurements to prove it was something else entirely: not a hang, just not enough clock.

commits.subject: ci(parity): rules parity runs against the Windows build the owner plays

body.text: **`rules parity (windows)` has now run on hosted CI for the first time ever**, closing BAL-06's gap and the CI half of `LF-105`, the project's only blocker-severity backlog item. The proof is a real check, not a diagnostic:
parity ok — 360 runs identical (gdscript vs python) [shard 0/4] [windows]

Why it matters, restated as a measurement rather than a claim: every one of the 1440 existing parity runs compares CPython against **Linux** Godot, and the owner plays the **Windows** build. Across 100,000 float64 samples, Windows Godot (MSVC UCRT) diverges from CPython and Linux Godot (glibc) on `atan2` 0.084%, `sin` 0.133%, `cos` 0.120%, `pow` 0.130%, `log` 0.031%, `exp` 0.069% and `tan` 4.32%. The rules use none of those operations today — `tools/check.py`'s `safe operations` check (decision 061) is what keeps that true by design — so cross-platform parity had held **by accident, not by design**, and until this run, nothing had ever watched it.
But the diagnosis is the story, because the first attempt failed in the most misleading way available

**Beat 1 — it looked exactly like a bug already on file.** The unsharded run died at 29 minutes: Godot printed its version banner, then produced nothing for the full 1700s internal timeout. That is the exact symptom `gate.yml`'s own header and decision 071 describe for a checkout that was never imported — a `class_name` global or a font `preload()` blocking on missing `.godot/` cache content. The coordinator read the log, matched it to the precedent, and called it near-certain.

**Beat 2 — it was not that, and it was proved rather than accepted.** An `--import` pass was added on that hypothesis and **measured** not to help: a CPU-time poll taken immediately after `--import` was identical to one taken before it. The import step was removed again; it survives only in the branch's diagnostic commits and in the workflow's header, which now warns the next person not to re-add it.

**Beat 3 — it was never hanging at all.** Single-anchor runs finished in 20–30s, ruling out a launch hang. A probe proved `DirAccess.open("res://data/anchors").get_files()` resolves in about 1ms, ruling out the one code path an unfiltered run takes that a filtered one does not. Sweeping anchors individually showed a rising cost trend — **24.1s, 33s, 39.1s, 48.1s** for anchor-01 through 04 — and **562s for 360 runs extrapolates to about 1800s for the full 1152, a hair over the 1700s timeout.** It ran out of clock. Sharding, not a longer timeout, was the fix — exactly what `parity-shard.yml` had already proved for Linux.

**Beat 4 — the false signal that made the wrong answer believable, and this is the keeper.** PowerShell's `$proc.CPU` / `Process.TotalProcessorTime` read a flat zero through a run that provably did correct work: anchor-05 alone completed with fully valid `PARITY_JSON` for all 48 of its combinations while the metric claimed 0% CPU the entire time. **"No output plus no CPU" reads as wedged when the real state was "working, slowly."** Filed as `LF-191`. The workflow header now says to check wall-clock against the single-anchor smoke baseline (about 20–30s) first, and not to trust `$proc.CPU` on this runner.

There is a general lesson worth naming: a symptom matching a known, well-documented, previously-expensive bug is exactly when you are most likely to stop looking. Decision 071 was real, its write-up was good, and its existence is what made the wrong diagnosis so easy to reach for.
The trigger, and its cost

Owner-approved and narrow on purpose: path-filtered to `sim/engine.py`, `scripts/anchor_sim.gd` and `scripts/test/parity.gd` — the only three files this check can catch a regression in — plus a weekly schedule and `workflow_dispatch` with a single-anchor smoke path that skips the matrix. **About 9.5 minutes per shard across 4 shards is about 38 job-minutes, billed at Windows' 2x rate, or roughly 76 Linux-equivalent minutes per full run.** Every-PR was rejected on that number. The cost is written into the workflow's first comment block so it is not re-litigated.
And one more thing landed alongside

**`main` was protected by nothing at all**, which nobody knew. A repository ruleset named `main` with enforcement `active` configured deletion protection, non-fast-forward protection and a pull-request requirement — but its `conditions.ref_name.include` was an **empty list**, so it applied to no refs. `GET /repos/.../rules/branches/main` returned `[]`. The classic endpoint actively misleads here: `/branches/main/protection` returns `404 Branch not protected`, which reads as "nobody set this up" rather than "somebody set it up and it targets nothing."

Same shape as decision 071's `nightly.yml` pointing at zero registered runners: configuration that looks live in the interface and is inert. That is now twice in this project, which makes it a pattern worth naming rather than an anecdote. The fix was drafted, diffed byte-for-byte against a live fetch, and held for owner approval before being applied, because it starts enforcing a PR requirement that had never actually been enforced. Filed as `LF-193`; confirmed here, against the live endpoint, that it is now applied — `/rules/branches/main` returns all four rules, including `required_status_checks` naming the three checks the repository actually wants required.

entries.title: An instrument that reclassifies itself when you tune the thing it measures
entries.summary: LF-186, found during decision 074's range pass: sim/coverage.py's verdict() calls an anchor (a) geometry or (b) range by comparing its geometric ceiling against the ceiling at double the current range — and both terms scale with data/towers.json. Raising every weapon's range flipped four of five LF-181 geometry calls to range or adequately-sited while their dynamic p10 went flat or worse. The ceiling was never wrong; the label read as a claim about slots when it was a claim about slots-and-range together. Fixed by recording and printing the range basis a verdict was computed against, not by changing the measurement.

commits.subject: fix(sim): record the ranges a coverage verdict was computed against

body.text: `sim/coverage.py`'s `verdict()` calls an anchor **(a) geometry** — the slots are simply far from the lane — or **(b) range** — the values are short — by comparing its geometric ceiling against the ceiling at double the current range. Both terms scale with whatever is in `data/towers.json` when it runs, and that is what LF-186 caught, during decision 074's range pass rather than by reasoning about the code: raising every weapon's base range flipped four of the five anchors the previous entry, `LF-181`, had declared "(a) geometry" — anchor-03, 04, 05, 07 — to "(b) range" or to sited adequately. Their actual dynamic p10 went flat or worse over the same change: 8→5%, 4→0%, 5→3%, 1→0%. The level did not change. The slots did not change. Only the yardstick moved.
The `ceil_p50 >= 0.5` early return is the sharpest edge in it: cross that threshold and the (a)/(b) question is never even asked.

None of this makes the ceiling wrong — it remains a true statement about the level given today's ranges. What is wrong is the **label**: it reads as a claim about slot geometry when it is a claim about geometry-and-range together. A true measurement, an untrue-sounding name.

The fix does not touch the measurement. A new `range_basis()` records the weapon ranges a report was computed against, plus a 12-character digest of them, carried on every report and summary, written into the `--json` artefact, and **printed above the table**, not merely stored — a JSON field nobody looks at would not have prevented this:

range basis 8189779cd568 — arc-node 3.8, flak-array 4.6, ion-lance 6.2, mortar-emplacement 7.0, pulse-turret 4.0
(verdicts below are RELATIVE to these; only comparable to a run with the same digest)
Two verdicts are comparable only if their digests match. When they do not, the thing to compare is the dynamic distribution, not the letter.

The digest was proved to discriminate rather than trusted: `8189779cd568` for today's ranges against `465958a1cc0a` for the pre-`LF-181` set, and stable across reloads — the same reasoning as the previous entry's audit checking itself for false positives. A fingerprint that failed to change when the ranges did would be worse than none.

Deliberately not done: the label is still computed against current ranges rather than a frozen campaign reference. That was the other option on file; it needs a baseline committed somewhere, which brings its own staleness question. Recording the basis makes the existing label honest, which is the smaller and better-evidenced change.

The third instrument this session found quietly untrustworthy, after a gate budget that had never been met and a journal renderer publishing invalid HTML — and the second where the fix was to make the measurement state its own terms, not to change the measurement.

entries.title: An emplacement has a position, not a slot
entries.summary: PLC-01 (issue #29), the first move on Pillar 2 of the PRD: `Placed.slot: tuple[int,int]` becomes `x`/`y` float64 in both engines. Representation only — legality is a stub that accepts exactly the anchor's authored slot positions, mirrored in one function per engine, so nothing about behaviour could change and nothing did (parity: 1440 runs identical, freshly verified, not from cache). Motivated directly by decision 074's finding that no range value reaches a pad too far from the lane. The bigger find was a look-ahead: four places still assume integer slot coordinates and would silently defeat free placement when PLC-02 opens the predicate, one of them meaning a player currently has no way to build off-grid at all no matter what the rules allow.

commits.subject: feat(rules): an emplacement has a position, not a slot

body.text: **Pillar 2 of the PRD starts moving: an emplacement has a position, not a slot.** PLC-01, issue #29. `Placed.slot: tuple[int,int]` becomes `x`/`y` **float64** in both engines.

parity ok — 1440 runs identical (gdscript vs python)
(digest 2efa855e11f7, freshly verified — not from cache)
**Why "freshly verified" is stated:** a cached digest pass would have proved nothing about a representation change, so it was forced.
Why this, now

The owner played the build and said most turrets could barely reach anything (`LF-176`). Decision **074**'s range pass then proved the residual is **slot geometry, not range values** — sweeping pulse-turret from 3.2 to **7.0**, more than double what shipped, leaves p10 pinned at literal **0.0%** while the median climbs sixteen points. No amount of tuning reaches a pad that is simply too far from the lane. Only moving the pad does. That is what makes this the next thing rather than a scheduled item.
The discipline that made it verifiable

The change is **representation only**. Legality goes through one stubbed function, mirrored in both engines, that accepts exactly the anchor's authored slot positions — so nothing about behaviour may change, and nothing did:

rows: a loop doing the identical elementwise float comparison

body.text: `PLC-02` replaces exactly those two bodies. The issue's own reasoning for splitting it: doing representation and rules in one commit means having **no way to tell which one broke parity**. It held.
A read-only `slot` property on `Placed` returning `(x, y)` kept `sim/coverage.py` — explicitly out of scope — reading real data unmodified, proved by its own selftest rather than assumed.
The part worth more than the diff

The agent was asked one extra question: is there anywhere left that still assumes integer slot coordinates and would silently break when PLC-02 opens the predicate up? It found **four**, all presentation, none in the rules — and finding them now is far cheaper than meeting them as a mystery later.

items: **`combat_fx.gd`'s `_beams` is keyed by `Vector2i(int(x), int(y))`.** Two emplacements in the same integer cell — `(4.3, 7.0)` and `(4.7, 7.0)` — collide, so a sustained beam can visually attach to the **wrong gun**. Load-bearing-wrong, not merely stale.
**`available_slots()` is tied to the fixed-slot concept, not to the predicate.** The moment PLC-02 accepts a position outside `anchor["slots"]`, it will not reflect it at all.

**The whole click/select UI is `Vector2i`-typed, and rounds the mouse before anything else sees it.** So there is currently **no way for a player to build at a non-integer position regardless of what the rules allow** — which is exactly how PLC-02 could ship green and change nothing visible in play. This is the important one.
`main.gd`'s scenario `build` verb truncates, so a fractional position in a scenario JSON would be silently floored.

body.text: Also worth a line: one `int()` cast was confirmed **correct and must not be "fixed"** — `_height_at(int(x), int(y))` is the intended world-to-tile truncation. A landmine list that flags a correct thing as wrong is worse than none.
Filed as `LF-197`.
Verification, all four bars

items: parity 1440 identical, fresh
24 anchors × 3 difficulties, **0 field differences**, compared field-for-field against a `git worktree` baseline built from `HEAD` rather than eyeballed
tier 2: 25 passed, 0 failed, with `safe operations` and `rules autoloads` called out specifically
a real screenshot with towers built

entries.title: Where you may build is now a rule, in both engines — and still unreachable
entries.summary: PLC-02 (issue #30) replaces PLC-01's exact-match stub with the real free-placement predicate — bounds, lane standoff, overlap — mirrored character-for-character in `sim/engine.py` and `scripts/anchor_sim.gd`. Parity holds at 1440 runs, but the entry's real subject is why that number could not have caught a wrong predicate, and how the rule was proved directly instead.

commits.subject: feat(rules): where you may build is a rule, in both engines
docs(backlog): per-tower footprint geometry, deferred out of PLC-02

body.text: **PLC-02 — where you may build is now a rule, in both engines.** Bounds, lane standoff, overlap, replacing PLC-01's exact-match stub that accepted only an anchor's authored slot positions.

parity ok — 1440 runs identical (gdscript vs python)
(digest 03a12e483b9d, freshly verified — not from cache)
But the parity result is the weak evidence, and that is the entry

Neither engine's `_try_build()` calls `_is_placeable()` at all. Both source their candidates from `_slot_priority()`, which reads the authored slots — expanding that set is `PLC-04`'s job. So none of the 1440 parity runs ever asks the predicate about a position outside `anchor["slots"]`. Identical parity therefore means *nothing regressed*. It does **not** mean the new rule is right.

A green gate that cannot see the thing you changed is a shape this project keeps finding — a tier-2 budget that was never actually met, a renderer whose output matched its input while both were wrong, a ruleset exercised against zero real references. This is the same failure mode, caught before it shipped as proof of something it did not prove.
So the rule was proved directly instead

items: **48,837 sampled positions**, grid step 0.37, across all 24 anchors, extending one tile outside every board edge, with two emplacements pre-placed per anchor to exercise overlap. Dumped from CPython and from a headless Godot `--script` run. `diff` between the two dumps is **empty**.
**Exact-boundary cases at 1e-9 either side** — the one-in-a-thousand parity failure the spec warns about — both engines agreeing on all three rejection reasons.

**Term order is identical character-for-character**, not merely algebraically equivalent: `abx*abx + aby*aby`, `dx*dx + dy*dy`, `r + FOOTPRINT_RADIUS`. Floating-point addition is not associative, and on an exact boundary that is the difference between legal and illegal — which is the entire reason the parity gate exists.

rows: exactly `r_i + r_j` from a placed emplacement

body.text: Squared comparisons throughout, no square roots. The path is sampled as **segments**, pairwise over waypoints, never at `_slot_priority()`'s `steps` resolution — that sampling is a grader heuristic and is allowed to be approximate, **a rule is not**.
And the honest ending

**A player still cannot build anywhere new.** `LF-197` is confirmed blocking at every layer it named: `anchor_view.gd`'s `hovered_slot = Vector2i(roundi(t.x), roundi(t.y))` rounds the mouse before anything downstream sees it, and `available_slots()` still enumerates `anchor["slots"]` rather than the predicate. The rule is correct and unreachable.

That matters because of what started this: the owner said most turrets could barely reach anything (`LF-176`), decision 074 proved the residual is slot geometry, and free placement is the fix — but only once `PLC-06`/`PLC-07` land. The owner's own play feedback since, `LF-200` (WASD should pan the camera, not step the cursor), belongs in that same change, because it touches the same input path. Two rule issues landed today and neither is yet visible in play.
Also filed

`LF-202` — `FOOTPRINT_RADIUS` is one shared 0.45-tile constant, not a field per tower. Verified harmless today: no two authored slots in any anchor are closer than 0.9 tiles. Becomes real the moment a player can place emplacements as close as the rule allows.

entries.title: Cliffs stop looking like floating tiles, with zero renders
entries.summary: TER-07 fills the gap elevation opened: a raised tile's surface moves up 32 px and nothing fills the drop beneath it. Cliff faces and ramps are drawn procedurally from the existing palette instead of rendered as assets — zero renders, zero atlas growth, asserted rather than claimed — and a bug the verification caught rather than review: a ramp declared on the low side was silently never drawn.

commits.subject: feat(terrain): cliffs and ramps drawn procedurally, zero renders
docs(decisions): 32 px is the right step, judged by eye rather than derived

body.text: **TER-07 — elevation stops looking like floating tiles.** Cliff faces and ramps are now drawn procedurally, from the same palette the rest of the board already uses — **zero renders, zero atlas growth**, checked rather than claimed: `pack_atlas.py --check` reports `nothing written`.
The gap the previous terrain work left open

Decision 057's terrain work made a tile's elevation real and proved it to the pixel. It also made a raised tile look wrong in a specific way: the surface moves up 32 px and nothing fills the gap where the ground used to be, so a plateau reads as floating slabs with see-through edges beneath them. The intuitive fix is to render cliff assets — and that is backwards. A rendered cliff set is roughly seventeen asset types, a `.blend`, a manifest entry and atlas space, all committed before anyone has looked at a single cliff in the game. Decision 066 already refused atlas growth on a measured VRAM projection, and the cheapest way to earn that cost later is to play the free version first. `TER-14`, which decides whether rendered cliff assets are worth it at all, now inherits an answer instead of a question.

body.caption: anchor-01's authored two-level plateau before TER-07: the raised tier reads as floating slabs, with a see-through gap at the drop where the ground used to be.
The same plateau after: solid stacked cliff tiers with a lit rim along the top edge of each face, and the authored ramp — previously invisible — now climbing between them.

body.text: The bug the verification caught, which review would not have

The first pass gated the ramp lookup inside the `if nh < h` cliff-only branch — so a ramp declared on the **low** side, climbing to a higher neighbour, was silently never drawn. anchor-01's actual authored ramp does exactly this: tile `(8,1)` climbing `+x` to `(9,1)`, height 0 to 1. The boundary just rendered flat. **That failure mode looks exactly like "no ramp was authored here", not like a defect** — it was found by capturing before and after and comparing the frames, not by reading the diff. The fix pulls the ramp check out to run regardless of which side is higher.

`terrain.ramps` has been in `data/schema/anchor.schema.json` all along, and `resolve_terrain()` in `sim/content.py` explicitly never consulted it. This is the first time that authored data reaches the screen: a per-corner-height tilted quad plus two filler triangles on the seam against flat lateral neighbours, keyed so a ramp suppresses the plain cliff at that boundary.
32 px, judged by eye for the first time

Decision 057 chose `Iso.LEVEL_PX = 32` because it lands a raised tile on a whole pixel and makes two levels exactly one tile height — correct arithmetic that said nothing about whether it looks right. Played on anchor-01's authored two-level plateau at zoom 1.0 and at 0.61: one 32 px face reads as a clean step without dominating the board, and two levels stack as two visually distinct tiers rather than one tall block. No case was found where it looked too small to notice or too large against a tile's 128×64 px footprint.

`AnchorView._draw` mean **0.383 ms**, p95 0.432 ms, over 300 frames on anchor-01. Faces are built once in `_rebuild_tile_cache()`, never per frame — the PRD's own risk 5 measures naive per-frame terrain at **52 ms/frame at 64²**, and decision 073 has since set the board target to 48², so per-frame terrain was never on the table.

Colour was pixel-sampled from a real rendered frame, not compared against the source `Color(...)` literals — the only way this project has ever caught the sRGB/linear class of error that made the board a flat grey slab three separate times before (`LF-023`/`020`/`022`). Both faces land within anti-aliasing rounding, and no literal `Color(...)` appears anywhere in the new code: every face traces to the existing `STONE_DARK`/`ALLOY_LIGHT` palette. Regression-checked against the 23 anchors that carry no `terrain` block — they render identically to before.

A placement detail worth a sentence: faces are appended into `_tile_cache`, the same painter-ordered array `_draw_board()` already culls and draws, which runs before `_draw_entities()` — so a face is guaranteed to draw under every unit standing on the tile above it. Putting them in `board_props.gd` would have been the natural-looking mistake; that layer's own `DRAW_Z` docstring explains why it sits above everything else instead.
A parallel worktree, and the class_name trap it hit on the way across

This work ran in an isolated git worktree, in parallel with a rules workstream, with disjoint file ownership — and the split held: zero cross-touches, and the cherry-pick onto a `main` that had moved two rules PRs ahead applied with zero conflicts. But bringing it across surfaced a known trap immediately. `board_props.gd` gained a `class_name BoardProps` so `anchor_view.gd` could call its `pillar_cap()`/`pillar_faces()` as static functions — a bare `preload()` constant resolves a script's plain constants but not its `static func`s, which Godot's checker only resolves through an actual class identity. A new `class_name` is invisible until the editor imports it, and the global class cache is gitignored: `gdscript parses` went from 35/35 to 34/35, reporting `Identifier not declared` rather than naming the real cause, until an in-place import registered the name. Exactly the trap CLAUDE.md already documents, hit the moment the work changed trees.

entries.title: Pillar 2 is true in the running game
entries.summary: PLC-06 gives the board a free, continuous cursor and closes out the loop PLC-01/PLC-02 opened: an emplacement carries a real float position and a real legality rule, but until now the mouse rounded to the nearest integer and every keyboard/gamepad step walked a fixed slot graph, so neither could ever be reached in play. A pulse-turret now builds at (8.06, 3.94) — not one of anchor-01's eight authored slots. The best part of the change is a removal: a lane magnet was built, played, and taken back out because it measurably fought the player.

commits.subject: feat(placement): a free board cursor — build where you want, and WASD pans
docs(chronicle): commit PLC-06's free-placement captures

body.text: **Pillar 2 of the PRD is true in the running game.** Build where you want — no slots. Three pieces landed across this workstream, and the first two could not be felt at all: **PLC-01** gave an emplacement float64 `x`/`y` instead of an integer slot (parity 1440 identical). **PLC-02** made legality a real rule — bounds, lane standoff, overlap — proved with 48,837 sampled positions matching between both engines. Neither changed what a player could do, because **PLC-06** (issue #34), the cursor, was the piece still missing: `hovered_slot = Vector2i(roundi(t.x), roundi(t.y))` rounded the mouse before anything downstream ever saw it, and keyboard/gamepad input walked a fixed slot graph. The rule was correct and unreachable.

body.caption: A pulse-turret built at (8.06, 3.94), sitting between the old teal build pads. anchor-01's authored slots are [[2,3],[4,4],[5,1],[6,4],[8,5],[9,3],[10,6],[12,6]] — (8.06, 3.94) is not among them. The HUD kicker reads EMPLACEMENT · (8.06, 3.94).

body.text: The motivation is not aesthetic. `LF-176` was the owner reporting that most turrets could barely reach anything. Decision 074 measured it and found the residual is **slot geometry, not range**: sweeping pulse-turret's range from 3.2 to 7.0, more than double what shipped, left p10 coverage pinned at literally 0.0%. No amount of tuning reaches a pad that is too far from the lane — the pads themselves were the ceiling. Free placement is the fix; this commit is what makes it reachable rather than theoretical.
The best thing in it is a removal
The spec called for a lane magnet: nudge the cursor toward good positions as the player moves it. It was built, played, and taken back out, with the measurement written down rather than a shrug:

The four cursor diagonals are each exactly 45° from any axis-aligned lane tangent, so on anchor-01's axis-aligned lanes **every** direction pressed counted as “aligned enough” — pulling the cursor back toward the lane it was trying to leave. Three presses of screen-right should reach (8.06, 3.94); with the magnet it reached (7.57, 3.61) — still refusing.

A helper that fights the player is worse than no helper. It was filed for a different formulation rather than shipped — the fifth measured refusal recorded this session, and worth naming as a pattern rather than a one-off.

body.caption: The red ghost, refused: WOULD REFUSE HERE · TOO CLOSE TO THE LANE. Legality is drawn continuously as the cursor moves, not revealed only on a failed click.

body.text: What actually shipped

items: **Snap on build, never on move.** Movement is free and predictable; `lf_build` ring-searches within 0.6 tiles of the cursor and builds at the nearest legal position, or refuses. Snapping during movement is exactly what the magnet did wrong.

**Live legality, not just on refusal.** An amber/red ring follows the cursor and the refusal reason shows continuously — PLC-02's rule returns which of the three tests (bounds, lane standoff, overlap) failed precisely so this could be shown before a click, not after.

**The sentinel had to die.** `NO_SLOT`, a magic `Vector2i`, does not survive the type change to `Vector2`, which has no spare value to mean “nothing selected.” It became an explicit `has_selection: bool`, and the fields were renamed — `cursor_at`, `selected_at` — deliberately, so no call site kept working by accident.

body.text: The owner's feedback, same day
I do not like the idea of wasd changing cursor position the way it is. WASD should allow to move the screen.

There was no keyboard camera pan on the board at all before this — WASD and the arrow keys both stepped the cursor. New `lf_pan_*` actions give WASD direct camera pan; arrows, d-pad and stick keep the cursor. The minimap legend had been claiming `ARROWS PAN`, which was only true while the minimap itself had focus; it now reads `WASD PAN · M FOCUS · ARROWS PAN`, which is finally true regardless of focus. Bindings were regenerated through `tools/godot/setup_input.gd`, never hand-edited — decision 042's own reasoning: a typo in a serialized `InputEvent` produces an action that silently never fires rather than an error.

One more worth a line: `data/scenarios/gamepad_build.json` exercises the snap mechanism through a real joypad event and now lands at (7.95, 4.65). Its old assertions passed by coincidence — any press used to park the cursor at `slots[0]` regardless of direction, because that is what the fixed slot graph's first step always did. A test that passes for the wrong reason is the kind of thing this project keeps finding. `scripts/anchor_sim.gd` is untouched by this commit, so no rules changed and no parity risk was introduced.

entries.title: The autoloop had no instrument panel and no brake
entries.summary: The owner started the autoloop for its first real unattended run and had to kill it — blind to what it was doing and with no safe way to stop it. Killing it left a branch checked out, which is why the loop's own notifier turns out to matter: a Title header containing an em dash raised a latin-1 encoding error before any request left the machine, and the except arm reported it as “ntfy unreachable,” blaming the network for a bug that never touched it. Since every notification in this module is written in the project's own prose style, most pushes had been silently failing since the feature landed two commits earlier. Both are fixed and verified end to end; the loop's spawned session dying instantly on iteration 1 is not, and is filed as LF-209.

commits.subject: fix(tooling): the notifier could not spell its own titles, and nothing could stop the loop
docs(backlog): LF-209 — the autoloop's spawned session dies instantly

body.text: The headline is not a bug fix, it is what the bug fix was *for*: the owner started `tools/autoloop.py` for its first real unattended run and had to kill it, because there was no way to see what it was doing and no way to stop it that did not just kill it. A loop built specifically to run unwatched had shipped with no instrument panel and no brake.

Killing it left a branch checked out. Every autoloop run afterward refused at preflight with `on branch 'lf/...', expected main`, with nothing in the message to say this was the debris of a kill rather than a new fault — which is its own small failure, fixed in the same commit.
The notifier had been lying about its own failure

HTTP header values are latin-1 on the wire, and `http.client` enforces it. A `Title:` header containing an em dash raised `'latin-1' codec can't encode character '—'` — before the request ever left the machine — and the `except` arm printed “ntfy unreachable,” which points straight at the network for a bug that never touched it.

Every notification title this module writes is composed in this project's own prose style, which is to say full of em dashes. Most pushes had therefore been failing since the feature landed, two commits earlier; the ones that arrived were the plain-ASCII minority. The irony worth naming: the project's house voice broke the one tool that exists to report on the project.

The fix ASCII-folds header values (`_header_safe`) rather than RFC 2047 encoded-words. ntfy does decode `=?UTF-8?B?...?=`, but only on recent builds, and an older self-hosted box would just display that raw string as the title. A hyphen where an em dash used to be is a loss nobody notices on a phone. The body is untouched — it travels as UTF-8 request data, not a header, so it was never broken.
Stopping is now a boundary, not a kill

items: `--stop` from any terminal, or one Ctrl-C from the loop's own — finishes the current issue and exits with the tree back on `main`.
A second Ctrl-C kills the child immediately, and warns before it does it.
`--status` is a snapshot, not a follower: lockfile liveness, the live status file, the tail of the running session's log, and the tree state — it prints the `tail -f` command instead of arming one.

body.text: Both defects were verified end to end rather than by inspection. A stub HTTP server confirmed the folded Title and the intact UTF-8 body actually arrive on the wire. A harness drove the real loop body with a fake session through both stop paths: graceful exits 0 after the issue completes with the stopfile cleaned up, double-SIGINT kills the child, exits 1, and says “CHECK THE TREE.”
The tail still open — LF-209

The loop's first spawned session died instantly, its entire log a 15-byte “Execution error.” That is why iteration 1 produced an empty branch and shipped nothing, and why iteration 2 then refused at preflight with `on branch 'lf/plc-placement-ghost', expected main` — debris of the kill, not a fault of its own. Plain `claude -p --model sonnet --output-format text` was verified working in this session; the untested difference is `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which this session was not permitted to run. Said plainly rather than papered over: the autoloop's own plumbing is fixed, and the thing it launches still does not work.

entries.title: Interrupted, not broken
entries.summary: The earlier entry today, “The autoloop had no instrument panel and no brake,” closed on an open question: the spawned session's first run had died instantly with a 15-byte log reading “Execution error,” filed as LF-209. That diagnosis was wrong, and the evidence had been on disk the whole time — the session transcript shows three minutes of real work ended by the owner's own Ctrl-C. The bug it uncovered instead was worse: Ctrl-C is delivered to the terminal's whole foreground process group, so it reached the child directly and the graceful-stop boundary shipped hours earlier could never have worked. LF-209 is dropped, not closed.

commits.subject: fix(tooling): Ctrl-C reached the spawned session directly, so the graceful stop was a lie

body.text: This corrects a claim made a few hours earlier in the same session, in “The autoloop had no instrument panel and no brake.” That entry ended on an open question, filed as `LF-209`: the autoloop's first spawned session had died instantly, its whole log 15 bytes reading “Execution error,” and the conclusion drawn from that was that the loop's plumbing was now fixed but the thing it launched still did not work. That conclusion was wrong, and the reason it was wrong is worth recording as carefully as the original claim was.
The evidence had been on disk the whole time

The session transcript under `~/.claude/projects/` for that run was never read before LF-209 was filed. Read afterward, it shows about three minutes of real work: `/session-start` completed, the PLC-07 spec was read, and a `godot-engineer` subagent was being dispatched when the transcript ends on `[Request interrupted by user for tool use]`. The session was not broken. It was interrupted — by the owner's own Ctrl-C. `claude -p` prints exactly “Execution error” when a run is aborted, and the log is 15 bytes for the plainest reason available: a session that never finishes emits no final text.
The real defect was worse, and it shipped in the fix hours earlier

Ctrl-C is delivered to the terminal's foreground **process group**, not to a pid. The child session lived inside the loop's own process group, so the terminal's signal reached it directly, and the parent's brand-new `SIGINT` handler — the one the earlier entry described as turning one Ctrl-C into a graceful stop — never got a turn to decide anything. “One Ctrl-C finishes the current issue” could not have held for a single run; it only ever looked like it might because nobody had pressed Ctrl-C against the fixed version yet. `start_new_session=True` now detaches the child into its own group, so a terminal Ctrl-C reaches only the loop.
Reproduced both ways, not reasoned about
A harness that signals the process group exactly as a real terminal does was run against both versions. Without the fix, the child prints:
CHILD KILLED BY THE TERMINAL Ctrl-C
and with it:
CHILD FINISHED ITS WORK
Detaching moves the risk rather than removing it

A detached child is a process-group leader, so a deliberate kill now goes through `killpg` rather than a plain `kill()` on its pid — killing the pid alone would strand its own subagents, its Godot, its Blender as reparented survivors, which on this project is a money bug and not fan noise. And because a detached child no longer dies for free when the loop does, its pid is now printed to the console and written to `.cache/autoloop-status.json`: a `kill -9` on the loop leaves a live agent session running with nobody watching it, and whoever has to end it by hand needs the number rather than a process listing to hunt through. That gap — the reaper does not yet know how to find or check that pid on its own — is open as `LF-210`.
LF-209 is dropped, not closed

The bug it described does not exist. The cheaper lesson is the one worth keeping: the transcript under `~/.claude/projects/` answers “what did the spawned session actually do” in seconds, and guessing from a 15-byte log instead produced a wrong diagnosis that survived a merge and into a published journal entry.

entries.title: A panel that cannot lie about a dead loop, and Opus on the main line
entries.summary: `--status` and `--stop` answered the right questions and were reachable only from the terminal that started the loop, which is not where the owner was the night they needed to stop one. `tools/autoloop_web.py` is one stdlib server and one self-contained page at localhost:8732 — state, live session log, and three buttons — that invents no state of its own and reuses the CLI's own stop, kill and preflight mechanisms rather than reimplementing them. It was nearly this project's second known leak after `tools/audio/serve.py`, and the fix is the same shape: a lease, and an idle shutdown verified live rather than assumed. In the same commit, decision 077 moves the main development line and all six subagents onto Opus, at the owner's instruction — re-reading decision 051 in that light, what it actually bought was every agent stating its model, not every agent being cheap. Three consecutive pull requests have now been infrastructure, on a project whose standing orders default to game-facing work; this panel is meant to be the last piece before the loop points back at real game issues.

commits.subject: feat(tooling): a control panel for the unattended loop, and Opus on the main development line

body.text: Two changes landed in one pull request because they are the same subject — how the unattended loop runs — not because unrelated work got batched: a web control panel for the loop, and decision 077, which moves that loop's model.
The lever within reach was Ctrl-C

`--status` and `--stop`, from the two entries earlier today, answer the right questions — but only from the terminal the loop was started from. The owner was not there: they started a night run, saw something they disliked, and Ctrl-C was the only lever within reach. `tools/autoloop_web.py` is one stdlib HTTP server and one self-contained page at `localhost:8732` — state, a live session log, and three buttons: Stop after this issue, Kill now, Start.

It invents no state of its own. It renders `.cache/autoloop.lock`, `.cache/autoloop-status.json` and the newest session log — the same files `--status` reads — so the page cannot disagree with the CLI, and every button reuses the CLI's own mechanism: the stopfile, two SIGINTs, spawning only after preflight passes. Two design points worth naming. Preflight now runs in the server *before* it spawns, so a refusal reaches the page instead of dying four seconds later in a log nobody opened. And a stale lockfile — what a `kill -9` leaves behind — reports as STALE LOCK rather than “running”, because a panel telling the owner a dead loop is alive is the one lie that would cost them a night.
Nearly the second known leak

`tools/audio/serve.py` is named in `reap.py`'s own docstring as a leak, because `serve_forever()` has no exit condition at all, and on this project a forgotten background process is a money bug, not housekeeping. The panel holds a lease and shuts itself down after `--idle` seconds with no request — the page polls every 2 s, so no requests means no browser has it open, which is exactly when it should stop. Verified live rather than assumed: it printed `no request in 60s — shutting down`, released its lease, and `reap.py` reported clean.
The obvious fix to that leak was considered and rejected

Adding the panel — and `autoloop.py` itself — to `reap.py`'s `OUR_TOOLS` looked like the tidy move and was wrong twice over. `reap.py --kill` runs from the `SessionEnd` hook, so an overnight loop would be killed by an unrelated session ending somewhere else entirely. And `autoloop.py`'s own preflight refuses to start unless the reaper reports clean — it would see the loop, then the panel, and refuse to start either. An unattended loop that runs all night is not a stray process; the reasoning lives in the module's own docstring, not only here.

items: Page loads 200, `/api/state` correct against both a running and a stopped loop.
Stop from the page is graceful — the loop logs `SIGINT — will stop after the current issue finishes`, ships its issue, exits 0.
Kill and Start both refuse correctly with no loop running and on a dirty tree.
An unknown route returns 404.

body.text: Decision 077 — the main line runs on Opus

At the owner's instruction: `autoloop.py --model` now defaults to `opus`, and all six subagent definitions in `.claude/agents/` are repinned from `sonnet`. This supersedes only the model half of decision 051 — its reaper and bounded-subprocess halves are untouched.

The insight worth keeping is what re-reading 051 turned up: the invariant it actually bought was that every agent *states* its model, not that every agent is cheap. All five agents 051 addressed had carried no `model:` key at all and silently inherited Opus, which is what had spilled the owner's subscription into paid credits in the first place. Read that way, the gate check (`agent models`) survives 077 intact and becomes *more* load-bearing, not less — with an expensive model chosen deliberately, drift off the pin is what would quietly change the bill. The value now lives in one constant, `AGENT_MODEL`, rather than a literal comparison.

The corollary inverts guidance this file has carried for a while: a five-way fan-out used to be the cheap move and no longer is. `CLAUDE.md` now says to dispatch the agent the work needs, not a panel of them.
A count that had already rotted, in the file that warns about it

`CLAUDE.md`'s own verification line for the agent pin said “→ 5” while six agent definitions already existed — a number written into prose, in the same file that names that exact failure mode and tells the reader not to trust a count without a check behind it. It now names the live count instead of a fixed one.
Said plainly, because the house style is not to round it up

Three consecutive pull requests have now been infrastructure — the loop's notifier and stop path, the Ctrl-C process-group fix, and this one — on a project whose standing orders default to game-facing work. None of the three were optional: an unattended loop that cannot be stopped safely or seen from another room is not one that should have been left running. This panel is meant to be the last piece of scaffolding before the loop is pointed back at real backlog issues rather than at itself.

entries.title: An arc is a dot product, and no angle ever enters the rules
entries.summary: Free placement made which way an emplacement points a real question for the first time, so this is the rule written down before the three weapons that need it exist. An arc looks exactly like a job for the inverse tangent; it is not. A probe of 100,000 float64 pairs across CPython, Linux Godot and Windows Godot found seven operations whose results differ between the two C libraries — the worst of them on 4.32% of samples — and the owner plays the Windows build. So an arc is two dot products against a cosine authored in the data, with no angle, no trigonometry and no square root anywhere in either engine. No shipped weapon changed. The more interesting half is what that costs: the branch is gated on a key no shipped row carries, which is the acceptance criterion itself, so the 1,440-run parity gate executes the absent branch every time and proves nothing about the present one. A gate that runs the whole game says nothing about a branch the shipped data never enters — hence a new check, `firing arcs agree`, and three deliberate breaks to prove it can go red.

commits.subject: feat(rules): firing arcs as dot products, so no angle ever enters the rules
test(rules): a firing-arc fixture and the two-engine harness that reads it

body.text: Until free placement landed earlier today, **which way an emplacement points was not a question anyone had to answer**. An omnidirectional gun bolted to a fixed slot is the same gun wherever it stands. A gun the player positions is not, and three weapons on the roadmap fire in a shape rather than a circle — the Siege Battery, the Cutting Lance and the Spine Driver. None of them exist yet. This is the rule written down first, so that when they arrive the arc is a thing that already works rather than a thing invented under pressure.
An arc looks exactly like a job for the inverse tangent. It is not.

The probe that settled it: **100,000 float64 pairs across five value regimes, 24 operations, raw IEEE-754 bytes compared** on CPython, Linux Godot 4.7.1 and — the part that matters — **Windows Godot 4.7.1**. Seven operations disagree between the Microsoft C runtime and glibc:

Stable across runs — this is a library difference, not nondeterminism. `sqrt`, `fmod`, `floor`, `round`, a hand-written hypotenuse and the four arithmetic operators come back **byte-identical on all three**. The rules use none of the divergent set today, which means cross-platform agreement currently holds **by accident**, and the owner plays the Windows build. An arc written as an angle difference would have ended that in the worst possible way: correct on every machine the gate runs on, and wrong once, unreproducibly, on the one machine that matters.
What actually shipped

Two comparisons, and nothing else: `dot(to_target, facing) >= 0`, and `dot*dot >= cos_half_angle² · |facing|² · d2`. The threshold is authored in `data/towers.json` as `cos_half_angle` — **the cosine of the half-angle, never the angle** — alongside a facing vector in tile space. Absent means omnidirectional, which is every one of the nine shipped rows. So this pull request lands the mechanism and the guard and **changes no shipped weapon at all**.
Three judgement calls, each of which rejected something

**The squared form removes the square root and is exact — but squaring loses the sign.** A unit standing directly **behind** the emplacement satisfies the squared comparison exactly as well as its mirror image in front does. The `dot >= 0` guard in front of it is load-bearing, not defensive tidiness, and it is written first in both engines with the derivation in both docstrings so nobody simplifies it away.

**The cosine is bounded at 0, not at −1.** A half-angle wider than 90° has a negative cosine, at which point the comparison inverts and the sign guard becomes actively wrong rather than merely redundant. The issue left this open — handle it or reject it, but deliberately. It is rejected, in the schema. An inverted branch that nothing exercises is a bug lying in wait for the first weapon that wants a 200° arc, and that weapon does not exist. A cosine of zero already gives a half-plane, which is wider than anything the design calls for.

**The facing vector is not normalised, and that is the whole trick.** Its squared length stays on the right-hand side of the comparison instead of being divided out at build time, which is what keeps a square root out of the rules entirely. `[0, 1]` and `[0, 3]` therefore author the identical cone. Normalising once at placement would have been defensible — one square root, on an operation that is provably safe — and it was rejected because it puts a square root in the rules to buy nothing, and because an authored non-unit vector would then be silently rewritten instead of simply working.
The gate that runs the whole game proves nothing about this branch

This is the finding worth more than the feature. `rules parity` drives the entire game through both engines — 1,440 runs, roughly fourteen minutes — and it is the strongest guarantee this project has. It **structurally cannot say anything about the arc rule.** The arc branch is gated on a key that no shipped row carries, and that is not an oversight, it is the acceptance criterion itself: no shipped weapon may gain an arc, so the path stays provably inert. Every one of those 1,440 runs therefore executes the **absent** branch. All of them pass. None of them touch the code that was just written.

And it would have kept passing, silently, right up until the first weapon shipped an arc — at which point a divergence between the two engines would have surfaced as an unexplained leak nine minutes into a parity run, with nothing pointing at the arc at all. The general form is the lesson: **a gate that runs the whole game proves nothing about a branch the shipped data never enters.**
So there is a new check

`firing arcs agree`, tier 3 — `tools/arc_parity.py`, `scripts/test/arc_parity.gd` and a fixture at `data/schema/fixtures/firing-arc.json` that lives under the schema directory because the data validator excludes that tree, making it non-shipping by location rather than by a promise to delete it later. Four emplacements face one lane down which a single walker travels with a million hit points, so that the fire pattern is never accidentally a statement about a kill. 280 ticks. The observable is whether each emplacement fired on each tick, which needs no new accessor on either engine and goes through the real targeting path on both sides.

It makes three claims, and the second and third are what make it worth having. Fire patterns must be byte-identical between the two engines. Every firing window must fall inside bounds derived from the **geometry** rather than from either implementation — so two engines wrong in the same way still fail. And the arc'd rows must fire **strictly less** than an un-arc'd control, so an arc test that never engaged at all cannot pass by looking omnidirectional.
Measured, green: `ok — 4 emplacement(s) over 280 ticks, 48 shots, python and godot identical and inside the analytic windows`.

body.caption: The four fixture emplacements' measured firing windows along one lane, plotted from the harness's own output. The two top rows are the claim that matters: `cone` and `scaled` author the same 60° cone with facing vectors of length 1 and 3, and they fire over windows of identical width — 1.87 tiles each — at different points on the lane. That equality is the entire un-normalised-facing argument, and it is the row that goes red the moment somebody “simplifies” the rules to assume a unit vector. The bottom row is the un-arc'd control, five times as wide.

body.text: Proved red three ways before it was trusted
A new check that has never failed is a decoration. Each of these was broken on purpose and each one was caught:

items: `--corrupt`, the harness's own self-test, collapses the first expected window — red.

Deleting the `dot >= 0` sign guard from `sim/engine.py`: **34 ticks of cross-engine disagreement** on the half-plane row, plus a window violation — that row began firing from x 0.07 instead of x 4.00, which is exactly the mirror-image-behind-the-gun failure the guard exists to stop.
Dropping the squared facing length from the Godot engine's arc gate: **25 ticks of disagreement** on the unnormalised row, whose window blew out from 13.87 → 15.73 to 9.40 → 18.27.

Separately, the static `safe operations` check was proved red on a deliberate inverse tangent appended to the Godot rules file — it named the file, the line and the 0.084% figure — and green again on revert.

body.text: A small embarrassment, recorded because it is the kind of thing that rots quietly

The issue's own acceptance criterion is a `grep` for banned operations across the two rules files, and it must return nothing. It returned two hits. Both of them were **my own prose** — comments in the rules files boasting that there is no inverse tangent, no cosine and no square root in them, written with the operation names spelled out. The gate's `safe operations` check strips comments before scanning, so it was green throughout and nothing was ever actually wrong; the issue's naive command was not. The comments were reworded to name the operations in words rather than as identifiers, so a future reader running that exact command sees a clean result instead of two false hits and ten minutes of confusion.
Tier 3, not tier 2, and that is a budget decision

`firing arcs agree` is the same shape and roughly the same cost as `terrain parsers agree`, which sits at tier 2 — the natural home for a cheap two-implementation agreement check. It went to tier 3 anyway, because tier 2 is already **over** its own 28,000 ms budget contract on a clean run, and this project decided once already, when it deleted a tuning constant rather than re-fitting it, that the answer to a budget nobody meets is to move the work rather than move the number. Not a judgement about importance. CI runs tier 3 on every pull request.
Verification, stated exactly

items: `rules parity` — **1,440 runs identical between the two engines, freshly run rather than served from cache** (digest `6062357c1cc8`), about 14 minutes. This is the acceptance bar: the arc code is present and provably inert.

`tools/check.py --tier 3` — **36 passed · 0 failed · 3 skipped · 210,575 ms**. The three skips are `music loudness`, `rules parity` and `rules parity (windows)`, all tier 4. `firing arcs agree` green inside the gate at 2,512 ms.
