`rules parity (windows)` was **not run locally.** CI runs it on every pull request that touches a rules file, and this one does — but nothing on this machine has executed the Windows build against these changes, and the whole premise of this work is that the Windows build is the one that differs. Stated plainly rather than folded into the line above.

body.text: What was not done

The issue lists mirroring the change into `scripts/test/parity.gd` as a task. The faithful report is that **the mirror was already free**: that harness indexes the raw tower rows and places through the same build path the game does, so both new keys reach the rules with no harness edit at all. An upgrade block still cannot override an arc — the merge would carry one through unchanged, but the schema does not admit the keys there and no weapon needs it. And whether the player will be able to rotate an emplacement while placing it is still an open design question rather than something this settled; facing comes from data and does not change.

entries.title: For fifty-one pull requests, merging closed nothing at all
entries.summary: The owner noticed something small: the loop ships a pull request, the pull request merges, and the issue is still sitting in the backlog. It turned out to have never worked once. PR #130 had merged thirty-seven minutes earlier carrying the line “Closes `PLC-03`”, and issue #31 was still open with closedAt null — because GitHub acts only on `Closes #31`, and a spec id in backticks is prose it reads straight past. Across all fifty-one merged pull requests in the repository, zero carried a closing keyword GitHub could resolve. The fix is not a script that closes things; it is making the merge itself the close, which is the only version that works when the owner merges by hand — and hand-merging is precisely the case every previous mechanism missed.

commits.subject: fix(tooling): a merged pull request now closes its issue, in both tracking systems

body.text: The report was one sentence: *the Python script runs, the task completes, it creates the pull request, I merge it — and the issue still sits in the backlog. Is that behaviour we anticipate?*

It is not. And the thing that made it worth stopping for was how recently it had failed. **Pull request #130 had merged thirty-seven minutes earlier**, closing the firing-arc work, with this line at the top of its body:
Closes `PLC-03`. Decision 078.

GitHub issue #31 was still `OPEN`, `closedAt: null`. **GitHub acts only on `Closes #<number>`.** A spec id in backticks is prose, and it reads straight past it. The line looked exactly like a closing keyword, was written in good faith, and did nothing whatsoever.
It had never worked, not once

rows: carrying a closing keyword GitHub can resolve
open backlog items named by an already-merged PR

body.text: That last number needs a caveat, and the caveat is the actual finding. **Forty is not forty stale items.** A pull request naming `LF-211` may have *filed* it rather than fixed it — which is exactly what #130 did. Nothing in the repository distinguishes “this PR fixed it” from “this PR mentioned it,” and *that indistinguishability is the defect*, not a footnote on it.
Three holes, none of them the one that was obvious

items: **No workflow observes a merge.** `gate.yml`, `parity-shard.yml` and `parity-windows.yml` all trigger on open and synchronize only. Nothing runs on `pull_request: closed`.

**`tools/issues.py close` is a line in a prompt.** It is a good tool, and it lives in the autoloop's brief and in step 8 of the ship skill — which means when the **owner** merges by hand, no code runs at all. Decision 051 exists because remembered rules fail. This was a remembered rule wearing a tool's clothes.

**Two tracking systems that had never been introduced.** `backlog.json` holds `LF-nnn` and closes with `backlog.py done`; `docs/issues/*.md` projects to GitHub and closes with `issues.py close`. The ship loop touched the second and never the first.

body.text: The fix is not a closing script

The temptation was a workflow on `pull_request: closed` that goes and closes things. That is another mechanism to forget, and it does nothing about the backlog file. The better answer was to ask what each system actually *is*.

A `docs/issues/` spec is projected to something **outside** the repository, so the close has to happen outside too — and GitHub already does it, atomically, on merge, **no matter who presses the button**. So the pull request body carries a *resolved* `Closes #31`, looked up from the id map rather than typed by hand.

A `backlog.json` item is a file **inside** the repository. Nothing external needs telling. It is marked done in the pull request's own commit, so merging is what lands the close and there is no second step at all.

Both halves read one declaration — a `Closes:` trailer in a commit message. **The colon is load-bearing.** It is git's own trailer syntax, so a sentence like “this closes the gap LF-105 describes” cannot be mistaken for a declaration. Both shapes were tested.
Proven red, then green, then red again

A check nobody has watched fail is a check nobody should trust. The new tier-1 `issue traceability` check was driven through both states on the real branch: green with `LF-212` marked done, then **red** after reopening it — naming the commit, the id and the exact command to fix it — then green again. The CI-side half was driven with the **literal body of PR #130**, which it correctly refuses, and with a body containing shell-injection-shaped text, which passes through the environment untouched because the workflow never puts a pull request body on a command line.
What this cost, said plainly

Tier 1 went from about 7.8 s to 8.3 s against a 10 s budget. **Tier 2 is at 33,386 ms against a 28,000 ms budget — over, and it was already over before this landed** (`LF-178`). This added roughly 370 ms to that. The budget did not move, because moving it is the thing decision 067 refused to do when it deleted `PRESSURE_FLOOR` rather than raising it. The honest state is: tier 2 needs a check taken out, not a bigger number.
Two traps found on the way

`actions/checkout` defaults to depth 1, so `git merge-base origin/main HEAD` finds nothing — and the new check would have reported *“skip: no merge base”*: green, and useless. That is the exact partial-run-that-reads-as-full this gate is built to refuse, so both jobs now fetch full history. The pack is about 7 MiB with LFS excluded.
And the `tier counts` check caught the docstring drift this change introduced on the very first run, which is precisely what it is for.

entries.title: The sweeper was lying about what it would delete
entries.summary: A blocker had been filed that morning, live, while two agents were running: the branch garbage collector proposed deleting the branch of an agent that was working in that worktree at that moment. It reads like data loss and it was filed as data loss. Reproducing it deliberately showed something more interesting — it could not have deleted anything, for two independent reasons, and the real bug was that `git branch --merged` decorates its output with a `+ ` for branches checked out in another worktree, which the parser did not strip. The tool was reporting a destruction it was incapable of performing. Which still cost a blocker-priority issue and a session's belief, and which stayed safe only by accident of a malformed name. The worse defect was found while fixing that one: every failed removal was silent and still counted toward “swept N items”.

commits.subject: fix(tooling): gc.py was lying about what it would delete, and counting failures as swept

body.text: `LF-201` was filed the same morning it happened, which is the best kind of bug report. Two agents were running; a dry run of `tools/gc.py` printed this:
branch   would delete  + worktree-agent-a7712cc56b9f06fe1  (merged into main)

That agent was working in that worktree at that moment. The issue was filed as a blocker, with an argument that is entirely correct in the abstract: **a killed process can be re-run; a deleted branch carrying an agent's work is gone.** It was ranked above everything else on the process queue.
Reproducing it first, which is what changed the answer

The condition needs a worktree whose branch points at `main` with no commits yet — that is what makes a live branch classify as *merged*. `git worktree add --no-checkout` produces it for free, with no 150 MB checkout. Then the two commands the tool would actually have run:

rows: `error: cannot delete branch 'lf/repro-201' used by worktree at …`

body.text: **Two independent guards, and the tool never got past either one.** The first because the name it had built was not a real ref; the second because git itself refuses to delete a branch a worktree holds. Nothing was ever destroyed, and nothing could have been.
So what was broken

`git branch --merged` **decorates its output**. `* ` marks the current branch — which the old parser did strip — and `+ ` marks *a branch checked out in another worktree*, which it did not. So a live agent's branch came back as the literal string `"+ lf/thing"`, matched nothing in the checked-out exclusion set that exists precisely to protect it, and got printed as a deletion.

The tool was **lying about what it would do rather than doing it.** That is a smaller bug than data loss and it is not a small bug: it produced a blocker-priority issue, and a session that believed agent branches were being deleted. It also stayed safe purely by *accident* — normalise that name in some future refactor and the exclusion has to actually work. So it was made to actually work.
The defect found while fixing it, which is the worse one
Both removal paths ran `subprocess.run(..., capture_output=True)` with **no return-code check**, then incremented the counter unconditionally:

Every failed removal was silent, and still counted toward **“swept N item(s)”**. That is the same class of instrument as the retry loop this project once had that committed nothing twelve times in a row without ever failing — a number that reports success for work that did not happen. `gc.py` now checks every return code, prints each failure by name, and exits 1 if any removal failed.
What changed

items: `--format=%(refname:short)`, so no decoration can ever reach the delete path.
`%(worktreepath)` from `for-each-ref` as the authoritative checked-out set, instead of parsing `worktree list` and hoping.

**Branches considered before `worktree prune`.** Pruning de-registers a worktree whose directory has vanished — and de-registering is exactly what disarms git's own refusal, the second of the two guards. Order matters here in a way it did not look like it did.
A `KEPT` line that names the worktree holding the branch, instead of a delete line that lies.

body.text: A selftest that is deliberately not in the gate

`gc.py --selftest` asserts both invariants against **this repository's real refs, not a fixture**. That is on purpose: the bug was a parsing bug against real `git` output, and a fixture of what someone *believes* that output looks like is exactly what let it through — the old parser was written against a correct mental model of `* ` and an absent one of `+ `.

It is not a gate check. It costs **1.45 s**, almost all interpreter startup, to guard a tool invoked once per session at wrap — while tier 1 has about 1.7 s of headroom and tier 2 is already **over** its own budget. Adding it would be the same bad trade as raising a budget rather than removing a check, which is the move decision 067 refused. So it runs where the tool runs: the ship skill's sweep step now reads `--selftest && --apply`.
The general lesson

The issue text was written from the dry-run output, which is the most reasonable thing to write it from, and it was **wrong about the mechanism** — it described data loss that could not occur. Reproducing before fixing cost about ten minutes and changed both the severity and the fix. The backlog entry has been superseded rather than edited, the same rule the decisions log follows, so the record still shows what was believed on the day.

entries.title: The guard denied the operation its own message recommends
entries.summary: Three false positives from one hook rule reached a live session in a single day, and the funniest of them denied an in-place reimport — the exact operation the denial message tells you to use instead. The test for “does this command write to the import cache” was, literally, whether a greater-than sign appeared anywhere in it, so `2>/dev/null` counted. The second gap denied the filing of the issue about the first gap, because the issue text quoted the path. The real cost was not the blocked commands: an over-broad rule does not just block, it hides, and one of the denied reads turned out to answer the open question at the top of the process backlog.

commits.subject: fix(tooling): the guard denied the operation its own message recommends

body.text: `tools/hooks/guard.py` is the file that turns this project's working agreement into something the harness enforces rather than something an agent has to remember. It is a good idea and this is the entry about it being wrong three times in one day, all in the same rule, all on the **allow** side — which its selftest covered thinly while covering the deny side well.
Gap 1: a greater-than sign, anywhere

The rule for “does this command write to the engine's import cache” was two tests: does a write verb appear, **or** does the command contain `>`. Not *a redirect to the guarded path* — just the character.
So this was denied:
du -sh .godot 2>/dev/null

And so was an in-place reimport piped to `tail`, followed by a `grep` **reading** the global class cache to confirm a new `class_name` had registered. Neither redirect touches the guarded path; `2>&1` touches no file at all.

**The irony is what made it worth fixing rather than working around.** The denial message tells the operator that the supported path is exactly the in-place reimport — which is what the command was doing. The rule denied the operation it recommends, whenever the operator also wanted to see stderr or verify afterwards. And verifying afterwards is the *correct* habit here, because a `class_name` that has not registered is a **hang**, not an error.
Gap 2: it denied the filing of the bug report about gap 1
Payload scrubbing existed — a path named inside a `-m` commit message is prose, not a filesystem write — but it only understood **flags**. A bare positional argument was still read as a command.

So `tools/backlog.py add "<text quoting the cache path and some example redirects>"` was denied. The issue about the guard's false positives could not be filed because of a guard false positive. It happened again twenty minutes later while filing a second report of the same thing, and was worked around by writing the prose to a scratch file and passing it by command substitution — which is not a fix, it is the next person hitting it.
The fix, and what was deliberately not done

items: A redirect is a write only when the guarded path is what it redirects **to**. `cat foo > <cache>/x` stays denied — the shell performs that write even though `cat` only reads — but `du -sh <cache> 2>/dev/null` writes nothing.
Prose positionals are scrubbed from an **explicit table** of `(script, subcommand)`, not a heuristic. “The last positional is probably prose” would silently un-guard `rm`.
Six selftest cases added, every one a command that was actually denied. 52 → 58, all green.

body.text: The part that actually mattered

The blocked commands cost minutes. What cost more is that **an over-broad rule does not just block, it hides.** One of the denied reads was asking whether a git worktree gets its own Godot import cache — the open question that `PRC-15` calls *“the single biggest reason worktrees are not free here”*, and worktree isolation is the top item on the process backlog.
With the false positive gone, the answer took one command:

A worktree gets a **fully populated, fully separate** cache. Godot has no cache-location flag — checked against `--help` on the real binary, where the only relevant flags are `--path` and `--import` — and `--path` implies the cache inside that directory. So the isolation is **by construction, not by configuration**, which removes the whole LF-075 class of risk from worktree agents rather than mitigating it. The cost is one import and about 128 MB.
That question had been asked once already, hours earlier, and the answer was sitting behind a denial. The rule was fixed for its own sake; the finding was the interest on it.

entries.title: The one blocker on the queue had already been fixed
entries.summary: Forty-five percent of the open backlog was tooling, against a standing order that says default to game-facing work. That order is true of how sessions are run and false of the queue they run against, so the correction was being reapplied one session at a time to a problem that regenerates. Applying it once properly meant checking every item against the tree instead of reading its title — and the very first thing checked was the single blocker, which asked for two fixes that both shipped weeks ago. Ten items closed on evidence, two dead tools deleted, and the queue went from 82 open at 45% tooling to 72 at 38%, with no blockers left.

commits.subject: chore(backlog): close ten items that were already done, delete two dead tools

body.text: Two `/insights` reports had just been read and neither could see this, because both read session transcripts and neither reads the backlog. Counted directly from `backlog.json`: **37 of 82 open items were `tooling`**, 45% of the queue, against a standing order whose exact words are *default to game-facing work*.

The order is true of how sessions are run and **false of the queue they run against**. So the correction was being applied one session at a time to a problem that regenerated faster than it was applied.
The blocker was not a blocker
There was exactly one item at `blocker` priority: `LF-105`, *“the gate never tests the build the owner plays”*. It names its own acceptance criteria — two fixes, both cheap:

items: **Run parity against the Windows build at least once per release.** `parity-windows.yml` runs on every pull request touching `sim/engine.py`, `scripts/anchor_sim.gd` or `scripts/test/parity.gd`, plus a weekly cron, plus manual dispatch — and `rules parity (windows)` sits at tier 4. That is considerably more than once per release.
**A gate check greping the rules for the unsafe operation set.** `safe operations`, tier 1, with a documented `# safe-ops-exempt:` marker mechanism.

body.text: Both shipped. The highest-priority item on the board, the one that ranks above everything, had been **done for weeks and simply never closed.** It was steering work by sitting at the top of a list.
Nine more, all verified rather than assumed

`LF-056` (`.editorconfig` carries `indent_style = tab`), `LF-116` (`MAX_CONCURRENT_CAPTURES = 2`, live), `LF-128` (the backgrounding rule is enforced by the guard, not just written down), `LF-175` (`XDG_DATA_HOME` isolation with an mtime assertion), `LF-180`, and `LF-194` — where the branch-protection ruleset was confirmed **active against the live API**, not taken from the item's own claim that it had been applied.

`LF-195` was closed as a duplicate rather than as done: its audit was finished, but its residual — *record the commit an item was observed at, so a stale item can be detected* — is `LF-156`, which stays open and carries it. One mechanism, one issue.
Two dead tools, and an honest note about deleting them

`tools/analysis_overdraw.py` and `tools/analysis_shield_wall.py` were verified dead three ways: nothing in the tree references them, both fail on import, and both hardcode a `sys.path.insert` pointing at `/Users/briangerhards/dev/defend-claude` — an old host **and** an old project name. They were non-runnable long before `PLC-01` renamed the data representation out from under them.

The part worth recording: **`docs/DECISIONS.md` cites both as “reproduce with …” for two decisions, and that file is append-only.** Deleting the scripts leaves two citations pointing at nothing, and the rule forbids quietly correcting them. They were *already* dead citations — the scripts could not run — so the deletion makes an existing loss visible rather than creating a new one. It is called out in the commit so a reader of those decisions can find it.
What it moved
The mechanism did the closing, which was the point

All ten closed through `Closes:` trailers on the commit — the convention landed a few hours earlier, when it turned out that across 51 merged pull requests **not one** had ever auto-closed anything. The tier-1 check reported `10 close(s) declared and backed` before the commit was allowed to stand. A cull is a one-time cleanup of a queue that regenerates; the mechanism is what keeps it drained. Doing them in that order was deliberate.

entries.title: The gate wrote its evidence into the cache it forbids everyone else to touch
entries.summary: A hook rule denies every writer access to the engine's import cache, because rebuilding it blanks the level for whoever is playing out of the same tree. The gate wrote three of its own scratch files straight into that directory — it was the one writer exempt from the rule it enforces, by being the thing that wrote the rule. The paths were also fixed rather than per-run, so two concurrent gate runs deleted each other's evidence while the accessibility analyser was still reading it. Fixing it also answered the question PRC-15 calls the single biggest reason worktrees are not free here, and the answer turned out to be that they are.

commits.subject: fix(gate): the gate wrote its evidence into the cache it forbids everyone else to touch

body.text: Three rendering checks each wrote to a **fixed** path inside `.godot/`, the engine's import cache: a game frame, a menu frame, and four accessibility captures with their JSON reports.
Two things wrong with that, and the second one is funnier

**Fixed paths mean two concurrent gate runs delete each other's evidence.** The accessibility analyser samples its background colours *out of those PNGs*, so it could read a frame another process had already unlinked. “Two agents ran the gate at once” had no defence at all — and that has to be true before parallel agents are safe at all.

**And `.godot/` is the directory the owner's running game reads from.** `guard.py`'s `rule_godot_write` denies every writer access to it, for exactly the reason LF-075 records: rebuilding or moving that cache pulls every texture out from under a live session, the menu still draws, the level comes up blank, and it reads precisely like a code regression. It cost a full diagnosis pass once.
So the gate was **the one writer exempt from the rule it enforces**, by being the thing that wrote the rule. Scratch files now go to `.cache/gate/`, alongside the leases and the parity digests.
One deliberate deviation from the spec
`PRC-15` asks for the temp directory to be removed in a `finally`. It is not, and that is on purpose.

The old code unlinked its frame **after** the assertions passed, and returned early on failure — so a failing rendering check left its frame on disk to be looked at. That is the entire value of a rendering check that failed. A blanket `finally: rmtree` would have been tidier and would have destroyed the evidence every time it mattered. Cleanup happens on **success** only; a failure keeps the directory, and the failure message now says where it is.

Both paths were driven directly rather than reasoned about — a synthetic passing check leaves nothing behind, a synthetic failing one keeps its file and reports the path, with the pid in the directory name so a hard-killed run leaves a trail rather than a mystery.
And the question that had been sitting under all of this

`PRC-15` calls one of its tasks *“the single biggest reason worktrees are not free here”*: does each worktree need its own import cache, and can it have one? Worktree isolation is the top item on the process backlog, so this is the number that gates it.

It gets one automatically. Godot has **no** cache-location flag — checked against `--help` on the real binary, where the only relevant flags are `--path` and `--import` — and `--path <dir>` implies the cache inside that directory. **Isolation is by construction rather than by configuration**, which removes the whole LF-075 class of risk from worktree agents instead of mitigating it. The residual cost is one import and about 128 MB.
A requirement withdrawn

The same spec requires worktrees to live **outside** the main checkout, citing LF-051 — six false nomenclature hits off an agent worktree under `.claude/`. But LF-051 was fixed differently and better: the gate enumerates with `git ls-files`, so an untracked worktree is *structurally* invisible to it, and `.claude/worktrees/` is gitignored besides. Both verified directly.

So the requirement's reason is gone, and the `Agent` tool's native worktree isolation — which puts them exactly there — is fine. Withdrawn in place, with the reasoning recorded, because a spec is not append-only and a stale requirement is worse than a corrected one.

`PRC-15` stays open. The ownership manifest, its hook rule and the `ownership sane` check remain — though worktree isolation may make the manifest unnecessary, since its entire purpose was to referee a **shared** tree.

entries.title: Three refusals that look different
entries.summary: Free placement took away the slot tiles, and with them the entire visual language of where can I build. The board came back continuous with no indication of where a build would be accepted — and the refusal had quietly become three different reasons that one red ring could not tell apart. This is the ghost, the buildable wash, and the three pictures. It also retires the tile_slot sprite rather than repurposing it as the wash, which is the decision the issue asked for and which the sprite itself settles. The interesting part is the thing the first screenshot killed: a lane-standoff treatment that was correct, and unusable.

commits.subject: feat(ui): a ghost, a buildable wash, and three refusals that look different

body.text: `PLC-01` and `PLC-06` between them deleted the slot set — an emplacement now stands at a fractional position and legality is a **predicate over a continuous board** rather than membership in a list of authored tiles. That was the point, and it left three things blank at once: the board no longer painted where you could build, the hover ring could only say yes or no, and the refusal had become three distinct reasons wearing the same red.
The decision the issue asked for, and the sprite that settles it
`PLC-07` names an explicit fork: retire the `tile_slot` sprite, or repurpose it as the buildable-area wash. Looking at it answers it.

It is a **raised, bevelled pad with a teal ring and four corner bolts** — discrete geometry with real height, a hardpoint. Tiled across a region it reads as a *field of hardpoints*, which reinstates the exact “these are the slots” language this issue exists to remove. A wash has to be a tint, not an object. So: retired.

Removing the **asset** is filed separately (`LF-216`) and deliberately not bundled in. It triggers the art pipeline and a re-import — the step that blanks the owner's running game if mishandled — and a red `sprite atlas` in a UI pull request would read as a UI regression. One correction to the spec while passing: it says dropping the sprite makes `sprite coverage` fall to 21 of 26. It would not. That check compares enemy and tower ids only; `tile_slot` is a prop, so `asset coverage` is what governs it.
What a legal placement looks like now

body.caption: The armed emplacement drawn where it would stand, at 45% alpha, facing the lane it would watch — the same idle-heading rule a real emplacement uses, so moving the cursor across the lane turns the ghost. Under it, the footprint as a projected 2:1 ellipse at the real FOOTPRINT_RADIUS the rules test against, not an artistic radius: the player can see the shape the refusal is about. Amber for legal, and the amber reach ring showing what it would cover.

body.text: The screenshot that killed the first design
The lane-standoff refusal is supposed to show the keep-out corridor. The first version drew it for **every segment of every lane**, which is correct and completely unusable:

body.caption: Before. About forty full-length offset lines webbed across the whole board, crossing tiles nowhere near the lane. Every one of them is a true statement about the standoff geometry, and together they read as scratches on the lens.

body.text: The information a player needs is **local**: *which* piece of lane, and by how much. So it finds the nearest segment, draws its two offset edges over that segment alone, and runs a connector from the ghost to the nearest point on it — the measurement the rule actually made, drawn.

body.caption: After. Three lines instead of forty, and they point at the answer. The corridor reads as a corridor.

body.text: The other two

body.caption: Overlap outlines the emplacement actually collided with, at ITS own footprint — so the two circles that are too close are both on screen at once, rather than the player being told a number about a thing they cannot see.
Out of bounds outlines the board edge the footprint crosses. The refusal has a visible thing behind it instead of being an assertion about coordinates.

body.text: Reading the rule instead of copying it

The wash is bounds and lane standoff, never overlap — overlap depends on what is currently built, so folding it in would invalidate the cache the moment anything is placed, and it is also the wrong picture. The wash answers *“where does this weapon fit on this board at all”*, which is a property of the level; what is in the way right now is answered at the cursor.

And it gets that answer by reading `_placement_reason()`'s **fixed test order** rather than re-deriving two of its three tests: the function returns the first failure, so `OK` or `OVERLAP` coming back is proof that bounds and standoff both passed. A second, drifting copy of a rule is precisely what `PLC-02` exists to prevent.
A measurement that was wrong, and the fix

“I can barely see the wash” is not a measurement, so it got measured — by diffing a frame with a tower armed against one without. **Zero pixels differed**, which briefly looked like the wash was not drawing at all.

It was drawing. `anchor_view.gd:253` arms the first unlocked tower **at boot**, so there is no unarmed state and both frames had a ghost and a wash. The experiment had no control in it. Re-run properly, by A/B-ing the constant itself, the wash changes **235,333 pixels** and lifts ground from `(35,40,41)` to `(41,53,52)` — a consistent +13 on green. Subtle by design; it sits under every sprite on the board and must not compete with the emplacements standing on it.

Worth keeping the failure: the first instinct on a zero-diff was that the code was broken, and the actual fault was in the instrument. On a board with one lane the wash is also close to tautological — “everywhere except near the lane” — and it earns its place on the multi-lane theatre-scale boards it was designed for, not on `anchor-01`.
One refactor, proven inert

`_cull_band()` is lifted out of `_draw_board()` so the wash culls with exactly the same arithmetic instead of a second copy — two passes disagreeing about what is on screen shows up as a strip of tint hanging off the edge of the board at one zoom level. Proven a pure refactor the only way worth trusting: the frame afterwards is **byte-identical**, zero pixels changed.

entries.title: The instrument measured the wrong quantity
entries.summary: LF-185 said six anchors carry slots no amount of range can rescue, gave their coordinates, and said move them. It was right about the slots and wrong about why. They are not far from the lane — several of them sit on top of it. What they cover is lane the enemies never reach alive. This is the pass that found the coverage instrument does not predict its own dynamic tail, replaced the metric with presence-weighted coverage, re-sited 21 slots across six anchors, and cut whole-game near-zero emplacements from 12.71% to 9.53% — along with the four things it did not fix and the one cell it made worse.

body.text: `LF-185` was confident because the other lever had already been tried and had failed decisively. Sweeping `pulse-turret` range from 3.2 to 7.0 tiles — more than double what ships — left p10 emplacement coverage pinned at literal **0.0%** at every step, while p50 climbed from 28.0% to 44.5%. The median moves and the tail does not. That is what proved the tail was geometry rather than range, and it is the entry immediately before this one.
So `LF-185` named six anchors, listed the slots, and said move them. It was right that they need moving. It was wrong about **which** geometry was failing.
The instrument does not predict its own tail

`sim/coverage.py` exists because of the owner's play feedback in `LF-176` — that most emplacements can barely reach anything. Its geometric half, `lane_coverage()`, answers exactly the question that complaint asks: what fraction of the lane's length falls inside this slot's range. `LF-185` assumed the named slots scored badly on it. They do not.

The slot with 17% geometric coverage is doing three times the work of the slot with 44%. Two implementations of one idea — the geometric ceiling and the simulated result — disagree, and the disagreement is not noise, it is inverted.
Where along the lane the coverage sits

The missing variable is *where* on the lane the covered arc falls. Measured over 20 policies × 3 difficulties, in live-unit-ticks per 5% of lane length: on these six anchors **half of all live unit time falls in the first 20–25% of the lane**, and the final quarter holds 4–5% of it. Kill-position p50 on the bad anchors is 22–47% of lane length — the wave is dead well before the halfway mark.

The contrast is anchor-20, one of the healthiest boards in the game at a 3.8% near-zero rate. Its profile is flat: half the presence is spent by 45% of the lane, and 11% of it is still in the final quarter.

**A gun covering lane the enemies never reach alive is idle no matter how close to the path it sits or how long its range.** That one sentence explains why doubling range did nothing, and it is a better statement of the owner's original complaint than the complaint was.

So the working metric for this pass became **presence-weighted coverage**: the share of live unit-ticks that fall inside a slot's range, rather than the share of lane length. The slots `LF-185` named score 2.2–26.9% on it.
What changed

21 slots re-sited across `data/anchors/anchor-{02,08,10,11,12,13}.json`. Slot arrays only; slot counts unchanged; no other key in any of the six files differs. One rule, applied identically to all six: **the legal integer position nearest the authored slot whose presence-weighted coverage is at least 42%, with a 2.0-tile dispersion floor** — the target relaxed in 2-point steps where 2.0-tile separation made 42% unreachable.

Two alternative rules were measured on the dynamic instrument rather than argued about: take the global presence maximum, and take the nearest position clearing 30%. Both were worse or equal on 4 of the 6 anchors.
A few rows are worth showing because of the column that goes the wrong way. `geo` is `lane_coverage()`; `live` is presence-weighted.
**The `geo` column falls on 7 of the 21 moves.** The old instrument would have scored a third of this change as a regression.
The numbers

Per anchor, all three difficulties, all 20 policies. The range digest was `8189779cd568` on both the before and after runs, so the verdict labels are comparable across them — `LF-186` is the entry that records why that has to be checked rather than assumed.
The other 18 anchors are **byte-identical** before and after. Across the whole game:

`sim/run.py` reports **24/24 anchors clean**; all six re-sited anchors grade `ok=True` before and after, and no untouched anchor's grade changed. Distinct viable builds went *up* on anchors 10, 11, 12 and 13, and on anchor-08 standard.

Legality was checked against the real engine rather than reasoned about. `Sim._placement_reason()` was called on every slot of **all 24** anchors, each with every other slot of that anchor loaded as a `Placed` — the strictest reading of the overlap term. Zero illegal slots. The minimum pairwise separation anywhere in the game is 1.0 tiles, on anchor-20, which this pass did not touch; every newly authored slot is at least 2.0 tiles from its neighbours.
Four things this pass did not fix

**1. `LF-185`'s own claim about `pulse-turret` did not reproduce.** It recorded pulse-turret as 66–79% of every near-zero sample. Measured on the *pre-change* data at today's ranges, it is **85.4%** — and after the change it is 84.3%, so the share did not fall. Its own near-zero rate dropped by a quarter, but it still dominates the tail, because the autobuild fills every leftover slot with it. That is `LF-053` and `LF-072`, untouched here.

**2. The tail migrated rather than vanishing.** After the change, anchor-11 (2,8) is near-zero in 45 of 51 samples and anchor-13 (10,4) in 34 of 57 — slots that were fine before. Killing units earlier steepens the presence profile, which strands the next rank back. Chasing near-zero to zero converges on every slot stacked at the lane entrance, which is fitting to the metric — decision 067's trap, by name. The pass stopped at the 21 slots `LF-185` named rather than chasing it.

**3. anchor-02 brutal lost two distinct winning builds, 6 down to 4.** Still clean, still four, death wave unchanged at 2 — and it is the only one of eighteen anchor-by-difficulty cells that narrowed. Filed as `LF-220` so it is not later rediscovered as an unexplained narrowing with no cause attached.

**4. The brief told the agent slots may be continuous floats now. They may not.** `data/schema/anchor.schema.json` still types slot coordinates as `integer`, even though `sim/content.py` loads them as float64 and `_placement_reason()` accepts any float. The search was therefore integer-only, and may have left better sub-tile positions unreachable. `LF-219`.
And the residual is not a siting problem

Act 3 already sits at 5% near-zero with a flat presence profile. Acts 1 and 2 sit at 16% and 11% with profiles that dump half the live time into the first fifth of the lane. Slot re-siting can move guns into the live zone; it cannot lengthen the live zone. The lever for the rest is enemy durability and spawn pressure in the act 1–2 wave tables — `BAL-04` territory, out of scope here, and it would move the grades.
Filed out of this

items: `LF-185` closed.

`LF-217` — the coverage instrument's geometric half does not predict its own dynamic tail, and `verdict()`'s label *(a) geometry: even 2x range does not recover coverage — slots are far from the lane* is the wrong sentence for the failure it fires on.
`LF-218` — the act 1–2 presence profile is the residual tail.
`LF-219` — the schema types slot coordinates as integer.
`LF-220` — anchor-02 brutal narrowed from six distinct winning builds to four.

body.text: The habit worth naming

This project built an instrument specifically to answer the owner's complaint, used it, and then found the instrument was measuring the wrong quantity — not by argument, but because the numbers it produced did not correlate with the numbers the simulation produced.

The fix was found by distrusting the instrument. That is the same move as `PLC-07`'s *the fault was in the instrument, not the code*, and the same move as `LF-201`'s *it reported a destruction it was incapable of performing*. Three times now, on unrelated work. It is becoming this project's most reliable debugging habit and it is worth naming.

The work landed on `lf/bal-slot-resiting` and was gated at tier 4. This entry states no verdict for that run — it was still in flight when this was written, and a gate result written before the gate finishes is exactly the kind of claim this journal exists to not make.

entries.title: The test of the instrument was red, and no tier ran it
entries.summary: The entry before this one proved the coverage instrument's geometric half does not predict which emplacements actually work. This is the repair: presence-weighted coverage becomes the predictor, `lane_coverage()` stays as a measurement because it is still a true statement about a level, and rank correlation against measured uptime goes from +0.520 to +0.748 across the whole game — +0.622 to +0.780 on the eighteen anchors last week's pass never touched, which is the number that is not circular. Underneath it was something worse: `sim/coverage.py --selftest`, the only runtime proof that the instrumented sim cannot change an outcome, had been failing on `main` for at least two merges, because no gate tier runs it.

body.text: The previous entry, an hour old as this is written, ended on a diagnosis: `sim/coverage.py`'s geometric `lane_coverage()` does not predict its own dynamic tail, and the slot with 17% geometric coverage was doing three times the work of the slot with 44%. That entry re-sited 21 slots on the strength of a scratch implementation of presence-weighted coverage. This one makes the replacement real, quantifies how much better it is, and finds that the test which guards the whole instrument had been red the entire time.

`lane_coverage()` is **kept**, not deleted. It answers a true question about a level — what fraction of the lane's length falls inside a slot's range — and that question deserves an honest answer. What changed is that it is no longer the thing the summary and the verdict label are computed from.
The metric now correlates
Spearman rank correlation of each metric against measured mean `uptime_combat`, one sample per (slot, tower) pair, over 20 policies × 3 difficulties.

**The 18-anchor row is the one that matters.** The six re-sited anchors were optimised against presence last week, so a gain measured on them could be circular — the metric scoring well on the boards it authored. It holds on the eighteen that were never touched, and that is what makes it a real result rather than a tautology.

Within-anchor ordering — which is the question `PLC-04`'s candidate lattice actually asks, since it never compares a slot on one board against a slot on another — went from **mean rho +0.442 to +0.773**. And `lane_coverage()` is outright **negative** on three anchors: anchor-02 at −0.301, anchor-10 at −0.244, anchor-13 at −0.019. On those boards it orders their own slots backwards. Presence-weighted coverage is positive on all 24.
The four inversion rows, recomputed

Two of the four slots the previous entry used to make its case — anchor-13 (6,0) and anchor-10 (7,13) — **no longer exist**. `5021a9e` deleted them, which was the point of that pass. They were restored into an in-memory copy of each anchor so that all four could be measured identically under today's code. That detail is what makes these numbers reproducible a year from now, and it is why the uptime figures differ slightly from the ones published an hour ago.

`lane_coverage()` ranks those four 36.8 > 43.9 > 36.9 > 17.1, against a true order of 54.0 > 23.5 > 0.6 > 0.4. **It is inverted at both ends** — it calls the best slot the worst and the worst slot the second best. Presence gets the order right.

One more, straight out of the shipped `--detail` output: anchor-10 `(11,9)` has **the highest lane coverage on the whole anchor at 71.7%**, and 29.2% presence. The single most attractive position on that board by the old instrument is a third-rate one by the new.
verdict() was calling the best-sited anchor in the game badly sited
The label `verdict()` printed for **anchor-01** — 83% median uptime, a 5% near-zero tail, the healthiest board there is — was this:
(a) geometry: even 2x range does not recover coverage — slots are far from the lane.
body.attribution: verdict(), on anchor-01, before this pass

body.text: The new labels compare an anchor's authored slots against **its own board's ceiling**: the median of the N best legal positions, where N is that anchor's own slot count, and legality comes from the engine's own `_placement_reason()` rather than from a re-derivation of the rule. Median-of-N against median-of-N, so no absolute presence threshold is needed — which matters, because presence share is not calibrated to uptime and a fixed cut on it would not be defensible.
Four outcomes, and they land where the evidence already was:

items: **no material near-zero tail** — 12 anchors, including anchor-01, which needed no diagnosis at all.

**(b) range/waves** — anchors 02–05, the four lowest board ceilings in the game. `LF-187` independently says decision 074's range numbers must be re-derived; this arrives at the same four boards from a different direction.
**(a) siting** — anchors 06, 07, 09 and 11. Slots that a better position on the same board would fix.
**(c) not geometry** — anchors 08, 10 and 13, which is exactly `LF-218`'s finding: re-siting moves guns into the live zone but cannot lengthen the live zone.

body.text: The worse thing underneath

`sim/coverage.py --selftest` is the **only** runtime proof that `InstrumentedSim` cannot change an `Outcome`. It runs the same (anchor, policy, difficulty) through both `Sim` and `InstrumentedSim` and asserts the results are field-for-field identical. Without it, a rules change in an unrelated workstream can silently invalidate every coverage measurement this project takes.
It was **failing on `main`**, and had been for at least two merges, because **no gate tier runs it**. Nothing was red anywhere. Nothing could be.

The mechanism is almost funny. The selftest builds a probe at `(500,500)` to prove that a slot with zero coverage measures zero. `PLC-02` gave the engine a real legality predicate, which started answering `out_of_bounds` for that position — so the scheduled build silently stopped landing, and the check failed with “the scheduled build never landed”: a message about the harness, not about coverage. A metric assertion that had quietly become a harness assertion.

Proved rather than assumed, by running `git show HEAD:sim/coverage.py` in isolation, which printed `HEAD placed slots: []`. Fixed by widening the in-memory probe anchor to 40×40 and moving the probe to (30,30) — still exactly zero coverage at the longest range in the game — and no file under `data/` was touched. Filed as `LF-221`, where **the bug is fixed and the gap is the item**: the selftest is about 2m43s in full, tier 2 is already over its own budget (`LF-178`), so it needs either tier 3/4 or a cheap single-anchor outcome-parity variant at tier 2.
The new assertions were proved red first
House style here, and it was actually done rather than claimed — by injecting bugs into an in-memory copy and confirming each new assertion fires:
FAIL presence bucket independence: worst |200 buckets − 800 buckets| is 0.0519 (tolerance 0.0200)
body.attribution: with BUG B injected — 800 buckets served at 25

body.text: FAIL presence share bounds: … whole board -> 52.095 (want exactly 1.0)
body.attribution: with BUG A (wrong normaliser) and BUG B injected

body.text: The refusal that was licensed and did not apply

The brief explicitly offered an out: if the presence profile turned out to be policy-dependent enough that a single pooled profile per anchor was meaningless, say so and do not ship. That out was **measured rather than taken**. Each of the 60 (policy, difficulty) cells was scored against its **own** profile and against the **pooled** one, mean within-cell rank correlation over 6 anchors:

Pooling costs 0.037 of a 0.378 gain — it captures about **96% of what a per-cell oracle would buy**. The refusal was licensed and did not apply, which is only worth knowing because it was checked instead of assumed.

But the per-run spread is real and wide: the worst slot swings **83.6 percentage points** across runs on anchor-02. So it is **reported rather than averaged away** — `per_run_min`, `per_run_max` and `per_run_std` on every record, and a `per-run lo..hi` column in `--detail`. A mean that hides an 83-point spread is the same class of error as the metric this entry replaces.
Cost, and the gate

**+6.3% to +9.8% wall clock**; a full 24-anchor run is 2m11s at `--jobs 8`. There is no new simulation — the presence profile is accumulated by the same walk that already computes uptime. One file changed: `sim/coverage.py`, **589 → 1008 lines**. No engine change, no data change, no game value moved.

The gate ran at tier 4: **38 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped**. The two skips are `rules parity` and `rules parity (windows)`, skipped by the content-hash cache because digest `f3e5a7b01020` had been verified fresh 40 minutes earlier against an identical set of rule and data files. That is **cached, not re-run, and a skip is not a pass** — said that way on purpose, in an entry that is entirely about instruments reporting something other than what they measure. `sim determinism` passed on this run.
Caveats that belong on the record

items: **The letter is a pointer to a column, not a result.** The classification is coarse at the boundary — anchor-11 at 0.72 and anchor-08 at 0.78 read as different letters two points apart. The docstring says so, so a reader of the tool learns it at the same time as a reader of this entry.

**The label is now relative to two things**, not one: `range_basis.digest` (`LF-186`) **and** the slot layout, because presence is measured on the authored board. `lane_coverage()` only ever needed the first caveat. A verdict computed before a re-siting pass is not comparable with one computed after — including, specifically, the verdicts in the entry before this one.
**Presence share is still not calibrated to uptime.** It predicts ordering well and says nothing reliable about magnitude, which is why every threshold in the new `verdict()` is relative.

body.text: Three times now

Two entries in a row where the fault was in the instrument rather than in the code. The previous one found the metric measuring the wrong quantity; this one found that the **test** of that metric had been failing unnoticed, because nothing ran it.

That is the same move as `PLC-07`'s **the fault was in the instrument, not the code**, and the same move as `LF-201`'s **it reported a destruction it was incapable of performing**. The habit is not scepticism about the code. It is scepticism about the thing doing the measuring, and it has now paid three times on unrelated work.

What this leaves for `PLC-04`, the next workstream: a public API of `presence_coverage()`, `bucket_points()`, `legal_positions()` and `board_presence_ceiling()`. The last of those is already the argmax over the candidate lattice `PLC-04` needs, so that work starts with its search function written and measured.

The work sits on `lf/bal-presence-coverage` and was not yet committed when this entry was written, so no commit hash is listed — the same call as last time, and for the same reason: a hash written before the commit exists is a claim this journal has no business making.

entries.title: The acceptance criterion was not a selector
entries.summary: `PLC-04` gives the grader a candidate lattice at ½-tile pitch, so it can finally stand a gun where no level author put a slot — `PLC-01` made placement continuous for the player months ago and the grader had been reasoning about a board the game no longer has. The ordering took five attempts, and the thing that decided it was not the grade table: the best-scoring candidate produced the worst board, and a different set of anchors failed under every ordering. So `PLC-04`'s own acceptance criterion — “every anchor still grades `ok`” — was withdrawn as a bar. Four anchors merge knowingly below it. Underneath, the one gate check that did fire named the wrong subsystem and said nothing at all.

commits.subject: feat(grader): a candidate lattice, and the grade table could not choose its ordering

body.text: `PLC-04` is the last open item in E3 Placement, and what it removes is `_slot_priority()` — the function that ranked an anchor's **authored slots** by distance to the path and handed them to the grader in that order. In its place is a deterministic candidate lattice at ½-tile pitch: the grader can now stand a gun anywhere the rules allow, including where no level author ever put a slot. `PLC-01` made placement continuous for the **player** months ago. The grader had been reasoning about a board the game no longer has ever since.

The lattice is built once per `Anchor`, filtered through `PLC-02`'s own `_placement_reason()` using the largest footprint in `data/towers.json`, and sorted once. `_try_build` consumes from an index and contains no sort at all. It is mirrored into `scripts/test/parity.gd`, which is what the 1,440-run parity gate drives — two independent implementations that have to pick the same candidate at the same step, every step.
The story is the ordering, and it took five attempts

The spec named the ordering: sort by `(d2_to_path, x, y)`, consume greedily from the front. **It is degenerate.** Every anchor's lanes are axis-aligned, so `d2_to_path` ties *exactly* across the entire band parallel to a lane — and the secondary key ends up doing all the work. `(x, y)` turns into a raster sweep.

Measured on all 24 anchors: the graded build collapsed into a **3–4 tile column at the board's left edge**, against authored slots that spanned 12–16 tiles. anchor-09 put twelve emplacements in a 4×10 block on a board whose second lane runs down `x=15` — never defending that lane at all — and went from 9/6/4 winning builds to **0/0/0**.

rows: all twelve in a 3–4 tile column, lane 1 undefended
spread along one path, the other lane favoured
lanes split 8/4, each packed at its own head

body.text: **Adopted: round-robin across lanes for whose turn it is; within a lane, the candidate whose arclength is farthest from every emplacement already on that lane.** Two orthogonal defects, and each fix does nothing whatsoever for the other:

items: **Lane-blindness**, cured only by round-robin — the one mechanism in the five that can express *“this lane has no guns on it”*.

**Front-loading**, which round-robin does not touch, because **any total order consumed greedily from the front packs at the front**. `(x, y)` packed at the board corner; arclength packed at the lane head. The same defect wearing a different axis.

body.text: Composed, anchor-09's twelve now sit on lane 0 at arclengths 0, 4.5, 9, 13.5, 18, 22.5, 27 and 36 of 37, and on lane 1 at 0, 3.5, 7 and 14 of 14. Eight guns and four.
The grade count did not choose it, and could not have

This is the part worth writing down. Minimum separation at 2.5 tiles scores **23/24**, the best of the five, while producing boards nobody would defend. The adopted ordering scores **20/24** while producing the only board of the five that is indistinguishable in shape from a hand-authored layout. Across five structurally different orderings, a *different set of anchors* failed each time, and the best-scoring candidate produced the worst board.

That is the signature of grades **co-tuned with the thing being replaced** — the 24 clean grades were swept against a grader confined to the authored slots — rather than of a better sort key waiting to be found. So `PLC-04`'s acceptance criterion 6, *“every anchor still grades `ok`”*, was **withdrawn as a bar for this issue**. Decision **081** records the withdrawal with all five candidates and their boards.

**This merges as a knowing regression, and it is not a footnote.** Four anchors go in below `ok`: anchor-01 (brutal unwinnable), anchor-04 (brutal single-solution), anchor-09 (brutal single-solution), anchor-11 (hard single-solution plus brutal unwinnable). Three of the four are brutal-only and all four boards are well shaped, which is the whole argument for shipping it — a grader that places well finds those tiers genuinely thin at the top difficulty. `LF-223` re-sweeps them and is the next workstream.
What was rejected

**Ordering the lattice by presence-weighted coverage** — despite the entry published an hour earlier proving that presence predicts real emplacement uptime far better than distance to the lane does, rank correlation **+0.748 against +0.520**. Two independent reasons, either sufficient. It is **circular**: the presence profile comes from running the sim, which depends on where things were built. And it **cannot be mirrored**: decision 078 restricts these two files to operations byte-identical across MSVC UCRT and CPython/Linux, and a coverage-weighted key is not one. There is an irony here worth exactly one sentence — the better metric, proven better sixty minutes earlier, is structurally unavailable to the thing that most wants it.

**The minimum-separation constant**, despite scoring highest of the five. It is a tolerance widened until the number came out right; it is **non-monotone in its own parameter** (2.5 gives 23/24, 3.0 gives 21/24); it fails on a different set of anchors at every value; and it never rescued anchor-09 at any setting.
The numbers

items: **Parity: 1,440 runs identical across both engines, first try.** anchor-09 — the two-lane case that would break first if lane assignment or the maximin tie-break disagreed — was checked alone beforehand: 60 runs identical.
Sharded parity **923,874 ms**, against 877,233 ms on `5021a9e` (+5.3%) and 832,967 ms for the spec-literal forward index (+10.9%). That is **71% of the 1,300,000 ms bar**.
The cost was **attributed rather than assumed**: anchor-01 wins *fewer* runs now and still costs 22% more, so it is the per-lane scan, not longer-surviving runs.
The Python grading leg is still **4.9% faster than HEAD** — the lattice is a net win and the scan gives part of it back.
`sim.run --jobs 8` against `--jobs 1`: empty diff, no order dependence.
Lattice built once per `Sim`: 60 constructions on one anchor collapse to 1 build.
`_try_build` is sort-free in both engines, verified by an AST walk rather than by reading it.

body.text: The tie-break, because a max-over-min has ties by construction

Two candidates equidistant either side of a gap tie exactly, and `LF-055` is the precedent where exactly that made the two engines disagree only when a wave happened to produce a tie. So the scan accepts only a **strict** improvement: the first index in the lane group wins, and that array is in ascending lattice order, which means ties resolve on the full `(d2, arclength, x, y)` tuple. Nothing leans on iteration order, and nothing leans on `sort_custom` being stable — GDScript does not guarantee that. `abs()` is written out as an explicit `if d < 0.0: d = -d` in both files so the arithmetic stays comparisons and `+ - *` only.
The second bug, found by being the first thing to fail

`sim determinism` — a gate check — returned `FAIL` on `sim/run.py`'s **exit code**, *before* comparing its two runs against each other. And `run.py --json` exits 1 whenever any anchor is not clean. So the moment the lattice made anchor-01 fail at brutal, the gate announced **“the sim is not deterministic”** — naming the wrong subsystem entirely — with `a.stderr` as its message, which is **empty**, because `run.py` writes its verdict to stdout. A red check, the wrong subsystem, and nothing after the check name. The two runs had been byte-identical the whole time.

Now: a crash with no output to compare is still fatal and is caught first; genuine divergence still fails; a non-zero exit on identical output is **reported** rather than raised. All four branches were proved red-or-green **by injection** before the check was trusted — house style here, and this is the case it exists for.

`LF-224` records what the fix removes: **nothing in the gate asserts that every anchor grades `ok`.** The conflation had been serving that role accidentally, under the wrong name, with an empty message. The real check must not be added until `LF-223` lands — a check that is red on arrival gets disabled rather than fixed.
Two more lines that belong on the record

items: `_slot_priority()` is **retained**, solely for `tools/analysis_lf014.py`, which reproduces the measurement decision **022** rests on. Repointing it at the lattice would move numbers a settled decision cites.

`LF-222` records that the lattice **enlarges** `LF-053`/`LF-095` rather than solving it. Every `Policy` is a total preference order and `_try_build` fills greedily, so a graded build is all-of-one-thing. With 12 slots that read as “twelve arc nodes”; with hundreds of candidates it is “as many as the cap and the money allow”. `BAL-02` is the fix, and this must not be read as one.

body.text: Gate, and what this entry does not have

The work sits on `lf/plc-candidate-lattice` at `e1896da` and is gated at **tier 4**, which was still running as this was written — so no verdict is stated here. Faithful reporting means the result goes in the entry that has it, not this one. There are also **no screenshots**: this is grader-side work, it changes no pixel, and no frame was captured. An invented one would be worse than none.
Three entries, and the same thing was wrong in all of them

The first of the three found that the metric was measuring the wrong quantity. The second found that the **test** of that metric had been failing unnoticed, because no tier ran it. This one found that the **acceptance criterion** was not a valid selector — and that the one gate check which did fire named the wrong subsystem with an empty message.

The thread is not “we found bugs”. In all three, the thing that was wrong was an **instrument** — not the game. The metric, then the test of the metric, then the bar the work was to be judged against and the check that announced the failure. None of them was a defect in what the player runs.

That is the same move as `PLC-07`'s **the fault was in the instrument, not the code**, and the same move as `LF-201`'s **it reported a destruction it was incapable of performing**, both already in this journal. The habit that keeps paying is not scepticism about the code. It is scepticism about the thing doing the measuring, and about the number it hands you — including, and especially, when that number is green.

entries.title: Four anchors, four different levers, and the one capacity that moved went down
entries.summary: `LF-223` is the re-balance the previous entry promised. `PLC-04`'s candidate lattice places better than the grader it replaced, and that exposed four anchors whose tiers had been tuned against a grader confined to the authored slots — anchor-01 unwinnable at brutal, anchor-04 and anchor-09 single-solution, anchor-11 both. All four are clean now, and the game is 24/24. Four anchors needed four different levers: a wave's arrival rate, a reactor capacity that was an exact multiple of a tower cost, a flank lane carrying 1.6% of the fight and a third of the guns, and an emplacement count that had quietly become the currency instead of power. The one capacity that moved went down.

body.text: The entry immediately before this one — **The acceptance criterion was not a selector**, `the-acceptance-criterion-was-not-a-selector`, merged as **#142** — shipped `PLC-04`'s candidate lattice and knowingly merged four anchors below the bar it had withdrawn. anchor-01 unwinnable at brutal; anchor-04 and anchor-09 single-solution at brutal; anchor-11 single-solution at hard and unwinnable at brutal. It named `LF-223` as the promised re-balance. This is `LF-223`.

The lattice grader places **better** than the one it replaced, and that is the whole reason those four went red. Their tiers had been tuned against a grader confined to each anchor's authored slots. Give the grader the board the player actually has and the tuning stops holding.
The result

**24 of 24 anchors clean.** Four anchors, **four different levers**, and the one reactor capacity that moved went **down**. The other twenty anchors are byte-identical in win counts, distinct builds, peak load, brownout and death wave — nothing was nudged sideways to make a neighbour work.

headers: before → after (wins, distinct builds) std / hard / brutal

body.text: anchor-01 — the wave table's arrival rate, capacity untouched

Five pulse turrets **is** the 60 MW bus — 5 × 12 — so anchor-01's damage ceiling is a fixed 60 dps and always will be. A brutal warden drone is 40 × 1.55 = 62 hp, which makes the maximum sustainable arrival 0.97 units/s: one per 1.03 s. The authored waves 4, 5 and 6 arrived at 1.00 / 0.90 / **0.80 s**. The terminal wave was demanding 77.5 hp/s from a bus that can supply 60 — **29% above the anchor's own ceiling**. The level had only ever survived on wave *length*, never on rate.

The discriminating measurement is the good part. **`lead_in` × 1.5 leaves brutal at zero winning builds; `interval` × 1.05 fixes it.** More time *between waves* does nothing, because nothing about the ceiling is a warm-up problem; more time between *units* is the whole thing. Money is inert too — the build is capacity-capped at five guns whatever the funds — and `max_emplacements` is inert at every value from 8 to 16.

So the intervals went to 1.05 / 0.95 / 0.90. **98 units in, 98 units out**; counts, capacity, funds and lives all untouched. Wave 6's interval is the entire knob and it is monotone: 0.80 unwinnable, 0.85 → 3 lives left, 0.90 → 6, 0.95 → 10. Chose 0.90 — margin without erasing the leak.
anchor-04 — reactor capacity, reduced 96 → 94

`96 = 8 × 12` **exactly**, so every greedy policy filled to the same eight pulse turrets and the build space collapsed to one board. 92, 93, 94 and 95 are green in **45 of 45** cells; 96 is the first bad value. That is a structural reason rather than a fitted one, which is why it survived when everything else was ruled out.

Everything else was ruled out **by measurement**. Starting funds is a **razor, not a gradient** — 480 ✗, 500 ✗, 520 ✓, 540 ✓, 560 ✓, 580 ✓, 600 ✗, 620 ✗, 640 ✗ — and picking a green cell out of that is choosing a fitted constant, not a design. No wave-rate variant of ten tried moved brutal off a single build. Lives from 10 to 22 produced no clean cell at all. `max_emplacements` from 8 to 16 had no effect whatsoever.

**The one capacity move tightens the power budget rather than loosening it.** anchor-04's brutal winners now run at 94–98% of capacity at peak and 91–96% at the *mean* — the bus sits near the line for most of the level, which is what the power currency is for.
anchor-09 — the wave table's lane allocation, and the instrument that found it

Capacity and funds untouched; total units unchanged at 160. What was wrong was **where** they arrived. `sim/coverage.py`'s presence metric — the one shipped two entries ago — was decisive here: the flank lane carried **14 of 160 units and 1.6% of all live unit-ticks**, while `PLC-04`'s lane round-robin correctly garrisons that lane with **4 of 12 emplacements**. A third of the board defending 1.6% of the fight.

Capacity is genuinely inert on this anchor: **zero clean cells across capacity 155–180 × funds 820–980**. No amount of power fixes a board where a third of the guns have nothing to shoot at. Sixteen pickets moved onto the flank instead — **130/30 rather than 146/14**, the same 160 units, the same hit points, the same leak budget — and flank presence went **1.6% → 4.9%**. Green in 15 of 15 cells.

That is worth saying plainly: **an instrument built three entries ago to answer a different question is what identified this anchor's actual defect.** It was built to explain why emplacements sit idle. It found a wave table that had allocated its units to a lane nobody fights in.
anchor-11 — an emplacement cap, and the currency was not power

Every cheap policy stopped at exactly **10 emplacements — `len(slots)` — for 120 MW of a 200 MW bus.** The *emplacement count* was the currency and power was inert; only builds expensive per slot could reach the bus at all, which is exactly why hard had one answer and only one. Capacity confirmed inert at 185, 190, 195, 200 and 205.

The lever is `max_emplacements: 13`, and it is monotone in its own parameter — 10 ✗, 11 ✗, 12 ✗, **13 ✓**, 14 ✓, 15 ✓, 16 ✓ — and green at every capacity from 185 to 205. Funds is a razor here as well (1210 ✗, 1240 ✓, 1270 ✗) and was rejected on the same grounds as anchor-04's.

Board saturation falls **42% → 32%**, which puts anchor-11 in line with anchor-09 at 30% and anchor-10 at 33% instead of being the act-2 outlier. Note the direction: **lower saturation means the bus covers less of a full board, so that is more power pressure, not less.**
Nothing was bought with power, and here is the number that proves it

The standing rule is that density is never paid for with reactor capacity. `docs/STATE.md` records what that failure looks like: anchor-24 once reaching 103% of board saturation, with the power decision having stopped existing on five levels. So the load figures are the acceptance evidence, not a footnote.

Grade-level peak ratios stayed at or above 130% on all four. No anchor gained slack. All four are money-bound at t=0, so power bites later, as designed. The capacity ladder stayed monotone — 60, 80, 92, **94**, 100, 104, 106, 110 | 170, 190, 200, 200, 250, 250, 260, 260 | 290 × 8 — and only anchor-04 moved, downward, forcing no other anchor.

Density moved the way it should: anchor-01 peak on screen 28 → 25, anchor-09 28 → 26, anchor-04 every column identical, anchor-11 saturation 42% → 32%. Units per wave, leak, hit points per wave and drain are unchanged everywhere.
The design position that was chosen rather than tuned away

**anchor-01 brutal is now single-solution — nine winning policies, one distinct build — and that is correct.** anchor-01 unlocks one emplacement type and its 60 MW bus is exactly five of them, so the entire build space contains five boards and only the maximal one survives 1.55× hit points. `tutorial: true` already waives the single-solution rule for precisely this reason.

The alternative was raising capacity to 72 for a sixth turret. That is a **20% power increase on the tutorial**, which would make the level easier at all three difficulties in order to fix a label the grader does not even apply to it. Refused.
Two gaps found on the way, both filed

**`tools/say_capacity.py` rewrites the spoken capacity and cannot see the second reference.** Its regex is anchored on the word “megawatts”, so anchor-04's brief was rewritten to ninety-four and still read:
Anchor fourteen. Ninety-four megawatts. Shield wall's signed off — forty of those **ninety-six** if you raise it.

The `dialog capacity` gate check stayed **green** throughout, because what it checks is the *spoken* figure and the spoken figure was right. Fixed by hand in this branch; `LF-225` carries the gap. It is the same shape as the `chronicle.py --check` failure already recorded in this journal: **a check that verifies output matches input cannot see a generator that is wrong in a stable, reproducible way.**

**anchor-11 is now the first shipped anchor where `max_emplacements` exceeds `len(slots)`.** That newly exercises a Godot-side autobuild fallback written for exactly that case and never entered by any shipped anchor until now. `rules parity` is verified clean on anchor-11 — 60 of 60 runs identical, `--no-cache` — so the rules half is proven. The *autobuild* fallback is not, because no scenario uses anchor-11. `LF-226`.

That is the same hole `firing arcs agree` exists to plug, and it is worth restating every time it turns up: **a gate that runs the whole game proves nothing about a branch the shipped data never enters.**
What this entry does not have

The work sits on `lf/bal-relattice-rebalance` and is uncommitted as this is written, so there are no commit hashes here. A tier-4 gate is in flight and **no verdict is stated** — the result belongs in the entry that has it. There are also no screenshots, and this time the reason is worth one line: the change is **four JSON files**. The entry is numeric because there is no frame to show, and an invented one would be worse than none.
Four entries, and the shape reverses at the end

The three entries before this one each found the fault in an **instrument**: the metric, then the test of the metric, then the acceptance criterion the work was to be judged against. None of them was a defect in what the player runs.

This one used those repaired instruments to find four **real** defects in the game. A tutorial wave arriving 29% faster than its own bus could ever answer. A capacity that was an exact multiple of a tower cost and so collapsed the build space to a single board. A flank lane carrying 1.6% of the fight and a third of the guns. An anchor where the emplacement count had quietly become the currency instead of power.
None of those four was visible before, and each needed a different lever. **That is what the three instrument entries were for.**

entries.title: The generator was not the deliverable. Thirteen tiles was.
entries.summary: `LF-080` builds `tools/genboard.py`, the large-board layout generator that decision 073's 48×48 target needs before any 48² content can exist — shipped anchors are 12–18 by 10–15, and hand-authoring a four-lane 48² theatre is not viable. Every budget it emits is a shipped-content ratio re-measured off `data/anchors/` at run time, not a constant somebody typed. But the tool is not the point. Run the repaired coverage instrument over its output and the top weapon needs about 13 tiles of range to cover the same fraction of a 48² lane it covers on a shipped board today — a number a whole balance epic can start from. Also here: a blocking discovery bug proved rather than described, and an instrument that fooled itself one entry after being repaired.

body.text: The previous entry — **Four anchors, four different levers**, `four-anchors-four-different-levers`, merged as **#143** — closed `LF-223` and put the game at 24 of 24 anchors clean. It ended by observing that the three entries before it had each found a fault in an **instrument**, and that it had then used those repaired instruments to find four real defects. This entry does the same thing to a board that does not exist yet.

`LF-080` — THEATRE SCALE 05 — is **the large-board layout generator**, `tools/genboard.py`. Decision **073** set the board target to 48×48. Shipped anchors are 12–18 wide by 10–15 tall. Hand-authoring a four-lane 48² anchor with a converging funnel and 78 sited emplacement slots is not viable, so the generator had to exist before the content could.
What it emits, shown rather than described

This is the first entry in five with something visual in it, and the reason the other four had none is that they changed JSON files and measured them. `--preview` renders the board as ASCII and writes nothing — the same preview-first method `tools/densify.py` uses. The default configuration, captured for this entry:

body.caption: `.venv/bin/python tools/genboard.py --preview`, default configuration, verbatim. The digit is the lane index — four lanes, `0` through `3`, laid in disjoint horizontal bands with buildable gutters between them and serpentining inside each band. `#` is a tile shared by more than one lane, which is what the converging funnel at `x=40` is made of. `o` is an emplacement slot, `S` a spawn point, `K` the keep at (44,24). The gutters are the point: every dot is buildable ground, and there is a great deal of it.

body.text: The full 48×48 grid is 52 characters wide including its row labels, which fits this page's column without scrolling — so it is shown at full size rather than reduced to a smaller `--lanes` configuration. The identity and budget block `--preview` prints underneath it has one line — the weapon-range summary, 118 characters — that is wider than the column, and it scrolls sideways rather than wrapping:

anchor-25  Generated 48x48 theatre, 4 lanes  ·  act 3
  grid            48x48 = 2304 tiles
  lanes           4  lengths 80 68 74 73  total 295  union 272 tiles
  spawn points    4  (2, 0) (0, 14) (0, 26) (8, 47)
  slots           78  (3.5 lane tiles each)
  capacity        1872 MW  = 50% of board saturation (78 x 48 MW)
  funds / lives   21917  /  244
  capacity decay  68.6 MW per wave
  unlocked        9 emplacements at id 'anchor-25' (unlocks follow the ID, not --act)
  weapon range    3.8-7.0 tiles  → one emplacement at max range covers 4.7% of the lane set, 17.5% of its longest lane

  wave  units  leak       hp   drain  per-lane
     1     39    55     5465     176  10 10 10 9
     2     51    67     6570     224  13 13 13 12
     3     63    83     8005     272  16 16 16 15
     4     74    94     8850     304  19 19 18 18
     5     86   108    10060     348  22 22 21 21
     6     98   122    11390     400  25 25 24 24
     7    110   140    13410     468  28 28 27 27
     8    122   160    15420     524  31 31 30 30
     9    134   174    16750     576  34 34 33 33
    10    146   186    17740     616  37 37 36 36
   tot    923  1189   lives 244 = 20.5% leak budget
body.caption: The same run's summary and generated wave table, verbatim. The one 118-character line runs past the column and scrolls rather than wrapping, because a soft-wrapped listing is not the listing.

body.text: Lane lengths 80 / 68 / 74 / 73 = **295 tiles**, union **272**, **78 slots**, **1872 MW**, **21,917 funds**, **244 lives**, **923 units** across 10 waves, from four spawn points on three edges.
Nothing in that block is a constant somebody typed

**Every budget is a shipped-content ratio re-measured off `data/anchors/` at run time, multiplied by a measured property of the generated board.** Slot count is union lane tiles divided by 3.5. Capacity is slot count × max draw × 0.50. Funds come from the shipped funds-per-slot ratio, lives from the act's leak budget, wave mass from the lane-length ratio. Change the shipped content and the generator's output moves with it, which is the only way a generator stays honest as the game it scales from is tuned.

Validated clean — **0 schema errors, 0 `check_anchor` errors, 0 warnings** — across nine configurations: lanes 2–5, sweeps 1–5, 32² / 48² / 64², acts 1–3. Deterministic: `--selftest` generates twice and compares byte-identical at **35,522 bytes**; two `--out` runs `diff` empty at the same sha256; verified cwd-independent.
The prerequisite that was genuinely blocking, proved rather than described

`LF-132`: `sim/content.py`'s `all_anchor_ids()` discovered anchors with a raw `glob('anchor-*.json')`, so **any untracked file dropped in `data/anchors/` was treated as real shipped content.** The backlog entry had predicted, in as many words, that this would bite again the moment anyone built the large-board generator — because a generate, grade, discard workflow is exactly that.
It was proved by doing it rather than by reasoning about it. The generated board was dropped at `data/anchors/anchor-25.json`, untracked, and the numbers taken on both sides of the fix:

The gate check **flipped which act it treats as the reference**, and that is the part worth naming: not a crash, not a red run — a silently different answer to the question the check exists to ask. After the conversion the generated file is still sitting on disk and every number is back where it was.
