`load_anchor()` was deliberately left alone, so an untracked board still grades **by name** — which is the whole generate-and-discard workflow, and the reason the fix belongs in **discovery** rather than in loading. Both synthetic anchors were deleted afterwards; 24 tracked.
The finding, which is worth more than the tool

`LF-187` predicted that decision **074**'s range numbers would not survive 48²: longer lanes mean a fixed absolute range covers a shrinking fraction of the board. **That is now measured rather than predicted.**
The target is **about 13 tiles for the top weapon**, being the range at which the median generated slot recovers the 48.9% own-lane coverage a shipped act-3 slot has today.

The demonstration is a control the generator ships with. `--budget shipped` puts a shipped act-3 anchor's **absolute** numbers — 12 slots, 290 MW, 4030 funds, 13.7 units/wave — onto the generated 48² geometry, unchanged. It grades like this:

With budgets **derived from the geometry** instead, the same board grades `ok` at all three. So the control does its job: it separates the range-and-budget question from the layout question, and the layout is not what is broken.

A second defect shows up in that same derived grade, and it belongs to `BAL-04` rather than here: **the winner set and the death wave do not move across difficulty at all.** Four distinct builds at each of standard, hard and brutal; all three dying at wave 7; the same four policies winning every time — burst, greedy-overdraw, anti-armour, overcharge-greedy. **Margin** moves — winners finish on 106–126 lives at standard and 10–64 at brutal — but **selection does not**. Difficulty is changing how close it is, not what works.
The presence profile: the shape is fine, the level has collapsed
Measured with the coverage instrument that entry 53 — **The test of the instrument was red**, `the-test-of-the-instrument-was-red` — repaired. Generated 48² against shipped act-3 anchor-20:

**`LF-218` does not get structurally worse at 48², and that was worth checking rather than assuming.** Cumulative presence reaches 25 / 50 / 75 / 90% at lane fraction 13 / 31 / 57 / 81% on the generated board, against 14 / 32 / 58 / 82% on anchor-20. The last quarter of the lane carries 13.6–14.1% per lane against anchor-20's 14.1%. The four lanes carry 26.9 / 23.8 / 25.3 / 23.9% of live unit-ticks, which is about as even as a four-lane board gets.

So **the attrition profile is scale-invariant** once slot count scales with lane length. What collapses is per-emplacement work, not the shape of the tail — which is precisely a range problem and not a layout one. That is the same 13 tiles, reached from a different direction.
The instrument fooled itself again, one entry after being repaired

`verdict()` printed “no material near-zero tail (6% of emplacements)” for a board whose own ceiling is **11.9%**. The `(0)` branch short-circuits on the near-zero fraction before branch `(b)` ever consults `board_presence_ceiling`. Filed as `LF-229`.

It is **invisible on all 24 shipped anchors**, because their ceilings are 75–95% and the short-circuit gives the right answer every time at those levels. Only a board unlike any shipped board reaches the hole.

Worth saying plainly rather than filing quietly: **entry 53 rewrote those exact labels earlier the same day**, and the rewrite has a hole. It is the same lesson as `firing arcs agree`, and it keeps arriving in different clothes — **a check that runs over all shipped content proves nothing about a branch the shipped content never enters.**
What `slots` is still for, after `PLC-04`

Checked against the tree rather than assumed, because the generator has to decide how much care to spend siting slots that free placement has arguably made decorative. The answer is a clean three-way split:

items: **The count is a real budget.** `_effective_cap()` takes `max_emplacements` else `len(slots)`, and it is the binding constraint in every run graded here — 12 of 16 policies fill all 78 and stop. It is also `validate_data.py`'s saturation denominator and `board_presence_ceiling`'s `n_slots`.

**The positions are an instrument input and a validator input.** `validate_data.py`'s bounds, on-path, duplicate, dead-slot and ramp/cliff checks; all of `sim/coverage.py`'s per-slot work; the editor overlay; `PLC-06`'s autoplay fallback (`LF-207`); and `_slot_priority()`, kept alive solely for decision 022's measurement.
**The positions are dead to both placement paths** — the grader's (7,402 lattice candidates on 48² against 579 and 763 on shipped boards), the player's, and the board render.

body.text: So the generator sites slots carefully **only because the coverage instrument reads them**. A generator that emitted `max_emplacements` and no `slots` at all would grade identically and be unmeasurable — which is a good argument for keeping the field and a bad one for believing it still does what its name suggests.
Two more filed on the way through

items: **`LF-228`** — `anchor_view.gd::_on_built()` computes the ward-engagement total as `placed + available_slots()`. With free placement that total **grows with every build**, so `wards-full` never fires; and on a slots-less anchor it equals `placed`, so `wards-half` and `wards-full` both fire on the **first** build.

**`LF-230`** — `InstrumentedSim`'s overhead is 2.1× at 12 emplacements and **6.8× at 78** (3.88 s → 26.41 s, same policy, `Outcome`s field-identical). A full coverage pass is 2.5 minutes on anchor-20 and **21 minutes** on the 48² board; a 64² board derives 131 emplacements. The rules got `WAR-03`'s spatial grid. The instrument did not.

body.text: Not a refusal, with one caveat worth recording

The sim cost does **not** explode at this scale. The candidate lattice builds in 125 ms, a plain run is 2.5–4.9 s, a full 60-cell grade about 7.5 minutes. Maximum `sim_seconds` observed was **1,397 against a `MAX_SIM_SECONDS` of 3,600** — so nothing is being killed by the clock. But that headroom is 2.6×, and a 64² board with slower act-3 units will approach it. Recorded now, while it is still comfortable.

And one thing that is not about scale at all: **all 16 policies reach the emplacement cap during wave 1's 22-second lead-in** — on the generated board **and** on shipped anchor-24. **Nothing is sequenced after the first decision.** That is inherited from the shipped funds-per-slot ratio rather than caused by the board size, which is exactly why it matters: scaling the ratio forward carries the defect forward with it.
What this entry does not have

The work sits on `lf/ts-layout-generator` and is uncommitted as this is written, so there are **no commit hashes** here. A tier-4 gate is in flight and **no verdict is stated** — the result belongs in the entry that actually has it, not in a hopeful sentence in this one.
Five entries, and the tool is the least of them

Five entries today. Four of them found the fault in an instrument — the metric, then the test of the metric, then the acceptance criterion, and then the four real defects those repaired instruments exposed. This one built a tool, ran the repaired instruments over its output, and got a number.
**The tool is not the deliverable. The measurement the tool made possible is.** Thirteen tiles is a whole balance epic's starting point, and it did not exist this morning.

entries.title: The instruments were standing where the player never stands
entries.summary: `LF-228` — a dialog cue that could never fire, and nothing noticed for two milestones. `anchor_view.gd` computed ward engagement as `placed + available_slots()`, and `available_slots()` is the authored slots still free — so once `PLC-01`/`PLC-02` made placement continuous the denominator grew with every build: 9, 10, 11 … 16 across eight free placements on anchor-01. `wards-full` was unreachable; `wards-half` arrived at the cap. On an anchor authoring no slots at all, both cues fired on the first build. It hid because every automated path in this project — the grader, the scenarios, the autobuild — builds on authored slots first, where the wrong expression is coincidentally correct. Fixing the trigger then made a second defect audible: the lines still quoted counts from when both anchors had six slots.

body.text: The previous entry — **The generator was not the deliverable**, `the-generator-was-not-the-deliverable`, merged as **#144** — built `tools/genboard.py` and closed on the observation that the measurement the tool made possible was worth more than the tool. This entry is one of those measurements, and it is not about scale at all. The generator authors **78 emplacement slots on a 48×48 board**, and running the game on a board that size made a bug visible that had been sitting in a shipped file for two milestones.
The expression, and why it can only be wrong

`scripts/anchor_view.gd::_on_built()` computed the ward-engagement total as `sim.placed.size() + sim.available_slots().size()`. `available_slots()` returns the **authored** slots not currently occupied, and occupancy is an exact `(x, y)` equality test. Free placement — `PLC-01` and `PLC-02`, decision **080** — made positions continuous, so a freely placed emplacement almost never lands exactly on an authored coordinate. **The denominator therefore grows with every build.**
Measured on anchor-01 with eight free placements, before the fix:

authored slots=8  max_emplacements=0   effective_cap()=8
build 1 -> n=1 OLD_total=9   NEW_total=8
build 2 -> n=2 OLD_total=10  NEW_total=8
build 3 -> n=3 OLD_total=11  NEW_total=8
build 4 -> n=4 OLD_total=12  NEW_total=8   <<NEW:wards-half>>
...
build 8 -> n=8 OLD_total=16  NEW_total=8   <<OLD:wards-half>>  <<NEW:wards-full>>
body.caption: anchor-01, eight free placements. `OLD_total` is the shipped expression, `NEW_total` the fix. `wards-full` never fires at all; `wards-half` — a halfway cue — fires on the last build.

body.text: And it is wrong in the other direction too. On an anchor that authors no slots at all — which `PLC-05` permits — `available_slots()` is empty, `total == placed`, and **both** conditions are true on the **first** build:

authored slots=0  max_emplacements=6   effective_cap()=6
build 1 -> n=1 OLD_total=1  NEW_total=6  <<OLD:wards-half>>  <<OLD:wards-full>>
build 3 -> n=3              NEW_total=6  <<NEW:wards-half>>
build 6 -> n=6              NEW_total=6  <<NEW:wards-full>>
body.caption: The slots-less case. The old expression plays a halfway cue and a fully-engaged cue back to back on the first emplacement anyone builds.

body.text: Why it hid for two milestones, which is the good part
**`--autoplay` builds on authored slots first.** The control case, with every build landing on an authored coordinate:

=== anchor-01, 8 builds ON the authored slots (autobuild's own ordering)
build 4 -> n=4 OLD_total=8 NEW_total=8  <<OLD:wards-half>>  <<NEW:wards-half>>
build 8 -> n=8 OLD_total=8 NEW_total=8  <<OLD:wards-full>>  <<NEW:wards-full>>
body.caption: When every build lands on an authored slot, `placed + available_slots()` is exactly the slot count and the old expression is coincidentally correct. Old and new agree on every line.

body.text: So the wrong expression is correct under **every automated path this project has** — the grader, the scenarios, the autobuild. Only a human free-placing hits it. That is worth stating plainly: a project that verifies almost everything through headless automation built a blind spot exactly where the automation and the player diverge.
The fix is a call, not a reimplementation
The denominator is now `sim.effective_cap()`:

func wards_total() -> int:
	return 0 if sim == null else sim.effective_cap()

`anchor_sim.gd:400` — `max_emplacements if max_emplacements > 0 else anchor.get("slots", []).size()` — is the same quantity `build_at()` refuses past and `Sim._try_build()` uses. One number, already shared between the two rule implementations, already parity-verified. **`anchor_sim.gd` was not modified.**
Proved end to end through a real scenario on anchor-01 with eight free positions:

DIALOG-TRIGGER wards-half frame=16 sim_t=0.233     <- build 4 of 8
DIALOG-TRIGGER wards-full frame=24 sim_t=0.367     <- build 8 of 8
body.caption: All 16 assertions pass. `view.wards.total` reads **8 on every build**, and each cue fires exactly once.

body.text: How it was verified, because it dodged a known trap

The hook is `export_state()` — `view.wards.{engaged,total}` — not a print marker. `tools/scenario.py` already relays its summary with every assertion's observed value, so the numbers are visible with **zero** new print prefixes. `shot.py` filters relayed markers by prefix and has silently eaten three working hooks before now; this change needed no edit to `main.gd`, `shot.py` or `scenario.py` at all. The bug was silent for exactly the reason the hook fixes: **nothing could see `total`**, and the only symptom was a line that never played.

An extra finding fell out of it. An anchor with **neither** `slots` nor `max_emplacements` has `effective_cap() == 0`, so `build_at()` refuses every build outright — the degenerate case is already unreachable in the rules, and under the fix the `total > 0` guard correctly keeps both cues silent.
Fixing the trigger made a second defect audible

The cues were authored when both anchors had **six** slots. anchor-01 now authors 8 and anchor-24 authors 12. So with the trigger restored, the player would hear a line naming three wards at the fourth of eight, and a line naming six of six at the eighth of eight — and on the finale anchor, at the twelfth of twelve. Shipping the trigger fix without the text would have been worse than shipping neither, so three lines were rewritten **so that no cue quotes a count at all**:

rows: Three wards engaged. Ring's half live.
Half the ring reads engaged. Rest when you can afford it.
Six of six. Ring's fully engaged.
That's the last ward. Ring's fully engaged.
Six of six. Last ring Meridian lights on this order.
Every ward engaged. Last ring Meridian lights on this order.

body.text: The constraint was structural rather than stylistic. `PLC-05` lets an anchor set `max_emplacements` above its authored slot count, `PLC-04`'s lattice places anywhere legal, and the `LF-080` generator derives **78** emplacements on a 48² board. **Nothing tracks the relationship between a dialog line and the anchor's capacity** — there is a gate check binding a mission brief to its reactor rating (`dialog capacity`) and no equivalent for this. So the lines were written to be true at any capacity: "half the ring" is the proportion the trigger actually tests, "the last ward" names the boundary it fires on, "every ward" is a universal quantifier.
One line was already correct and was left alone as the model — Okonkwo's **"Full ring, eleven-year-old hardware, and it still locks true. Somebody built this to last."** It never quoted a number.
`LF-207` was assessed and deliberately not done

`PLC-06` left a 1-tile fallback scan in `anchor_view.gd` because `PLC-04` did not exist yet, and `LF-207` says to replace it with `PLC-04`'s ordering once that landed. It landed this morning. The assessment says **leave it**, and the reasoning is worth recording rather than re-deriving next time.

`PLC-04`'s GDScript lattice is a **private method on a `SceneTree` MainLoop** (`parity.gd:472-587`), not a class and not preloadable, depending on two file-local consts. The Python side is module-level and memoised on the `Anchor` dataclass, so extraction has no Python counterpart to mirror. Reuse therefore means a new preloadable module that both `parity.gd` and `anchor_view.gd` load — which drags in a `tools/check.py` `safe operations` registration, an edit to the one file whose failure mode is 1,152 empty dictionaries rather than an error, and a full tier-4 re-baseline including the Windows leg.

And a second point that outlives the ticket: **even after extraction, `anchor_view.gd` would gain only the ordering.** `PLC-04`'s actual candidate choice is `_try_build()`'s lane round-robin by per-lane maximin, entangled with policy preferences, caps, overdraw, reserve and per-lane arclength state. "One candidate ordering in the project" is achievable for the lattice; **the consumption rule is a second thing**. `autobuild()`'s own docstring already claims it "builds the way the cheap-mass policy would" — which it does not, and would not, from the lattice alone.

The current divergence is real but narrow: the fallback runs only when authored slots are exhausted **and** `placed < effective_cap()` — today that is anchor-11 alone, and only under `--autoplay`. Revisit when `LF-226`'s anchor-11 autobuild scenario is written, since that is the one thing that would exercise it.
Filed

items: **`LF-232`** — the audio cue is still counted. `_on_built()` plays `ward_engage_%d` with `clampi(n, 1, 6)`, so builds 7 through N all replay `ward_engage_6`. **The sound effect stops counting at exactly the number just removed from the text.** At 78 emplacements a counted cue is meaningless, so the recommendation is proportional rather than counted.

**`LF-233`** — rename `available_slots()` to `unoccupied_authored_slots()`. Three callers left, all meaning "an authored position nobody has taken yet". **The name is what made the bug read as correct.**

body.text: What this entry does not have

The work sits on `lf/eng-ward-engagement` and is uncommitted as this is written, so there are **no commit hashes** here. A tier-4 gate is in flight and **no verdict is stated** — that belongs in the entry that actually has the result. There is also **no screenshot**, deliberately: the proof here is a denominator that reads 8 on every build and two trigger lines with frame numbers on them, and a picture of a board with eight emplacements on it would show none of that.
Six entries, and the last one found this one

The generator built in the previous entry found this bug — it authors 78 slots on a 48×48 board, which made a growing denominator impossible to miss. And the bug survived two milestones because every automated path in this project builds on authored slots, so the wrong expression was right everywhere the machines looked.
**The instruments were not wrong this time. They were just standing somewhere the player never stands.**

entries.title: The net one fix removed, and the branch no shipped board could enter
entries.summary: Two verification holes, both opened by today's own work, both closed here. `LF-224`: `sim determinism` used to return FAIL on `sim/run.py`'s exit code, and `run.py --json` exits 1 whenever an anchor is not clean, so it had been serving by accident as an all-anchors-clean assertion under the wrong name and with an empty message. Entry 54 made the check do what its name says, which removed the accidental net; the deliberate one — `anchor grades`, tier 3, printing every failing anchor's own problem strings — is built now that entry 55's re-balance has all 24 back to `ok`. `LF-229`: `sim/coverage.py`'s `verdict()` short-circuited on the near-zero tail before it ever consulted the board's own presence ceiling, and printed "no material near-zero tail" for a generated board whose best 78 legal positions reach 12% of the live wave. And the ticket's own premise turned out to be wrong in a way that lands on act 1.

body.text: The previous entry — **The instruments were standing where the player never stands**, `where-the-player-never-stands`, merged as **#145** — found a dialog cue that could never fire, because every automated path in this project builds on authored slots and the wrong expression is coincidentally correct there. This entry is the seventh and last of the day, and it is about the instruments again, from the other side: **two holes that today's own work opened**, and what it takes to notice that your own fix removed something.
`LF-224` — the net nobody meant to have, removed by a correct fix

`sim determinism` used to return `FAIL` on `sim/run.py`'s **exit code**, before it compared its two runs at all. And `run.py --json` exits 1 whenever an anchor is not clean. So the check had been serving, by accident, as an all-anchors-clean assertion — **under the wrong name, with an empty message**, because `run.py` writes its verdict to stdout and the check reported stderr.

Entry 54 — **The acceptance criterion was not a selector**, `the-acceptance-criterion-was-not-a-selector` — fixed the check to do what its name says. That is right, and it **removed the accidental net**. Entry 55, **Four anchors, four different levers**, then restored all 24 anchors to `ok`. The deliberate replacement was deferred until the grades were clean, on the reasoning that a check which is red on arrival gets disabled rather than fixed. They are clean, so it is built now.

`tools/check.py` gains **`anchor grades`**, tier 3. It shells `sim/run.py --jobs 8 --json`, parses the report, and puts **every failing anchor's own `problems` strings** in the message. It restates none of `run.py`'s thresholds — what counts as unwinnable, as a single-solution level, as difficulty not biting, stays `run.py`'s business. A second copy of a rule is the drift this project keeps paying for.
Proved red first, against two deliberately perturbed anchors:

anchor grades  FAIL   59733 ms
2 of 24 anchors do not grade ok (sim/run.py --jobs 8):
  anchor-14  standard: unwinnable — no policy clears it
  anchor-14  hard: unwinnable — no policy clears it
  anchor-14  brutal: unwinnable — no policy clears it
  anchor-19  hard: every distinct build clears it — difficulty is not biting
  anchor-19  brutal: every distinct build clears it — difficulty is not biting
body.caption: The perturbation lived in a **scratchpad shadow tree** with no `.git`, so the real `data/` was never touched and `git status --porcelain data/` stayed empty throughout — the working tree is shared with whoever else is running, and a red-first proof must not be the thing that breaks them.

body.text: And green on the real tree: `24 anchors grade ok at every difficulty (--jobs 8)`.
Why tier 3, and the reasoning is the interesting part

**Tier 2 is unavailable.** It is already *over* its own 28,000 ms budget (`LF-178`), and decision 067 refused to raise a threshold so the data would fit once already — the fix there is to move a check out, not to move the number again. **Tier 4 was rejected** because the regression this catches arrives almost exclusively as a **data-only pull request**: entry 55 moved four anchors' capacities and slot layouts and nothing else. Tier 3 is the PR tier, and a check that only runs nightly lets an unwinnable anchor sit on `main` until the next scheduled run. The cost is named rather than hidden: **tier 3 goes from 204 s to 265 s**.

One thing worth a line on its own. `tier counts` is a tier-1 check that asserts `check.py`'s own docstring counts against its `CHECKS` registry on every run, so **adding a check without updating the prose turns the gate red**. That is deliberate — a count written into prose here rots within a day, so it is asserted rather than trusted. Docstring updated in the same change: tier 3 = **38**, tier 4 = **41**.
`LF-229` — the branch that no shipped board could reach

`sim/coverage.py`'s `verdict()` printed **"no material near-zero tail (9% of emplacements)"** for a generated 48x48 board whose **own presence ceiling is 11.9%** — a board where the best legal positions available anywhere reach 12% of the live wave. The `(0)` branch tested the near-zero tail and returned before `(b)` ever consulted `board_presence_ceiling`.

ceiling top_n_median 11.9%   near-zero tail 8.7%   site-eff 0.57
uptime p10/p50/max   11% / 18% / 61%

BEFORE: no material near-zero tail (9% of emplacements)
AFTER:  (b) range/waves: the board's own best 78 positions reach only 12% of the live wave
body.caption: The mechanism is that `NEAR_ZERO_UPTIME` is an **absolute** 0.10, so the tail measure only ever sees a *bimodal* board. A board that is uniformly mediocre has no tail to find and is nonetheless broken everywhere.

body.text: `(b)` is now tested **first and unconditionally**. The order is `(b)` then `(0)` then `(a)` then `(c)`. **All 24 shipped anchors keep their exact verdict — 0 of 24 moved**, verified by running the pre-change and post-change `verdict()` over one cached 24-anchor report set, so the comparison cost no simulation at all.
The ordering argument was made for all four branches, not just the pair

This is the part worth recording, because it is the part that would otherwise be re-derived. `(a)` deliberately stays **after** `(0)`. It is a **ratio** against the board's own ceiling — headroom, not outcome — and promoting it above the tail test relabels **twelve** shipped anchors from "no material tail" to "(a) siting", on boards where every emplacement is doing work. `(b)` is an **absolute** claim that no outcome is reachable anywhere, so it needs no tail to be true. Outcomes rank above headroom; a claim about what could have been better ranks below both.
The correction — and it lands on act 1

`LF-229`'s own ticket said all 24 shipped ceilings are 75–95%, so the short-circuit could only ever mask a low ceiling on a board unlike any that ships. **That premise was wrong.** Measured while fixing it, at range basis `8189779cd568`:

No label moved when the ordering was fixed, but **only** because those four already carry large near-zero tails and were reaching `(b)` by another route. (`LF-234` records that band as 22–31%; `sim/coverage.py`'s own note says 19–31% — the conclusion is the same either way, and the discrepancy is recorded here rather than smoothed over.) So the masking window is **narrower than the ticket claimed and real** — and what sits under the threshold is **act 1's entire opening stretch**.

Those are boards where the level's own slot-and-range budget is the limit, not the player's siting. Filed as **`LF-234`**. It is the same conclusion `LF-187` reaches from the other direction — a fixed absolute range covers a shrinking fraction as lanes lengthen — and the same four anchors entry 55's re-balance found thinnest. Worth treating as one finding rather than three.
Two smaller things

items: A new selftest case locks the branch ordering on **synthetic** summaries — free, no simulation, and red on the pre-fix `verdict()`. But `sim/coverage.py --selftest` is **still in no gate tier** (`LF-221`, open), which entry 53 already flagged. **The cheapest guard in the file is the one nothing runs.**

The irony worth naming: entry 53 — **The test of the instrument was red, and no tier ran it**, `the-test-of-the-instrument-was-red` — rewrote these very labels **the same day**, and the rewrite shipped with this hole. The fix was not to add a fourth branch. It was to re-argue the order of all of them.

body.text: The gate, and what this entry does not have

A **tier 4** run finished before this was written: **39 passed · 0 failed · 2 skipped**, out of **41 checks** — up from 40, and the new one is among the 39 that ran and passed. The two skips are `rules parity` and `rules parity (windows)`, held back by the content-hash cache at digest `78921592b4c5` because no rule or data file changed in this branch. **That is cached, not run** — it is not a pass, and it is stated that way here for the same reason the gate's own tally line names every check that did not run: a green partial result that reads like a full one is the failure the tiering exists to prevent.

The work sits on `lf/prc-verification-holes` and is uncommitted as this is written, so there are **no commit hashes** here. And there is **no screenshot**: the evidence in this entry is a check message with two anchors' problem strings in it and a verdict label that changed on a board that does not ship, and neither of those is a thing a picture of the game can show.
Seven entries in one day

Three of them found the fault in an instrument rather than in the game. One built a tool that then found a real bug. One fixed four anchors with four different levers. One found a cue the player could never hear. And this one closes the two holes the others opened.

**A verification layer is not a thing you build once. It is a thing that acquires holes exactly as fast as the code under it changes, and the only defence is noticing when your own fix removed something.**

entries.title: The dialog stopped counting. The sound kept counting.
entries.summary: LF-232, and it is the other half of the previous entry. Entry 57 fixed the ward dialog triggers and rewrote three lines so that no cue quotes a count. The audio cue was still counting: _on_built() played ward_engage_%d clamped to 1..6, so the sound effect stopped counting at exactly the number just deleted from the text. anchor-01 authors 8 emplacement slots and anchor-24 authors 12, so both shipped anchors carrying ward cues hit it — builds 7 through 12 all replayed the top note of a six-note phrase written so the sixth is unmistakably the last one. The fix is proportional rather than counted, reusing the existing six-rung bank with no new audio, and it was proved on a 78-emplacement generated board by reading the cue index out of the running game rather than predicting it.

body.text: The previous entry — **The instruments were standing where the player never stands**, `where-the-player-never-stands`, merged as **#145** — fixed a ward dialog cue that could never fire, and rewrote three lines of Control's dialog so that **no cue quotes a count**. This is `LF-232`, and it is the other half of that fix. The *audio* cue was still counting.
The cue stopped counting at exactly the number the text stopped quoting

`_on_built()` played `ward_engage_%d` with `clampi(n, 1, 6)` — one sound per emplacement, six sounds in the bank. **anchor-01 authors 8 slots and anchor-24 authors 12**, so both shipped anchors that carry ward cues run off the end of it. Read out of `export_state()` on each build, anchor-24 before the fix:

n= 1..5 -> ward_engage_1..5
n= 6/12 -> ward_engage_6
n= 7/12 -> ward_engage_6      <- bug
n= 8/12 -> ward_engage_6
n= 9/12 -> ward_engage_6
n=10/12 -> ward_engage_6
n=11/12 -> ward_engage_6
n=12/12 -> ward_engage_6
body.caption: The count stopped counting at six, which is the number `LF-228` had just removed from the dialog text one entry ago. The text stopped saying it and the sound carried on saying it.

body.text: The fix, and the one line that matters
**Proportional, not counted**, reusing the existing `ward_engage_1..6` bank. **No new audio was authored.**
rung 6 the instant the board is full, otherwise rungs 1..5 spread evenly over the builds before it — `1 + (n - 1) * 5 / (total - 1)`, integer division.

rows: rung 1 on 16 builds, 2 on 15, 3 on 16, 4 on 15, 5 on 15, and **6 exactly once**, at n = 78

body.text: **Why the full-board case is a separate branch rather than a plain `n * 6 / total`.** The bank's `WARD_STEPS` is a rising major pentatonic G3 to E4 at +0.30 dB per rung, with everything except pitch held identical across all six, authored “so the sixth is unmistakably the last one”. The split keeps rung 6 reachable **only** at `n == total`, so the top note lands on the last build and lands once — the same build the `wards-full` dialog line fires on. Both endpoints are pinned deliberately, because the endpoints are where the old bug lived: `n = 1` is always rung 1, and `total <= 1` is rung 6, because a one-emplacement board is full on its only build.

And a detail worth recording on its own: **on a six-emplacement board the sequence is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6** — rung for rung identical to the counted cue it replaces. That was the bank's design case, and the proportional mapping reproduces it exactly rather than approximating it.

The denominator is `wards_total()`, which is `sim.effective_cap()` — **called, not reimplemented**, the same number entry 57 established as the one the rules and the parity harness already agree on. `anchor_sim.gd` is untouched by this change.
How it was proved, which is the methodological bit

The 78-emplacement row was **measured, not predicted**. `ward_cue_step()` is static and pure, so a temporary `export_state()` field emitted the whole n = 1..78 table from the *running game*, and a scenario assertion printed it. Under the old code the same field read `1,2,3,4,5,6,6,6,…,6` — **73 consecutive top notes** on a board the generator will happily produce. Both the temporary field and the temporary old-mapping line were removed afterwards; a grep for the marker they carried returns nothing, and the shipping diff is only the change itself.
One permanent addition survives from that scaffolding: **`view.wards.cue` in `export_state()`** — derived, not stored, so it cannot drift from what was played.
The reason both halves were silent, and it is the same reason

`LF-228` and `LF-232` hid for the same structural cause: **the cue index was visible nowhere outside `_on_built()`.** Filed as `LF-235` — `AudioDirector.sfx()` has no cue log, so **no scenario can assert what the game actually played.** Every audio assertion in this project is really an assertion about the *caller's arithmetic*.

A bounded ring buffer of recent cue names would make “the brownout duck fired”, “the deny tone played and not the build tone” and “rung 6 played exactly once” assertable. **None of those can be checked today.** `LF-174` already lists `audio_director.gd` among the zero-coverage scripts; this is the concrete mechanism behind that entry on the list.
The gate, and what this entry does not have

A **tier 4** run finished before this was written: **39 passed · 0 failed · 2 skipped**, out of **41 checks**. The two skips are `rules parity` and `rules parity (windows)`, held back by the content-hash cache at digest `78921592b4c5` because no rule or data file changed in this branch. **That is cached, not run** — it is not a pass, and it is stated that way here for the same reason the gate's own tally line names every check that did not run.

The work sits on `lf/aud-proportional-ward-cue` and is uncommitted as this is written, so there are **no commit hashes** here. There is also **no screenshot**, and for once that is not an omission: this entry is about a sound. A frame of the board at n = 7 looks exactly like a frame of the board at n = 7 looked yesterday, and the bug was never anywhere a camera could reach.
Eight entries in one day, and this is the smallest

One expression, one bank reused, no new sound. But it finishes something. Entry 57 fixed a cue the player could never hear and rewrote the lines that would have said the wrong number; this one stops the *sound* saying it.

**A fix that lands half of a thing is a fix that leaves the other half looking correct.** The dialog stopped counting and the audio kept counting, and the two halves sat one entry apart in the same file. Only writing them down together made the mismatch obvious.

entries.title: The output matched the source, and both were wrong
entries.summary: `LF-211` and `LF-231`, and they are one defect three times over: a prose field that skips the inline renderer. A straight double quote in an entry summary ended the meta description's attribute early and spilled the rest of the summary into the tag as attributes — measured on two already-published pages, one of which a real HTML parser reads as **101 attributes on a single tag**. Nothing scanned for single-asterisk emphasis at all, which prints literally by design. The ticket asked for `render_inline` over the summary and that would have been wrong: an attribute value cannot hold a tag, so the fix is a new `render_plain` that **removes** markup using the identical pairing machinery. The lone-asterisk check ships as a shrink-only ratchet rather than a plain assertion, because a strict one is red on 54 spans across 15 already-published entries and this journal is append-only.

body.text: Every page in this journal is projected out of `chronicle.json` by `tools/chronicle.py`, and `tools/chronicle.py --check` regenerates the whole site into a scratch directory and diffs it against what is committed. That check has been green for 59 entries. It asks whether the output matches the source, and it cannot see a generator that is wrong in the same way in both.

Entry 56 — **The generator was not the deliverable. Thirteen tiles was.**, `the-generator-was-not-the-deliverable`, merged as **#144** — carried the first of these as a side fix. Table headers were the one prose field in `render_block` that never went through `render_inline`, and two headers reading `lane_coverage()` had already shipped to entry 53's published page with their backticks printed literally. This entry is the rest of them: `LF-211`, and both halves of `LF-231`.
Three defects, one pattern: a prose field that skips the inline renderer

**`LF-211` — one escaper doing two jobs.** `esc()` escaped the ampersand and the angle brackets and deliberately left quotes alone, which is right for element content and wrong for an attribute value. Every attribute in the file took it. A straight double quote therefore closed the attribute early and the tail of the prose leaked into the tag **as attributes** — parsed as attribute names by a browser, read as text by nobody.

The ticket was filed against an image caption reaching `alt`. The field it actually broke on the live site is the entry summary reaching `<meta name="description">`, and it had broken there twice. This is `entries/quality-is-not-just-looks.html` exactly as published, read with `html.parser` rather than by eye:

BEFORE   entries/quality-is-not-just-looks.html, as published to the site

  html.parser sees 101 attributes on that one <meta> tag:
    name    = 'description'
    content = 'The owner delegated four questions that had sat gated for
               sessions, in one message, with one instruction: '
    quality = None
    speed   = None
    cost,   = None
    ...       96 more, every remaining word of the summary parsed as the
              name of a valueless attribute on the tag

AFTER

  html.parser sees 2 attributes:
    name    = 'description'
    content = the whole summary, quotes escaped and intact
body.caption: Two published pages did this: `quality-is-not-just-looks` at 101 attributes and `the-net-the-fix-removed` at 39. Every other page was correct by luck — a summary with no straight double quote in it. Nothing was red anywhere, because the committed HTML matched `chronicle.json` exactly. It was the projection that was wrong, identically, in both places.

body.text: The `alt` half had to be proved on synthetic input, because no caption on any published page happens to contain a straight double quote — the workaround of authors typing curly quotes had held there, which is precisely what makes it not a mechanism:
BEFORE alt a browser actually parses: The AFTER alt a browser actually parses: The "before" frame - alt text ends here, id=x onerror=boom
body.caption: Synthetic, and deliberately so. Each of the three was proved broken first, on input written for the purpose, and never by editing a real entry to make it fail.

body.text: **`LF-231`, half one — the summary reached the meta description unrendered.** Same field, second and independent defect in it: even on the pages where the attribute did not break, the summary arrived with its markup verbatim. That tag is what a search result and a link unfurl read, so backticks and asterisks are what they read.

**`LF-231`, half two — nothing checked for single-asterisk emphasis at all.** A lone `*x*` prints literally by design; that is `LF-173`'s measured reversal, argued at length in `render_inline`'s docstring. So a lone asterisk pair in prose is **always** unrendered markup, and `audit_markup` — the one check that exists to catch exactly this — scanned only for the double asterisk. The scan was widened, then proved to fail on a synthetic entry carrying a single span:

BEFORE   audit_markup verdict: PASS   (the defect is invisible to it)

AFTER    unrendered emphasis in entries/...: 1 lone-asterisk span(s) - '*wrong*'
           single-asterisk emphasis prints literally by design (LF-173) -
           use ** for emphasis, or backticks if it is a path or a glob
         audit_markup verdict: FAIL   (caught)
Two decisions taken against the ticket, and both are the interesting part

**The ticket said to run `render_inline` over the summary. That is wrong** — worth writing down, because the two functions look interchangeable. An attribute value cannot hold a tag: `render_inline` emits a `<strong>`, the attribute escaper then escapes it, and the description would read `<strong>first</strong>` — trading unrendered asterisks for **visible tag names**, which is worse than what it replaced. `<title>` is RCDATA and would show them for the same reason.

So the fix is a new `render_plain()`, which **removes** the markup rather than rendering it, using the **identical** pairing machinery as `render_inline` — the same `_hide_code_spans`, the same `_wrap_pairs` with a null tag. Sharing it is the point: two parsers that have to agree about what a delimiter is will eventually stop agreeing. It is applied to the meta description, to `alt`, and to `<title>`.

Worth stating plainly, because it is the part that generalises: **the ticket was written by an agent, not by the owner, and it was wrong.** The brief for this work said to argue rather than comply, and arguing is what produced the better fix.
The second decision: a check that is red on arrival gets disabled rather than fixed

Widening the lone-asterisk scan is the fix `LF-231` asked for. Running it over the corpus for the first time returned **54 lone-asterisk spans across 15 of the 59 published entries** — `*before*`, `*merged*`, `*current accepted bank*` — every one of them live on the site right now, printing bare asterisks at readers. This journal is append-only: those entries record what was true on the day they were written and are not editable to make a check green. A plain assertion could therefore not be both correct and green.

It is a **ratchet** instead. A frozen set of those 15 entry ids is exempt, anything else fails, and it is exact in **both** directions: an exempted id that stops producing a span, or that no longer renders at all, fails as a **stale exemption**. The list can only ever shrink. Per-entry granularity is safe precisely because an entry is immutable once published — an exemption cannot come to cover a later addition to an older page, because there are no later additions.

a-panel-that-cannot-lie                       3
four-anchors-four-different-levers            7
gc-was-lying                                  4
measuring-the-fifth-non-negotiable            1
merging-closed-nothing                        6
no-instrument-panel-no-brake                  1
placement-rule-both-engines                   1
the-acceptance-criterion-was-not-a-selector   6
the-blocker-was-already-fixed                 4
the-gate-was-exempt-from-its-own-rule         3
the-guard-denied-its-own-advice               3
the-instrument-measured-the-wrong-quantity    6
the-net-the-fix-removed                       2
the-sound-kept-counting                       4
three-refusals-that-look-different            3
                                     15 entries, 54 spans
body.caption: The exemption list, and the number of live unrendered spans each id is exempt for. It is written as entry ids rather than as the spans themselves, because an id is stable and a span is a string somebody could quietly add one more of.

body.text: That is the same shape as `LF-224`'s lesson from earlier the same day: **a check that is red on arrival gets disabled rather than fixed.**
Every prose field was audited, not only the two the tickets named

items: `site.subtitle` into the index page's meta description — the same defect as the entry summary, one page over.
`title` and `site.title` into `<title>`, which is RCDATA and so takes plain text for the same reason an attribute does.

`body[].attribution` into `<cite>`, which was **the last field still bypassing the renderer** — the same class as entry 56's table headers. An attribution here is nearly always a file, a function or a check name, which is exactly the shape that wants backticks.
The previous and next navigation's link **text**, which took the escaper while the same title takes the renderer in the page header and on the index card.
The previous and next navigation's `href`, which **was not escaped at all**. Also `superseded_by`, and the `id`, `date` and `file` interpolations.

body.text: Left alone because they were already right: `body[].text`, list items, table headers and rows, commit subjects, the footer. Left alone because they are **not prose**, and now documented in the file as such: tags, decision ids, commit hashes, and `pre` block text — a listing's backticks and asterisks are content, not markup that failed to render. The rule the file now states is mechanical: **an interpolation inside a quoted attribute takes the attribute escaper; an interpolation in element content takes the inline renderer unless it is an identifier.**
The measured result

`tools/chronicle.py` is **+180/-25**. The regenerated diff is **37 files and 41 lines**: **34 meta descriptions and 7 `alt` attributes, and nothing else**. Of the 34 descriptions, 17 changed only by escaping a quote or an apostrophe, 5 only by having markup removed, and 12 by both. All 7 `alt` attributes gained an escaped apostrophe, and 2 of them also lost backticks that a screen reader would have read out. `index.html` did not change at all — the site subtitle carries no markup and no quote.

`chronicle.json` is **byte-identical to `HEAD`**. That is the property which makes a change like this safe to run across an append-only corpus at all: it alters how entries render, and not one word of what any of them says.

All 60 pages were then re-parsed with a real HTML parser rather than a regular expression: **zero unexpected attributes on any tag, zero raw angle bracket or double quote in any attribute source, and zero attribute values still carrying a backtick or a `**`.**
One thing for the owner, and it is genuinely theirs

**The 54 legacy lone-asterisk spans are live on the published site**, showing bare asterisks to readers across 15 entries. Append-only means they can only be addressed by superseding those entries, or by reversing `LF-173` and rendering `*x*` as emphasis after all. `LF-173` was a settled, measured decision and this work deliberately did **not** re-open it — but the corpus it was measured against was **2 strings**, one of which was a false positive, and that corpus is now **54**, all of which read as genuine emphasis, with **zero glob false positives** under the guarded pattern. Recorded here as an open question, not as a recommendation.
What this entry does not have

The work sits on `lf/prc-chronicle-rendering` and is uncommitted as this is written, so there are **no commit hashes** here. The gate was run at **tier 1** and nothing above it: **17 passed, 0 failed, 25 skipped**, with `chronicle current` green over the 59 entries that existed when it ran, and `banned terms` clean across 290 tracked files. No screenshot either — the whole subject of this entry is a class of defect that a picture of the page cannot show.
Wrong in a stable, reproducible way

Four rendering defects in this tool have now been found by the people writing entries with it, and none by the tool itself — table headers, `alt`, the meta description, and an emphasis form nothing scanned for. Every one of them was invisible on the page and visible only somewhere else: in a browser's attribute parser, in a search result, in a link preview.

**A journal that checks its own output against its own source cannot see a generator that is wrong in a stable, reproducible way.** That is a sentence this journal has already written once, about a different tool — a gate that runs over all shipped content proves nothing about a branch the shipped content never enters. It is now true about the journal itself.

entries.title: The schema was a fuse, not a fix
entries.summary: `LF-219`. `data/schema/anchor.schema.json` typed slot coordinates as `integer`, contradicting `PLC-01`'s continuous positions — both rule engines have modelled position as a float since free placement landed, but a fractional slot in an anchor file was a schema error. Widening it to `number` is four lines. The entry is what widening it exposed: **three integer assumptions in `validate_data.py` that the schema had been keeping unreachable**, one of them a hard crash that names no anchor, and two that would have silently stopped covering the case they exist for. Plus one trap in GDScript found, bounded, and shipped as a warning rather than as silence.

body.text: `data/schema/anchor.schema.json` typed a slot coordinate as `integer`. Both rule engines have been continuous end to end since free placement — `sim/content.py` loads slots through `float()` into float64, and `Sim._placement_reason()` accepts any float and always has. So the schema was the **only** thing forcing authored slots onto the integer grid, and it was doing it while `PLC-01`, `PLC-04` and several agent briefs said the opposite.

It had already cost something concrete, which is why it was a ticket rather than a note. The `LF-185` re-siting pass was briefed that slots could be fractional, discovered the schema only after it had started, **searched integer positions only**, and may have left better sub-tile positions unreachable on six anchors. The ticket was filed in the pass entry 56 covers — **The generator was not the deliverable. Thirteen tiles was.**, `the-generator-was-not-the-deliverable`.
The widening is `integer` to `number` and a rewritten description. **The audit is the entry.**
Three integer assumptions were hiding behind the schema, and one was a crash

The schema had been doing the validator's job for it. Every one of these was written correctly against a world where a slot is an integer, and every one of them was already sitting in `validate_data.py` waiting for the day it was not. Widening the type without looking would have shipped all three.

**A hard crash.** `check_terrain`'s ramp and cliff slot loop calls `height_at(sx, sy)`, which is `grid[ty][tx]`. Measured on a fixture, not predicted: `TypeError: tuple indices must be integers or slices, not float`, raised as a stack trace **with the anchor id nowhere in it** — from the one tool whose entire job is naming the offending anchor. Each slot now resolves to its containing tile first, through a new `slot_tile()` helper: slot coordinates are tile centres, so tile `t` spans `[t-0.5, t+0.5)` and the containing tile is `floor(v + 0.5)`, which is the identity for an integer slot.

**Two checks that would have silently stopped covering the thing they are for.** Neither would have crashed, neither would have gone red, and both would have started accepting inputs that both engines refuse:

items: Bounds tested `0 <= x < w`. A slot at `(13.1, 3)` on a 14-wide board **passes that** — and `_placement_reason()` refuses it, because a footprint of radius `0.45` at a tile-centre coordinate needs `x + 0.45 <= w - 0.5`, and 13.55 is past 13.5.

The on-path test was `tuple(s) in all_tiles`. A slot at `(1.0, 5.6)` beside a lane running along y=5 is 0.6 from the centreline — **illegal to both engines**, which want a standoff of `0.95` — and it lands in tile (1,6), which is not a lane tile. So it passed.

body.text: Both are now the engines' own predicate rather than an integer restatement of it: footprint-aware bounds, plus a lane standoff of `lane_half_width + FOOTPRINT_RADIUS`, with `FOOTPRINT_RADIUS` **imported from `sim/engine.py` rather than copied**. For an integer slot the acceptance set is provably identical — an integer point at least one tile off an axis-aligned integer polyline is at distance at least 1.0, and `0 <= x <= w-1` satisfies the footprint interval exactly — and the full validator output is **byte-identical to the pre-change baseline across all 58 documents**. It was also checked against `Sim._placement_reason()` directly on the same three positions, and the two agree at the 0.95 boundary. A duplicated point-to-segment walk in the dead-slot check was collapsed into the same shared function while the file was open; there were two implementations of distance-to-nearest-lane in one validator, which is the drift this project keeps paying for.
That is the shape worth naming. **A schema constraint was the only thing keeping three validator bugs from being reachable.** Widening the type did not create them. It exposed them.
The trap that was found and named rather than shipped

`AnchorSim.available_slots()` returns `Vector2i(int(sx), int(sy))`. It **truncates**. It has two callers that matter here — `anchor_view.gd::_next_autobuild_candidate()` and `main.gd`'s `--build` hook — so on a fractional-slot anchor those two site an emplacement at the **floor** of the authored position rather than at it. If the floor happens to be illegal, `build_at()` returns false and the build **silently does not happen**: no hang, because the autobuild loop exits on its own `placed_one` flag, and nothing anywhere is red.

That was **not** a reason to refuse the widening. The trap is bounded to two headless verification hooks, no shipped anchor can reach it, and nothing else in GDScript truncates — the rules read only `slots.size()`, the editor overlay already draws through `float(slot[0])`, and the particle code hashes **placed** positions rather than authored slots. But it was not shipped in silence either. `validate_data.py` now emits a **warning** on any fractional slot, naming that exact call site. It is silent for all 24 shipped anchors, which all still author integers, and it fires the moment one does not. `LF-238`.

One line of irony worth keeping. `available_slots()` is the same accessor behind `LF-228` — the ward engagement cue that could never fire, written up in entry 57, **The instruments were standing where the player never stands**. Its **name** cost a bug there, and `LF-233` is open to rename it. Its **return type** has now cost one here. One function, twice, for two unrelated reasons.
Proof, both directions

A fixture anchor — anchor-01 with eight **half-tile** slots, every one of them `_placement_reason() == ok` — written into the scratchpad and **never** into `data/anchors/`. Run against HEAD's schema and HEAD's validator in a shadow tree, it fails fourteen ways:

ERROR anchor-99: /slots/0/1: 3.5 is not of type 'integer'      (x13)
ERROR anchor-99: CRASH in check_anchor: TypeError: tuple indices must be
                 integers or slices, not float
-- 14 error(s), 0 warning(s)
body.caption: BEFORE. Thirteen type errors and one crash. Note what the crash line does not contain: any indication of which of the twenty-four anchors produced it.

body.text:
warn  anchor-99: 8 slot(s) are fractional: [[2.0, 3.5], ...] — the rules and
      both graders are continuous, but GDScript's AnchorSim.available_slots()
      truncates to Vector2i, so --build/autobuild will site at the floor of
      these (LF-219)
-- 0 error(s), 1 warning(s)
body.caption: AFTER. Legal content, with the one known consumer that has not caught up named in the message rather than left for whoever hits it.

body.text: The other direction matters more, because a check that accepts everything is not a check. Proved separately, on fractional input: **out-of-bounds, on-path, standoff and duplicate all still fire.** The new predicate is not vacuous — it refuses fractional slots for the same four reasons it refuses integer ones.

And the fixture loads and grades, through the real `grade_anchor()` — which is `sim.run.grade()` minus the `data/anchors/` read, so this is the shipping grader on a board whose every build point is a half tile:

standard  5 of 11   75.6 MW 126%   12%  wave 2
hard      2 of 11   81.0 MW 135%    8%  wave 2
brutal    1 of 10   75.6 MW 126%    6%  wave 2
ok = True
body.caption: Columns are the grader's own: distinct winning builds of distinct builds tried, peak load in MW and as a share of capacity, brownout share, and the earliest wave anything died on. Nothing here is a balance claim about anchor-01 — the board is a fixture that was never in `data/anchors/`. It is evidence that a half-tile board is content the engine will actually play.

body.text: What was already float-safe, because that matters too
The audit found more ready than not, and the list is worth recording so the next pass does not re-derive it:

items: `sim/content.py`, which has loaded slots as float64 since free placement landed.
`_placement_reason()`, `_is_placeable()` and `_effective_cap()` in the Python rules.
`sim/coverage.py` and `tools/density.py`, both of which already do continuous geometry off the authored positions.
The dead-slot range check, which was already a float distance — the one part of the validator that had been thinking in the right space all along.
On the GDScript side: the editor overlay draws through `float(slot[0])`, the rules read only `slots.size()`, and the particle code hashes placed positions rather than authored slots.

body.text: **Most of the codebase was ready. The schema and three validator checks were not.**

`tools/genboard.py` changed **only in a docstring**, and that is deliberate. It had cited the old schema as its reason for emitting integer slots, which is no longer a reason at all, so it now cites the real ones: `render()` indexes an ASCII preview grid by slot, the generator binds the **count** far more than the positions, and moving the positions moves every generated board's numbers including the ones `--selftest` asserts byte-identical. Sub-tile emission is real work with its own evidence and is tracked as `LF-239`, not smuggled in behind a schema change.
What this entry does not have

The work sits on `lf/data-fractional-slots` and is uncommitted as this is written, so there are **no commit hashes** here. The gate was run at **tier 1** and nothing above it: **17 passed, 0 failed, 25 skipped**, with `game data` green over **58 documents against 7 schemas and no warnings**, and all 24 shipped anchors validating with output byte-identical to the pre-change baseline. Parity and coverage were not run, and neither was anything that launches Godot — so the `available_slots()` truncation above is read from the source and from its two call sites, and is **not** something this pass watched a running game do. There is no screenshot either: the subject is a type in a schema file and four arithmetic predicates, none of which a frame of the board can show.
A constraint upstream of a bug is a fuse

This is the fourth time in two days that widening or fixing one thing revealed that something else had only ever been correct **by accident**. The grader ordering that worked because authored slots happened to be spread. The ward denominator that worked because autoplay happened to build on slots. The verdict branch that worked because no shipped board had a low ceiling. And now three validator checks that worked because the schema happened to forbid the input that would break them.

**A constraint upstream of a bug is not a fix. It is a fuse, and nobody knows it is load-bearing until it is removed.** The practical corollary is what turned a four-line ticket into a day of work: when you widen a type, the job is not the widening. It is finding everything downstream that had quietly been relying on the narrower one.

entries.title: The derivation was right. The prediction was wrong. The grade table said nothing.
entries.summary: `BAL-04` / `LF-187`, decision 082. `range` in `data/towers.json` is an absolute distance in tiles, tuned against 18×15 boards whose lanes run 24–51; decision 073 moved the board target to 48×48, where the generated lanes run 68–80. `tools/range_derive.py` holds own-lane coverage fixed and bisects for the range that recovers it — a per-emplacement ladder from 1.36× to 1.86×, with the mortar landing on 13.0 exactly. Then the honest check. The confident prediction that applying the ladder now would gut the shipped campaign was **measured, and it is wrong**: all 24 anchors still grade `ok`. What the grade table cannot see is that the top difficulty dissolves.

commits.subject: feat(balance): range derived from lane length at 48 squared, and the grade table cannot see what it costs

body.text: `range` in `data/towers.json` is an absolute distance in tiles. It was tuned against 18×15 boards whose lanes run 24 to 51 tiles, and decision 073 then moved the board target to 48×48 — where the generated board's lanes run 68 to 80. A constant absolute range covers a shrinking share of a wave's route as the board grows, and it shrinks **silently**: nothing anywhere in the campaign goes red about it. This is the range half of `BAL-04` and `LF-187`, and it was the top item on the priority list because every theatre-scale board is behind it.
The invariant is own-lane coverage, and the two better metrics could not be used

`tools/range_derive.py` (new, 561 lines) holds exactly one quantity fixed — **own-lane coverage**, the share of **one** lane's length a slot can reach, taken as the median over a board's authored slots — and bisects for the range at which a generated 48² board recovers what a shipped act-3 slot has today. Two coverage metrics already exist in `sim/coverage.py` and neither one is the right instrument here, which is worth saying because both were considered first:

items: `lane_coverage()` is length-weighted across every lane, so it divides a well-sited gun's score by the lane count and reads four lanes as a range problem. A board with more lanes would ask for more range purely for having more lanes.

`presence_coverage()` is much the better predictor of real uptime — rank correlation **+0.748** against **+0.520** (`LF-217`) — but it is measured from a live run on the board's own slots. It does not exist until the board has been graded, and this solve has to run **before** there is any content to grade. So the geometry is the derivation and the grader is the check, in that order.

body.text: The ladder

Eight shipped act-3 anchors (median lane 41 tiles, 96 slots) against a generated 48² four-lane board (lanes 68–80 tiles, 78 slots). The middle column is the quantity being held constant across the move, not an output.
Plus the four `upgrade.range` overrides, solved the same way — 4.4→7.1, 5.4→9.0, 6.8→12.3, 8.0→15.2 — because an upgrade whose range does not scale with its base becomes a downgrade.

**The mortar lands on 13.0 exactly.** A previous session posted a target of about 13 tiles to issue 17 by a completely different route, and that number is the whole reason this pass had a target at all. Reproducing it from lane geometry turns it from an input into a check.
Two things a single multiplier would have got wrong

**The ladder does not scale uniformly.** 1.36× at the short end against 1.86× at the long: a short range on a winding lane sits on the steep part of the coverage curve and a long one does not, so one factor applied to every row is wrong in both directions at once.

**The support emplacements belong in the derivation, and decision 074 left them out.** `shield-wall` (slow), `scan-relay` (reveal) and `anchor-damper` (damp) have their range tested against **unit** positions by `Sim._covered_by()`, with the same squared-distance compare the firing loop uses — they are lane-coverage quantities exactly as much as a weapon's range is. Holding them fixed at 48² would have silently halved the Act II damper decision that decision 027 exists to create.
One field that reads as tuning and is not

`restorer.range` is never read by either rules implementation. `Sim.capacity_now()` (`sim/engine.py:608`) adds `effect_value` for every online restorer with no distance test at all, and `scripts/anchor_sim.gd:383` mirrors it. That is a measurement rather than a reading of the code: anchor-20 was graded with the restorer's range at 1.0 and again at 40.0 and `by_difficulty` came back identical field for field — and the same assertion returns `False` when pointed at `pulse-turret`, so it discriminates rather than being vacuously true. The restorer is therefore excluded from the ladder, because scaling nothing is nothing. It is the only emplacement in the game whose siting is free. `LF-242` carries the real question, which is whether it should be.
What the ladder buys on the board it was solved for

On the generated 48² board at the **authored** ranges, brutal is a single-solution level — 1 winning build out of 16 tried — and all three difficulties die on wave 8. At the derived ranges it is 4 of 16 at all three, it grades `ok`, and the death wave separates for the first time: 9 / 9 / 8.

body.caption: The board the ladder was solved against, straight out of `tools/genboard.py --preview`. Four lanes of 68 to 80 tiles across 48², 78 slots. A digit is a lane index, `#` a tile two lanes share, `o` an authored slot, `S` a spawn and `K` the anchor. The last line is the problem in one sentence: at the ranges the campaign ships today, an emplacement at maximum range reaches 17.5% of the longest lane it sits on and 4.7% of the lane set.

body.text: The prediction was made confidently, checked, and was wrong

This is the part of the session worth keeping. Before anything had been measured, the position stated plainly in this session was that applying the ladder now **would gut the current game** — a 13-tile mortar on a 41-tile lane is absurd on its face, so the shipped campaign would fall over. `--shipped-impact` was written to **check** that claim rather than to assert it.
It is wrong. **All 24 shipped anchors grade 24/24 `ok` at the derived ranges, completely unchanged.** Not one of them notices.

What actually happens is a failure the grade table has no column for: the top difficulty dissolves. On brutal the share of tried builds that **win** goes **25% → 43%**; the median anchor's distinct winning builds goes **3 → 6**; anchor-02, 09 and 11 go from 2 winning builds to **8, 7 and 8**. And not one anchor trips `sim/run.py`'s difficulty-is-not-biting rule, because that rule fires only when **every** distinct build clears — the closest any anchor came was anchor-14 on standard, at 13 of 14.

So this is the **second independent proof that the grade table is not a valid selector**, after decision 081 found board quality and grade count anti-correlated across five lattice orderings. There a green grade could not choose the right answer; here a green grade cannot see the wrong one. `LF-243` carries the candidate replacement — win **share** per difficulty, required to fall monotonically across the three tiers. The shipped campaign is 40 / 30 / 25 percent today, monotone and discriminating; at the derived ranges it is 55 / 47 / 43, still monotone but compressed. That needs a derivation and a decision entry of its own, not a constant fitted to today's data — which is exactly why `PRESSURE_FLOOR` was deleted in decision 067.
Deliberately not done

items: **The patch is printed and never applied.** It lands with the first 48² content, per decision 082. Nothing under `data/` changed in this commit; the diff is one new tool, the decision, and the backlog.

**No dynamic coverage pass on the generated board.** `sim/coverage.py`'s `InstrumentedSim` is 6.8× overhead at 78 emplacements and one pass is about 21 minutes (`LF-230`). The geometric solve is the derivation; `--grade` is the check that was run instead.
**`LF-234`'s act-1 presence ceilings are not re-measured** against the derived ladder — anchor-02 68.3%, 03 65.3%, 04 50.1%, 05 41.8%. Decision 082 puts that with the content rather than here.

body.text: Gate: tier 2, **26 passed, 0 failed, 16 correctly skipped**, 32,372 ms. No rules file and no data file changed, so tier 2 is the bar. `python syntax` went from 63 files to 64 — the new tool tracked **before** the run rather than after it, which is the trap where a new untracked file is invisible to the gate, avoided on purpose this time.

entries.title: 1,440 runs of the whole game per parity check, and not one of them ever pressed the sell button
entries.summary: `LF-244`, decision 083. `Sim._dispatch_one()` accepts eight scheduled verbs. Across all **twenty** policies the grader ever builds, exactly two are ever scheduled — so every one of the 1,440 `rules parity` runs executes the **absent** branch for `sell`, `upgrade`, `set_online`, `build`, `target_mode`, the shutter and `speed`. Those six are precisely the ones with a key bound to them in `project.godot`. A fixture, a harness and a `verbs agree` gate check at tier 3 close it. The route here was not a hunt for parity holes — it was a wrong first read of the campaign's economy.

commits.subject: test(gate): the six verbs nobody graded are the six with a key bound to them

body.text: The previous entry, an hour before this one — `the-grade-table-said-nothing` — derived emplacement range from lane length and then found that the grade table could not see what the change cost. That left a question hanging about the instrument rather than the content: what **else** can the grader not see? The answer turned out to be most of the player's interface.
The measurement

`Sim._dispatch_one()` accepts eight scheduled verbs — `speed`, `call_wave`, `ability`, `target_mode`, `sell`, `upgrade`, `set_online`, `build`. `standard_policies()` returns **twenty** distinct policies, and sixteen of them schedule nothing whatsoever. Of the four that do anything at all: one schedules `call_wave`, once, on the first tick; two schedule `ability`, 53 actions between them, and only the surge and the overcharge — never the shutter; and the fourth opts into veterancy rather than pressing a button. `chain_bounty` is set by no policy in the set.

So every one of the 1,440 `rules parity` runs executes the **absent** branch for `target_mode`, `sell`, `upgrade`, `set_online`, `build`, the shutter ability and `speed`. `scripts/test/parity.gd:317` has carried a mirrored `upgrade` dispatch since `BAL-01`, and nothing has ever driven it.

**One number in the record needs correcting, and this entry is where that happens rather than in the record itself.** `LF-244`'s backlog title, the commit message above and decision 083 all state that `ability` is scheduled by **three** policies. Re-running `standard_policies()` against the tree at `b3e861a` and counting says **two** — `surge-on-peak` (20 actions) and `overcharge-greedy` (33). The 53-action total those three places also record is exactly right; it is the policy count that is off by one. Nothing about the finding moves: fewer policies pressing buttons makes the hole wider, not narrower. It is written down here because `docs/DECISIONS.md` is append-only and so is this journal.
Why this is worse than an unauthored firing arc, and it is checkable rather than rhetorical

An unauthored `cos_half_angle` (decision 078, `PLC-03`) is inert in the shipped game **by construction** — the acceptance bar for that work was that no shipped emplacement row gains one, so the untested branch is a branch nobody can reach. These six are different in kind. They are the player's entire interface, and `project.godot`'s action map has one bound action for each of them:

An `upgrade()` that merged its stats differently in the two engines would mean every balance conclusion about an upgraded board describes a game nobody plays — and the owner plays the Windows build, which is the whole reason decision 078 exists in the first place. This is the third instance of the same principle: **a gate that runs the whole game proves nothing about a branch the shipped data never enters.**
What landed

`data/schema/fixtures/scheduled-verbs.json` (154 lines — four emplacement types, one walker spawned three times, ten scheduled actions, 320 ticks), `tools/verb_parity.py` (481 lines), `scripts/test/verb_parity.gd` (204 lines), and a `verbs agree` check at tier 3 costing 2,573 ms. The Python side drives `Sim._dispatch_one()` itself; the GDScript side drives `scripts/anchor_sim.gd` through a mirror of `parity.gd`'s match block. Same shape `tools/arc_parity.py` established. Five claims:

items: The two engines agree **byte for byte** on fire pattern, funds, spend, bus load, emplacement count, and every unit's distance and hit points, on every tick.

The money trajectory matches arithmetic done **in the harness** from the fixture's own costs: 2000 − 100 − 200 − 300 = 1400, −150 upgrade = 1250, −400 build = 850, + floor(400 × SELL_REFUND) = 1090. Two engines wrong the same way still fail.
`upgrade` is proved **geometrically**, not by reading a stat back out — the next section.
`set_online` and the shutter are priced on the bus to the exact megawatt, and the unit inside `hold_tiles` is held at a standstill for all thirty ticks the shutter is down.

`speed` is **proved** to be the no-op `sim/engine.py`'s own comment claims it is, by re-running the whole fixture with the speed actions stripped and requiring identical output. That is the demonstration `BAL-01`'s task list asked for and never got.

body.text: Claim 3 is the one worth copying: an upgrade proved by geometry, not by a read-back

The obvious way to check `upgrade` is to apply it and read `range` back out of the emplacement. That proves a write happened, in one engine, and nothing else. So the fixture does it structurally instead. `verb-probe-reach` is built at (10, 0) with range 3.0, and the lane runs straight along y = 4 — a 4.0-tile standoff. It **cannot fire at all**: not at a poorly chosen target, not at a distant one, not at any target, no matter where anything on the board stands. After the upgrade merges range 8.0 it reaches sqrt(8² − 4²) = 6.9282 tiles of lane either side of x = 10.

So the check is: **zero** shots from that row before tick 150, and after it, every tick it fires on must have a unit within 8.0 and **none** within 3.0. An engine that merged the wrong key, or merged nothing, or merged into the wrong emplacement, cannot satisfy that in either direction.
The fixture, tick by tick

tick  funds  spend    load placed units  verb(s)
      0   1400    600    60.0      3     1
     30   1400    600    60.0      3     1  speed
     60   1400    600    60.0      3     2  target_mode
     90   1400    600    30.0      3     2  set_online
    120   1400    600    60.0      3     2  set_online
    150   1250    750    60.0      3     2  upgrade
    180    850   1150   100.0      4     2  build
    200    850   1150   100.0      4     3  speed
    210    850   1150   155.0      4     3  ability
    240    850   1150   100.0      4     3  ability
    270   1090   1150    60.0      3     3  sell
    319   1090   1150    60.0      3     3

ok - 7 verb(s) over 320 ticks, 112 shots, python and godot identical and
     matching the fixture's own arithmetic
body.caption: Regenerated for this entry with `.venv/bin/python tools/verb_parity.py --report` — about three seconds, one headless windowless Godot. `load` is the bus in MW; `verb(s)` is what the schedule dispatched on that tick.

body.text: The bus column is where the identification lives. 60 → 30 → 60 MW as emplacement 2 goes offline and back: no other subset of the fixture's draws {10, 20, 40} sums to 30, so the drop names **that row** rather than merely reporting that something changed. Then 100 → 155 → 100 as the shutter comes down and lifts. And the funds column is compared against the harness's own arithmetic rather than against either engine, so two engines wrong the same way still fail.
Proved red first, five ways, and the last two are the interesting ones

`--corrupt upgrade | refund | bus | target | engine`. The first three break an **expectation** — they change a number the harness asserts. That is necessary and not sufficient: all three would still go red against a comparator that compared nothing at all, because they fail against the fixture's arithmetic rather than against the other engine. So the last two break **behaviour** instead. `target` makes the mode switch a no-op; `engine` perturbs one tick of one engine's result. A vacuous comparator passes those two, and this one does not.
A bug found in my own check, which is this entry in miniature

The first `--corrupt target` run did not go red. It **crashed** — an `IndexError` out of `check_target_mode()`, which indexed `hps[tick + 1]` while guarding only on `hps[probe]`. A check that raises instead of reporting is not a passing check and is barely a failing one: it proves the harness ran, not that the engines agree. It was fixed in the same change. It is a small instance of exactly the thing this whole entry is about — the verifier itself being unverified.
The alternative, measured rather than dismissed, and rejected here only

Adding upgrade-buying and selling **policies** to `standard_policies()` is the obvious move. It would put the verbs into the real 1,440-run parity set instead of a fixture, and improve the grader at the same time. It was measured, not waved away: a prototype `upgrade-ladder` policy — preference byte-identical to `cheap-mass`, plus a schedule walking `upgrade` by index in three passes so an unaffordable upgrade is retried once kills have paid for it — spends **2,280** on act-3 anchors against the base mean of **1,835**, and adds a new distinct winning build on **10 of 72** anchor-by-difficulty cells. It never trivialises anything: no cell reaches distinct-winning equals distinct-tried, and it wins exactly one brutal cell in the whole campaign.

It is rejected **here and only here**. A twenty-first policy moves `distinct_builds_tried` on every anchor in the campaign and adds 72 rows to the parity set — that is a re-grade, and a re-grade is `BAL-04`'s blast radius, not a verification change's. `LF-245` carries it with its numbers.

`call_wave`, the surge and the overcharge are deliberately **out** of the fixture: those three are what shipped policies already schedule, so `rules parity` covers them across 1,440 runs and the fixture would only add cost. The harness asserts its own scope rather than trusting it — if the fixture ever stops scheduling one of the seven in-scope verbs, the check fails rather than quietly shrinking to whatever is left in it.
How this was actually found, including a first read that was wrong

The route here was not a hunt for parity holes. It came from measuring the campaign's economy across all 24 anchors, where **55–62% of every fund the player ever has is never spent** (act 1 58%, act 2 55%, act 3 62%; anchor-24 finishes with 4,358 unspent). The first read of that was that the economy is dead — a resource the game hands out and never asks for back.

That read is **wrong**, and the correction is what exposed the verb hole. Counting the cost of upgrading every emplacement on the board the grader actually built absorbs most of the surplus, leaving 22 / 16 / 28% unspent by act — and anchor-10 and anchor-11 go **negative**, at −1% and −10%, meaning a fully-upgraded board is not affordable there at all. So the surplus is an artefact of the **grader's repertoire**, not of the game's design: no policy in `standard_policies()` has ever bought an upgrade. That is the moment the question stopped being about money and started being about which verbs the grader has never pressed.

One more number from the same pass, filed under `LF-245`: by act 3 the board stands at **97–100%** of its final size before the first enemy spawns, with only 1.1–1.4 waves carrying any build at all — one act-3 anchor reaches a flat 100%. Upgrades are the only shipped mechanism that could sequence that. Issue 17's sequencing note predicted it; this measured it.
API traps found, so the next session does not rediscover them
