items: `AnchorSim` has **no `call_wave()` verb at all**. `parity.gd`'s `"call_wave"` branch sets a local flag that its own wave lead-in loop consumes; there is nothing to call.
`parity.gd`'s `build` verb takes `args["slot"]` as a two-element array, not `x` / `y` keys. A fixture that writes `x` / `y` silently exercises a different contract instead of failing.

`data/schema/fixtures/` is excluded by `validate_data.py`'s `discover_documents()` but is **not** excluded by `parity_inputs_digest()`. Adding this fixture took the digest's data set from 78 files to 79 and forced a full tier-4 re-comparison on **both** platforms. That is the conservative behaviour and it is correct; it is written down so the next person adding a fixture expects the cost rather than discovers it.

body.text: The gate

Tier 4: **43 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped**, 2,177,204 ms — about 36 minutes. Both parity legs freshly verified at the new digest `205413f5378e`, 1,440 runs identical on each. `reap.py` clean afterwards. The new check sits at tier 3 rather than tier 2 for the same two reasons `firing arcs agree` does: it is one headless windowless Godot of the same class, and tier 2 is already over its own 28,000 ms budget (`LF-178`, measured at 37,669 ms on a clean run at the start of this session), where the standing answer is to move a check out rather than move the number again.

No screenshot with this one, because nothing visible changed — this is a verification change end to end. The tick table above is the artefact, and it regenerates in three seconds from the tool rather than sitting in a PNG that can go stale without anything going red.

entries.title: At 200% interface scale the playfield was 4 px wide, and every accessibility check passed
entries.summary: `LF-247`, decisions 084 and 085. The two instrument panels are 948 px that do not shrink when the interface scale shrinks the logical viewport, so the board was drawn into a strip 4 px wide at 200% — completely covered, on every anchor. `accessibility` reported 192 text items clean throughout, and `scenario a11y-worst`, which runs at exactly that scale on exactly that anchor **because** it is the worst case, passed. A derived bound, an undocking threat panel and a 9 ms tier-1 check close it. Decision 084 is the other half: it corrects a number inside an owner-taken decision and finds the decision's answer survives anyway.

commits.subject: fix(ui): the playfield was 4 px wide at 200% and every accessibility check passed

body.text: Third entry of this session, and the three share a theme worth naming rather than leaving for a reader to notice. `the-grade-table-said-nothing` derived emplacement range from lane length and then found the grade table could not see what the change cost — all 24 anchors still graded `ok` while the top difficulty's bite was halved. `never-pressed-the-sell-button` found that the parity check had run the whole game 1,440 times per invocation and never once pressed the sell button. This one found a board 4 px wide behind an accessibility audit reporting 192 text items clean. **Three times in one session, the instrument was the thing that was wrong.**
The defect

The strip the board is drawn into is `vp.x − 2·gutter − COL_W − THREAT_W`. `COL_W` is 420 and `THREAT_W` is 528 — **948 px of instrument panel that does not shrink when the interface scale shrinks the logical viewport.** The viewport does: 200% means a 960×540 logical design space. On every anchor:

The 4 px is not the plain subtraction — that goes negative. `Ui.gutter()` is itself derived from whatever is left over and clamps at 4 px a side, so the arithmetic bottoms out instead of crashing, and what it bottoms out at is a board four pixels across. The two panels cover it completely; it is drawn **behind** them. A zoom-to-fit at that width clamps to `ZOOM_MIN_FLOOR` and shows nothing at all. **200% is an offered, shipped setting on which the game cannot be played.**

body.caption: The defect. anchor-24 at 200% interface scale, before the fix — the instrument column on the left, the threat panel and minimap on the right, and between them no board. There is a playfield in this frame; it is the four-pixel seam.

body.text: Why nothing caught it, which is the part worth keeping

Decision 050 measured these panels' **vertical** fit exhaustively and made both scroll, with their controls pinned outside the scroll region. That work is correct and it stays. It is also about **text** — WCAG SC 1.4.4 and 1.4.10, content not lost at 200%. `tools/validate/a11y.py` audits text items, and **a playfield is not a text item.** So `accessibility` reported 192 items clean, and `scenario a11y-worst` — which runs at `ui_scale: 2.0` on anchor-24 **precisely because** that is the worst case decision 048 identified — asserted that the inspector showed the emplacement it had just selected, took its frame and its text inventory, and passed over a 4 px board.

Sharper: the measurement already existed. `scripts/display_settings.gd` recorded that at 200% interface scale the strip is 4 px wide on anchor-24 and that the two panels eat nearly all of a 960 px design space — and used it to justify one thing, defaulting edge-scroll off, because a 48 px edge-scroll margin does not fit inside a 4 px strip. The number was right, it was written down, it was read, and the consequence was never drawn. **A number written into a comment is not a number anything checks.** That comment now says so about itself, at the same call site.
How it was found: by taking a frame decision 073 said to take

Not by auditing the interface. By generating the first 48×48 theatre-scale board with `tools/genboard.py` and looking at it in the engine — the thing `docs/STATE.md` and the previous entry both noted had never actually been done, because no shipped anchor is that size (anchor-24, the biggest, is 18×15). Two separate findings fell out of that one capture: the camera could not fit the board, and at 200% there was no board on screen at all.

body.caption: The first 48×48 board this project has drawn in the engine, and the frame that produced both `LF-247` and `LF-248`. 2,304 tiles against the 270 of a shipped anchor. Decision 073 chose this size in the abstract; this is the first time anyone looked at one.

body.text: The fix

`Ui.PLAYFIELD_MIN_W := COL_W` — **the board is at least as important as the narrowest instrument panel this project already treats as usable.** Derived rather than picked: `COL_W` was solved against the 16 px type ladder (decisions 045 and 046) and is the smallest width anything in this interface is permitted to be, so a board given less than that is being told it matters less than the readout beside it. Around it, `threat_docked()`, `reserved_w()` and `strip_w()`, so the rule lives in exactly one place and is read by both `anchor_view.gd`'s `_strip_geometry()` and `hud.gd` — the two of them have to make the same call about where the panel goes, and two copies of that is one too many.

Above the width at which docking both panels would breach the bound, the threat panel stops reserving strip width and becomes an overlay toggled on `lf_threat_toggle`. The threshold is derived from the widths themselves and never written as a scale number — it lands near 137% today, and writing 1.37 into the source would be a constant that stops being true the moment either panel width moves. The binding was generated through `tools/godot/setup_input.gd` per decision 042, not hand-edited into `project.godot`'s `[input]` block.

body.caption: The same screen after. The threat panel and minimap have undocked and reserve nothing; what is left in their place, top right, is the affordance `INCOMING · MAP — I` naming the key that brings them back. Without it a player at 150% and above has no way to discover the tactical map still exists.
Zoom-to-fit at 200% after the fix: the whole board framed inside the strip. The same control at the same scale before the fix clamped to `ZOOM_MIN_FLOOR` and drew nothing.

body.text: The claim worth making about those numbers is not that they look right — it is that the running game and the gate's arithmetic produce the **same** number rather than two plausible ones. `scenario a11y-worst` was re-run for this entry against `74f1f7c` rather than quoted from the commit:

frame  assertion                                    got
    3  hud.selected        == "pulse-turret"       pulse-turret   pass
    3  hud.threat_docked   == false                false          pass
    3  hud.threat_open     == false                false          pass
    3  view.strip.w        >= 420                  508.0          pass
    3  view.strip.zoom_min >  0.05                 0.240530303    pass
    7  hud.threat_open     == true                 true           pass
    7  view.strip.w        >= 420                  508.0          pass
   10  hud.threat_open     == false                false          pass

SCENARIO pass=true  anchor-24  ui_scale 2.0  300 frames
body.caption: `.venv/bin/python tools/scenario.py data/scenarios/a11y-worst.json`, re-run at `74f1f7c` for this entry — one headless, windowless Godot. Frames 5 and 8 press `lf_threat_toggle` through `Input.parse_input_event()` and the assertions land on the frame after, because the press queues (`LF-139`). The strip is 508 px both while the overlay is shut and while it is open, so `the overlay does not take the width back` is part of the same run. And `zoom_min` came back at 0.240530303 against a board that projects to 2112 px wide: 508 / 2112 is 0.240530303 exactly.

body.text: A measured refusal, and it went against the ticket
`LF-247` proposed two ways to keep the minimap on screen when the threat panel undocks. **Both were built, measured, and rejected**, and the minimap travels with the overlay instead.

items: **A minimap-only sliver kept docked on the right.** `MINIMAP_MAP_W` plus padding is 244 px, which leaves the board at 264 px at 200% — it breaches `PLAYFIELD_MIN_W` on its own, so it does not solve the bug it exists to work around.

**Relocating the minimap into the instrument column.** It fits horizontally — a 508 px strip against a 420 px column, no overlap — and it looked right in a capture. It costs 203 px of a 540 px viewport: the column's scroll budget drops from 426 px to 223 px and the nine-button build bar, whose content ends at y=383, goes below the fold. That trades **nine controls for one readout**, which inverts decision 050's own rule that controls are pinned and readouts scroll.

body.caption: The rejected attempt, kept because a refusal with a picture behind it is a different thing from a refusal with an argument behind it. The tactical map is in the instrument column and reads well; there is not one emplacement button on screen. This is the frame that decided it.

body.text: What `CAM-04`'s risk note objected to was the minimap **scrolling away unbidden** — something the player did not ask for, cannot see happen and cannot undo except by hunting for a scrollbar. A deliberate toggle with a permanent on-screen affordance is a different thing, and it is exactly the status the threat readout beside it now has. The two are read together anyway: what is coming, and where it is.
The new check, and the four ways it was proved red

`playfield width` — tier 1, **9 ms**, text-only, no Godot and no frame. It parses the constants out of `scripts/ui_theme.gd`, the scale ladder out of `scripts/display_settings.gd` and the base viewport out of `project.godot`, then evaluates the bound at every offered scale. The interesting part is `STRIP_FORMULA`, which pins the four geometry expressions **verbatim** against the GDScript: rewrite `strip_w()` and the check fails by name rather than quietly continuing to evaluate a formula the game no longer uses. That is what makes a text-only mirror safe to trust — it can only go stale loudly.

It was proved red four separate ways before it was trusted: against the pre-fix tree, against a rewritten `strip_w()`, against a 250% scale added to the ladder, and against `COL_W` raised to 480. The tier-1 docstring counts moved 17/26/40/43 to 18/27/41/44 and `tier counts` stayed green.

[  ok  ] playfield width           9ms  playfield >= 420px at all 6 scales:
        1x 940px, 1.1x 765px, 1.25x 556px, 1.5x 828px (undocked),
        1.75x 645px (undocked), 2x 508px (undocked)

tier 1 — 18 passed · 0 failed · 26 skipped · 7105ms
body.caption: Re-run for this entry. Six scales, not the five in the defect table above: `Display.UI_SCALES` also offers 110%, where the strip was already 765 px and the panel stays docked. The check reads the ladder out of `display_settings.gd` rather than carrying its own copy, so a scale added to the options screen is a scale it covers on the next run.

body.text: Decision 084: a correction inside an owner-taken decision, whose answer survives it

The same measurement that found the shipped defect found a wrong number in decision 073, which chose the 48² board target. Part of 073's case was a zoom-to-fit row that divided by the **full viewport** instead of this strip: it tabulates 0.312 at 100% and 0.156 at 200%, which are `1920/6144` and `960/6144`. The real capture comes back at **0.1530**, which is `940/6144` exactly — 2.04× out at 100%, and 223× out at 200%, where the real strip was 4 px and the real fit was 0.0007.

That is not pedantry, because that row is where the table's **sprite on screen** figures came from, and sprite legibility is the row that **rejected 64²** — 073 says 64² draws a sprite at 30–60 px, below the threshold at which one enemy type can be told from another. Corrected against the real strip at 100% interface scale, sprite width is `256 × zoom`:

**Every candidate now falls inside or below the band 64² was rejected for — including the 32² option 073 called the only size that needs no concession at all.** A row that rejects all three selects nothing.

So the resolution is to **strike the row, not redo the arithmetic**. Zoom-to-fit is the wrong reference for legibility, and decision 073 supplies the reason itself: it concluded that at 48² the board is never fully visible in the playfield and that the minimap does the wide read. Nobody plays at the zoom floor. Legibility belongs at playing zoom, where a sprite is 256 px at zoom 1.0 on a board of any size and board dimension does not enter it. **The board size stays 48².** 073's answer survives its own broken premise, because the discriminator was never valid for any candidate — and that is worth saying out loud rather than quietly banking. The live reasons to prefer 48² over 64² are the ones 073 lists elsewhere and which do not touch this row: `Iso.TILE_W` cannot grow, decision 066 refused a larger atlas cell on a measured VRAM projection, and 64² would commit the project to silhouette-first art.
Treat 32² and 48² as arithmetic on a measurement, not as measurements — if either becomes load-bearing for a further decision, take the frame directly.
One number in the record needs correcting, and this is where that happens

The commit message above states that `scenario a11y-worst` **now runs 8 assertions (was 3)**. Eight is right — the re-run above lists them. Three is not: the scenario file as it stood at `1e59d71`, immediately before this change, carries exactly **one** assertion, `hud.selected == "pulse-turret"`. Nothing about the finding moves, and it moves the wrong way for comfort: the worst-case accessibility scenario, at the worst scale on the worst anchor, asserted precisely one thing about the screen, and that one thing was which emplacement was selected in the inspector. It is written down here because the commit is not editable and neither is this journal.
Not done, deliberately

At 200% the undocked overlay's left edge covers the instrument column's rightmost 20 px — its padding and its scrollbar gutter, no text. The alternative was pushing it clear and losing 12 px of the threat panel's own scrollbar off the right edge of the screen: a covered scrollbar on a panel the player is not reading beats an unreachable one on the panel they are. It is documented at the call site in `hud.gd` and, as far as this entry could find, nowhere else — there is no backlog item behind it, so the call-site note and this paragraph are the whole record.
The gate

Tier 3: **41 passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped** (the three tier-4-only checks), 340,433 ms. `accessibility` 192 items clean, worst contrast 5.08:1 — the audit that missed this is still green, and still correct about the thing it measures. `reap.py` clean. No `.godot` rebuild and no import, so nothing was pulled out from under a running session. Re-run for this entry at `74f1f7c`: tier 1 green in 7,105 ms with `playfield width` at 9 ms, `scenario a11y-worst` green on all eight assertions, and `reap.py` clean afterwards.

The through-line of all three of this session's entries is one sentence and it is not about any of the three bugs. A check that runs the whole game proves nothing about a quantity nothing in it ever asserts on. The grade table ran every anchor and asserted `ok`. The parity check ran 1,440 games and asserted the two engines agreed on what it happened to drive. The accessibility audit ran the worst screen in the game and asserted on text. All three were green, all three were honest, and none of them was looking at the thing that was wrong.

entries.title: Autoplay built twelve dampers, and the render check reported the same two numbers either way
entries.summary: `LF-236` / `LF-250`, and `LF-251` is what the fix uncovered. `Content.unlocked_at()` returns ids alphabetically and `--autoplay` took the first affordable one, so from anchor-10 on it built nothing but anchor dampers — damage 0, twelve of them, a board that cannot kill anything. A tier-3 gate check has been driving that board for its three captures. The fix is a policy, not a sort, and it is small. What fell out of it is not: `game renders` reported `coverage 0.95, 114 tones` before and `coverage 0.95, 114 tones` after, across a board that changed completely.

commits.subject: fix(engine): autoplay built twelve dampers and the render check reported the same numbers either way

body.text: Fourth and last entry of this session, and it closes a run with one sentence running through it. `the-grade-table-said-nothing` ended with a grade table that could not see the top difficulty dissolve. `never-pressed-the-sell-button` ended with a parity check that had run the whole game 1,440 times per invocation and never once pressed the sell button. `four-pixels-of-playfield` ended with an accessibility audit reporting 192 text items clean over a board four pixels wide. This one is the fourth, and it arrived carrying a fifth. **Five times in one session, the instrument was the thing that was wrong.**

rows: brutal's win share went **25% → 43%**, the median anchor's distinct winning builds **3 → 6**
**six of eight** scheduled verbs were never dispatched once
anchors 03–05's authored slots reach **36–47%** of what the board's slot budget admits
slot **positions** have been vestigial since `PLC-04` — only the count still binds
`accessibility`, 200% interface scale on the worst-case anchor (`LF-247`)
**identical numbers before and after the board changed completely**

body.text: Three of those five have an entry above them and a change landed against them. `LF-246` has neither — it is the one whose consequence is a report describing data the grader stopped reading, and nothing has been done about it yet. This table is the whole of its record in this journal so far, which is worth saying outright rather than leaving a reader to hunt for a page that does not exist.
The defect

`Content.unlocked_at()` ends with `out.sort()`. It returns ids **alphabetically**, and `_autobuild_step()` walked that array first-affordable-wins. The alphabet begins `anchor-damper`, `arc-node`, `flak-array`, `ion-lance`, `mortar-emplacement`, `pulse-turret`. So from anchor-10 on, where the damper unlocks, `--autoplay` **could never build anything else** — and it looked fine on anchor-01 only because `pulse-turret` happens to sort ahead of everything affordable there.

Measured with the engine's own facing dump rather than by eye: `tools/shot.py anchor-24 --facings` printed **24 FACE lines, every one of them `anchor_damper_base` or `anchor_damper_head`** — twelve emplacements at two drawables each, damage 0, nothing on the board that shoots. `autobuild()`'s docstring has promised for fifteen anchors that it builds the way the `cheap-mass` policy would, while doing nothing of the kind: `cheap-mass` is `rest(has("pulse-turret"))` in `sim/engine.py`, and it leads with the turret.

body.caption: anchor-24 under `--autoplay` before the fix. Twelve anchor dampers, and the inspector on the left states what that means without needing any interpretation: `damage none — support`. The reactor bus reads **216 / 290 MW** — twelve times the damper's 18 MW draw, exactly — for a board that cannot kill anything. Wave 1 of 10 has not spawned yet; when it does, nothing in this frame will fire at it. The grey cylinder at the centre is the build ghost under the cursor, not a placement.

body.text: What it invalidated

`tools/check.py`'s `game renders` drives `--autoplay --anchor anchor-24` for all three of its captures — `game-100`, `game-200` and `game-brutal`. So a **tier-3 gate check has been reporting on a board with no damage on it**. Every `--autoplay` screenshot of an act-2 or act-3 anchor is the same, **including ones in this journal**.

Which ones is not a question this entry can answer, and the reason is a gap worth recording as a gap. `chronicle.json` stores an image's file name and its caption; it does not store the command that produced the frame. So the journal cannot be asked for every image captured under `--autoplay` on an anchor above 09 — the evidence needed to enumerate them was never written down in the first place. Nothing above is being corrected: past entries are not rewritten here, and an image captioned as a board under autoplay was captioned truthfully. But an act-2 or act-3 autoplay frame published before today should be read as a picture of the interface and the terrain, not as a picture of the game being played.
The fix is a policy, not a sort

The tempting fix is to change what `unlocked_at()` returns, and it is the wrong one. `sim/run.py` sorts that same list so the GDScript preference tail matches the Python port's — **that sort is a parity input.** Re-ordering it would move an input the 1,440-run `rules parity` check depends on, in order to fix a smoke policy that has nothing to do with parity: trading a real guarantee for a convenience, at the exact moment the previous entry in this journal was about how much that check has been trusted for.

So the change is an `AUTOBUILD_LEAD` constant and an `_autobuild_preference()` that puts `pulse-turret` first and keeps everything else in `unlocked_at()` order, reproducing `cheap-mass` exactly — which is what the docstring already claimed. A named constant rather than a literal because it is the one thing tying the smoke policy to the graded policy it imitates, and a literal would not say so. Thirty-four lines in one file, `scripts/anchor_view.gd`. After: **24 FACE lines, every one `pulse_turret`.**

body.caption: The same capture after. Twelve pulse turrets, amber, muzzles up, on the same board at the same point in the same run. The two panel readouts settle the count without anyone counting sprites: the reactor bus falls **216 → 144 MW**, and funds rise **$790 → $2,830**.

body.text: Those two readouts are worth one more line, because between them they verify the claim from inside the frames rather than from the commit message. The bus falls by 72 MW, which is twelve dampers at 18 MW replaced by twelve turrets at 12 MW. Funds rise by **$2,040**, which is twelve times the $170 by which the turret is cheaper. And both frames imply the same starting purse — `790 + 12 × 270` and `2830 + 12 × 100` are both **$4,030** — so the pair really is one anchor at one point in one run with a single variable moved. That is what a before-and-after is supposed to be able to demonstrate, and it is precisely the kind of thing `game renders` could have asserted and does not.
And the thing that fell out of it, which is worth more than the fix

`game renders` reported `coverage 0.95, 114 tones` **before** this change and `coverage 0.95, 114 tones` **after** it. The same two numbers to the digit, across a board that went from twelve support structures to twelve weapons. **The check is insensitive to what is standing on the board.**

What it actually measures is that the frame is not blank and carries enough distinct colour: `coverage` is the fraction of non-background pixels and `tones` is the count of distinct quantised colours, and both are dominated by terrain, the two instrument panels and text rather than by twelve sprites. That is a real thing to check — it is what catches a blank frame, and it is what catches the flat-grey atlas regression this project has already had once. The defect is not the measurement. It is the **message line**, which names a running game and invites a reading the numbers cannot support.

`LF-251`, with a recommendation that costs nothing to implement: assert the emplacement count and the distinct emplacement ids out of the facing dump **the capture is already printing**, rather than rewording the message to promise less. Rewording is the cheaper fix and the worse one — it would leave the gate taking three captures of the running game and still holding no assertion about the game. A capture that already knows what it drew should say so.
The gate
Tier 3: **41 passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped** (the three tier-4-only checks), 340,419 ms. `anchor grades` 24/24 at every difficulty. `reap.py` clean.

`scenario lf226-fallback` and `scenario gamepad` both pass unchanged — **30 assertions and 9**, counted out of `data/scenarios/lf226_lattice_fallback.json` and `data/scenarios/gamepad_build.json` at this commit for this entry rather than taken from the commit message. Both of them **drive autobuild**, and neither depended on which emplacement it chose. That is not a footnote about the fix being safe. It is the same finding one more time, smaller: two scenarios that exercise the autoplay path carry 39 assertions between them, and not one of them had anything to say about what autoplay built.
How all five were found, which is the part to keep

Not one of the five came out of auditing checks. Every one came from looking at the thing the check was standing in front of. The range work came from grading a generated board. The verb hole came from measuring where the campaign's money goes. The playfield came from generating the first 48-square board this project has drawn and opening it in the engine. This one came from a screenshot of that same board, and from noticing that every object standing on it was identical.

So the lesson is not "write better checks". Every one of these five is arithmetically correct about the quantity it computes — the grades really were `ok`, the two engines really did agree on what they were driven through, the slot arithmetic is right, the text really is legible at 200%, the frame really is not blank. Not one of them was computing the quantity that mattered, and no amount of care inside a check can fix that, because a check cannot know what it is failing to look at. **A check earns trust only against an independent look at its subject.** Five green runs, five honest measurements, five things wrong anyway, and the only thing that found any of them was somebody looking at the game.

entries.title: The bound the ticket asked for was looked for and is not there, so the claim was weakened until it needed no constant
entries.summary: `LF-243`, decision 086, and the first landable slice of `BAL-04`. The ticket asked for win share per difficulty **with a bound on the top tier**. Both campaigns were graded in full — the shipped one and the derived-range one decision 082 refused — and every **shape** statistic came back indistinguishable: pooled share falls strictly in both, the drop ratio is 0.405 against 0.411, the constant-hazard fit 1.143 against 1.121. Only the **level** differs, and bounding a level needs a number fitted to today's data. So there is no bound in what shipped. Three candidate metrics were measured and rejected, and one of them turned out to be **backwards**.

commits.subject: feat(balance): the grade table could not see brutal dissolve, and the bound it wanted is not there

body.text: This is the first piece of `BAL-04`, the campaign re-grade, and it deliberately is not any re-grading. `BAL-04`'s headline acceptance criterion is that all 24 anchors grade `ok` at all three difficulties — and by the time this session opened, the grade table had been proved twice over not to be a valid selector for anything. Decision 081 measured board quality and grade count as **anti-correlated** across five candidate lattice orderings, and withdrew "every anchor still grades ok" as a criterion. Decision 082 then graded all 24 shipped anchors at the 48-square derived ranges and got **24/24 ok, unchanged**, while the top difficulty's share of tried builds that win went 25% to 43%. Re-grading first would have produced a green table that means nothing. So the instrument came first.
The entry above this one, `the-grade-table-said-nothing`, is where that second proof was written down. This is what was done about it.
What was asked for, and what is not there

`LF-243` asked for a metric — win share per difficulty, `distinct_winning_builds / distinct_builds_tried` — that falls monotonically across the tiers **and holds the top tier under a bound**. The falling half was easy. The bound was looked for, over both campaigns graded in full at 1,440 runs each keeping every per-policy outcome, and it is not there to be found. Every statistic about the shape of the difficulty curve is indistinguishable between the shipped campaign and the one that dissolved:

Monotonicity, spacing and curvature all pass on the campaign that dissolved. **Only the level differs.** Which means any test that catches it has to bound a level — and a bound on "how forgiving is too forgiving" is a number fitted to today's data, which is precisely the thing decision 067 deleted `PRESSURE_FLOOR` for rather than tune. Hunting for the constant that separates 24.2% from 42.6% would have been fitting to the sample, dressed up as a rule.
The claim that survived
The top difficulty's win share must fall strictly below the bottom one's, on every anchor. Nothing else.

That is the weakest statement about difficulty that is not vacuous, and it contains no number at all. It is also strictly stronger than the rule it joins: the old guard fired only when a tier's win share hit exactly 1.0 — every distinct build tried clears it — which is a knife edge silent one build short of itself, and is how a change that roughly doubled how forgiving the top tier is passed the campaign's own instrument without moving a single verdict.

`sim/run.py`'s `verdict()` was extracted as a **pure function of the grade table**, with no `Sim` and no content behind it, for a reason worth stating plainly: three of its four rules cannot fire on any anchor that ships. A gate that grades the shipped 24 and asserts they pass therefore only ever exercises the **green** path of each one. `--selftest` drives 12 synthetic tables — 6 that must produce a problem, 4 that must stay silent, 2 structural — and `tools/check.py` runs it as `grade verdict` at tier 1 in about 220 ms, with no Godot and no content load. It was proved red four ways by breaking behaviour rather than an expectation: comparison inverted, rule deleted, the tutorial exemption widened to every anchor, and the top tier mis-read as the middle one. Same argument as `firing arcs agree` and `verbs agree`, one level up.

campaign win share over 24 anchors (distinct winning builds / distinct builds tried, pooled)
  standard 40.6% (134/330) · hard 30.0% (100/333) · brutal 24.2% (80/331)
  falls strictly across the tiers: yes   [reported, not asserted]
  hard does not fall below standard on 2 anchor(s): anchor-08, anchor-15   [reported, not asserted — only brutal is a problem]

24/24 anchors clean
body.caption: The new footer on a full grade, re-run for this entry at `.venv/bin/python -m sim.run --jobs 8`. The pooled campaign figure is written under `docs/STATE.md`'s grade table by `tools/session.py` on every wrap — labelled `reported, not asserted`, because it falls strictly in both campaigns and so discriminates nothing. It is there as a trend line across sessions, not as a test.

body.text: Does it actually catch anything

Yes, and this is where a number in the commit body needs correcting. **0 of 24 shipped anchors fail. 3 of 24 fail at the derived ranges** — anchor-02, anchor-07 and anchor-23. A **fourth** anchor, anchor-01, trips the same rule at the derived ranges (3 of 5 builds win on `standard`, 3 of 5 on `brutal`) and is relaxed because it is declared a tutorial in data, so it reports `ok`. The commit message and decision 086 both compress that to "4 of 24 fail … and anchor-01, which is exempt as a tutorial", which does not sit with the tool's own summary line of `21/24 clean`. An exempt anchor does not fail. Recording the discrepancy here rather than editing either document, because both are append-only.

anchor              standard             hard           brutal  verdict
anchor-01       2->3  of 5       2->2  of 5       1->3  of 5    ok
anchor-02       5->6  of 10      3->6  of 10      2->8  of 11   brutal: win share 73% (8/11) is not below standard's 60% (6/10) — the top difficulty is not harder than the bottom one
anchor-07       4->4  of 14      3->5  of 14      3->4  of 14   brutal: win share 29% (4/14) is not below standard's 29% (4/14) — the top difficulty is not harder than the bottom one
anchor-23       4->5  of 15      3->5  of 15      3->5  of 15   brutal: win share 33% (5/15) is not below standard's 33% (5/15) — the top difficulty is not harder than the bottom one

21/24 clean at the derived ranges, against 24/24 at the authored ones
regressed or still broken: anchor-02, anchor-07, anchor-23
body.caption: `.venv/bin/python tools/range_derive.py --shipped-impact --jobs 8`, re-run for this entry; the twenty passing rows are omitted. Before this change the same command printed `24/24` on **both** sides — the tool that found the blind spot could not report it. The `anchor-01` row is the tutorial exemption doing real work: without it that line would read as a fourth failure.

body.text: The exemption carries a trap worth writing down for whoever adds the next rule. It filters the anchor's `problems` list **by substring**, so a new rule whose message happens not to contain a matching phrase is silently **not** relaxed on anchor-01 — and anchor-01 is the one anchor where relaxation is load-bearing, with five distinct builds tried against thirteen to sixteen everywhere else, which quantises its win share into 20-point steps.
Three metrics measured and rejected
All three separate the two campaigns. All three were thrown away, with their numbers, in decision 086 — and the rejections are the more useful record.

rows: survival of standard's winners into `brutal`, bounded under 50%

The shipped margin is **4.5 points**, and the pooled figure is carried by three act-2 anchors — anchor-09/10/11, surviving at 0%, 14% and 12% — that `BAL-04` is about to re-tune. A test whose verdict turns on three anchors the next workstream will move is not an instrument.
fewer than 8 distinct winning builds on `brutal` — the 8 read as a per-tier ceiling

Separates cleanly and was the most attractive candidate for hours. It **misreads decision 044**: `ROBUST_ENOUGH = 8` caps `standard_wins + brutal_wins` inside a **scorer** — a point of diminishing returns for a search, never a floor or a ceiling on one tier. Reusing the digit while discarding what it measured is how a number acquires authority it was never given.
a power-discipline gap that widens with difficulty
Not weakly supported. Backwards. See below.

body.text: The second of those has a consequence beyond this change. **`BAL-04`'s own acceptance criteria make the same misreading**, from the opposite side: its second bullet asks that every anchor carry **at least** 8 distinct winning builds, citing decision 044. One reading turns the number into a ceiling, the other into a floor, and the shared error is treating a scorer's saturation point as a bound on a tier at all. The shipped campaign does not meet the floor and never has — anchor-01, 02, 03, 04 and 08 are all under it on the sum — so `BAL-04` would be graded against a criterion its own baseline fails. That bullet needs rewriting before the re-grade runs against it, which is `LF-255`. Worth being exact about the scope: two of `BAL-04`'s eight acceptance criteria are phrased in terms of the grade table, not all of them. The other six are capacity saturation, rebased wave density, `PRESSURE_FLOOR`, dialog capacity, wave composition and rules parity, and none of them is touched here.
The one that came back backwards

The third candidate was the session's first hypothesis and by far the most appealing, because it needed no constant of its own. `sim/engine.py`'s `DIFFICULTIES` table carries a comment saying the top tier's 1.55 multiplier was swept to be "the point where brutal kills the overdraw build but leaves the disciplined one alive". If that were true, the gap between the win rates of disciplined boards and overdrawing ones should **widen** as difficulty rises — a parameter-free test, handed over by the code itself.
Measured over all 1,440 runs of the shipped campaign, splitting on whether a run ever browned out: **runs that brown out win far more often than clean ones.**

Overdrawing the reactor bus is worth roughly twenty points of win rate at every difficulty, and the advantage **narrows** as difficulty rises rather than widening. It is not one greedy policy dominating the sample — 171 to 173 runs per difficulty brown out, out of twenty policies, so many of them do it. The likely mechanism is that the overdraw penalty is priced against a board that is otherwise the same, while an overdrawing board has **more guns on it**, and more guns at reduced output beats fewer guns at full output.

That is a real finding about the currency this whole game is built on, and it is filed as `LF-253` rather than acted on here — nothing in what shipped depends on the answer, because the metric it came from was rejected. It belongs to `BAL-04` and should be settled **before** the capacity rebase, since a capacity ladder tuned on top of an inverted incentive tunes the wrong thing. One more wrinkle: at the derived ranges the trend inverts again, the gap going −11.9 to −22.2 and widening, so range interacts with it.
What was deliberately not done

**Only the top tier is asserted.** The middle tiers are reported and not tested, and the reason is measured rather than cautious: `hard` does not fall below `standard` on **anchor-08** (3 of 14 builds win on both) or **anchor-15** (6 of 13 on both) today. Both are real "hard is not biting here" findings — on those two anchors the tier's 1.35× enemy health and 0.90× bounty buy nothing, the same builds clear either way — and both are filed as `LF-254`. They are not asserted because a check that is red on arrival gets disabled rather than fixed, which this project has already watched happen (`LF-224`). Instead both anchors are **named on every full grade and every wrap**, in the footer above, so it cannot go quiet.

The thinnest passing anchor is worth naming while the margin is known. anchor-21 grades 4 winning builds of 15 tried on `standard` and 4 of 16 on `brutal` — the **same absolute count**, passing only because `brutal` happened to try one more build, on a win-share margin of **+1.7 points** against a campaign median around +11. The count-based form of the same rule fails on anchor-21 and on no other shipped anchor. `LF-256` records it so that when `BAL-04` loosens something and this check goes red there, it is a known thin margin and not a surprise — and so nobody weakens the rule to accommodate it.
The general lesson

When two candidate states of the world differ only in level and not in shape, no amount of ratio-taking will separate them, and the honest move is to weaken the claim until it needs no constant — not to keep hunting for the constant that happens to fit.

The commit records a tier-4 gate across the change: **43 passed, 0 failed, 447,360 ms**, with both parity legs reporting a cached skip because no rule file and no data file moved, so the content digest is unchanged. A cached skip is not a pass, which is why the tally is 43 and not the registry's 45. The same commit records `tools/sweep.py anchor-20` still returning 27 of 27 clean cells under the tightened rule. Neither of those two was re-run for this entry; the two listings above were, and the tier-1 `grade verdict` check re-measured at 220 ms.
No screenshot on this one. It is a change to a grading instrument and it has no visual surface in the game at all — the two listings above are the whole of what there is to look at.

entries.title: Filed high in the morning, closed the same afternoon — indiscipline does not win, the policies that overdraw are simply the strong ones
entries.summary: `LF-253` and decision 087, the immediate sequel to `the-bound-was-not-there`. That entry reported a finding it called **backwards**: across all 1,440 shipped runs, boards that brown out the reactor bus win 53.2% on `standard` against 31.4% for clean ones, a 21.8-point advantage to indiscipline against the whole point of the power economy. It is an artefact. Whether a run browns out is decided by the **policy's build rules**, not by the price — the clean/browned split does not move by a single run when the penalty is swept to four times its shipped value. Compare each policy against **itself** and three quarters of the effect goes and the sign flips on the top tier. Two more claims made in between are withdrawn with it, and the price is not the lever anyway.

commits.subject: fix(balance): "indiscipline wins" was an artefact of which policies overdraw, and the price stays

body.text: The previous entry — `the-bound-was-not-there`, linked at the foot of this page — closed with a section headed "the one that came back backwards". This is the correction to it, written the same day, one commit later. Decision 086 is append-only and is not edited; decision 087 corrects one of its rejection **reasons** and confirms decision 022. The rejection itself still stands: the metric was rejected and stays rejected.
The claim, and it was ours

While deriving decision 086, the hunt was for a difficulty metric that needed **no constant of its own**, and `sim/engine.py`'s `DIFFICULTIES` table appeared to hand one over. Its comment says the top tier's 1.55 multiplier was swept to be "the point where brutal kills the overdraw build but leaves the disciplined one alive". If that is true, the gap between the win rates of disciplined boards and overdrawing ones should **widen** as difficulty rises. Splitting all 1,440 shipped runs — 24 anchors, 20 policies, 3 difficulties — on whether a run ever browned out gave the opposite:

Decision 086 recorded that as "not weakly supported, it is backwards", and it was filed as `LF-253`, a `high` design bug against the mechanic this entire game is built on. Power is the real currency; if overdrawing the bus is worth twenty points of win rate at every difficulty, decision 022 priced it wrong and the capacity ladder `BAL-04` is about to rebase would be tuned on top of an inverted incentive. That was the right severity for the number as it stood.

One note for anyone reading the two pages side by side: `the-bound-was-not-there` writes these gaps as **negative** (clean minus browned-out, `−21.8 pts`) and everything from here on writes them as **positive** (browned-out minus clean, `+21.8%`), which is the sign convention `sim/run.py` now prints. Same magnitudes, opposite sign; nothing changed but which way round the subtraction goes.
The control that was missing

The previous entry did look for a confound, and the check it used does not control for one. It reads: "It is not one greedy policy dominating the sample — 171 to 173 runs per difficulty brown out, out of twenty policies, so many of them do it." That rules out a single outlier and nothing else. **Many policies browning out is not the same as browning out being what distinguishes them.** The twenty policies differ in far more than their power discipline, and the split is drawn by what they build.

The decisive test is the cheapest one available and it should have been the first: if the penalty is what makes browned-out runs win, then changing the penalty should change something about the browned-out set. Sweeping `BROWNOUT_SLOPE` from its shipped 1.5 up to 6.0 and re-grading the whole campaign at each value, **not one run crosses the line** — the figures below are identical at 1.5, at 4.0 and at 6.0, each re-measured for this entry, and the commit reports the same at 2.5 and 3.0.

Whether a run browns out is decided by the policy's build rules, which do not read the penalty. So the raw comparison is largely a statement about **which policies overdraw**, and those turn out to be the strong ones: the ion lance is the best weapon in the game — 48 damage against the mortar's 26 — and it also draws the most, 34 MW against 30, so a lance-led board overdraws almost by construction. The split is not disciplined boards against undisciplined ones. It is one set of strategies against another.

Compare each policy against **itself** — its own browned-out runs against its own clean ones, so the strategy is held fixed and only the overdraw varies — and three quarters of the effect goes, and the sign flips where the `DIFFICULTIES` comment made its claim:

Eighteen of the twenty policies produce both clean and browned-out runs and can be paired with themselves; the other two never split and are dropped rather than pooled. A thing that helps on **under a third** of the approaches that try it is a judgement call — which is precisely what decision 022 set out to build, against the flat −40% penalty `LF-014` had measured as making "never exceed capacity" unconditionally correct. `BROWNOUT_SLOPE = 1.5` and `BROWNOUT_MAX_PENALTY = 0.70` are unchanged, and `LF-253` is closed as not a defect.

campaign win share over 24 anchors (distinct winning builds / distinct builds tried, pooled)
  standard 40.6% (134/330) · hard 30.0% (100/333) · brutal 24.2% (80/331)
  falls strictly across the tiers: yes   [reported, not asserted]
  hard does not fall below standard on 2 anchor(s): anchor-08, anchor-15   [reported, not asserted — only brutal is a problem]

overdraw advantage — does browning out the bus help? (decision 087; reported, not asserted)
                 raw    within policy   helps on
  standard    +21.8%            +6.0%   7/18 policies (309 clean, 123 browned-out runs)
  hard        +17.6%            +5.2%   6/18 policies (310 clean, 122 browned-out runs)
  brutal      +15.6%            -3.7%   4/18 policies (307 clean, 125 browned-out runs)
  The raw column is confounded by WHICH policies overdraw and must not be read alone.

24/24 anchors clean
body.caption: The new footer, re-run in full for this entry at `.venv/bin/python -m sim.run --jobs 8`. **Both columns print, always** — printing the raw one alone is how this was misread, and printing only the adjusted one would hide what was misread. `tools/session.py` writes the same table under `docs/STATE.md`'s grade table on every wrap; it now passes `--detail`, because a within-policy figure cannot be recovered from the per-anchor aggregates. The run counts on the right are the paired subset — the runs belonging to the eighteen policies that split — not the campaign totals of 309/171, 310/170 and 307/173.

body.text: The price is not the lever anyway
This is the measurement worth keeping, and it would have mattered even if the raw effect had been real. The whole campaign was re-graded at each slope. Nothing else was changed.

The gap reaches zero on `brutal` somewhere near slope 4.2 — where **five anchors no longer grade at all**. On `standard` and `hard` it never reaches zero: at four times the shipped price it is still **+10.7** and **+8.2** points. So the penalty could not have fixed the raw figure without the content moving with it, which is `BAL-04`'s joint re-tune and not a constant anyone can turn on its own.

Three of the five rows above — 1.5, 4.0 and 6.0 — were re-measured independently for this entry, by patching the constant in memory before the grading pool forks rather than by editing `sim/engine.py`, so the shared working tree never held a modified rules file and neither parity leg was disturbed. Every figure reproduced exactly. The 2.5 and 3.0 rows are quoted from the commit and were **not** re-run here. One detail the re-run adds: the `standard` gap reading **+10.7% at both 4.0 and 6.0** is not a transcription slip, it is the column having gone flat — `BROWNOUT_MAX_PENALTY = 0.70` caps the penalty, so past a certain slope the price stops rising for any board already deep enough into the red, and raising it further only removes anchors.
Two more claims withdrawn
Between the two decisions, two further results were derived off the same uncontrolled split and both are withdrawn. Neither should be cited again.

items: **That the effect reverses across the 11-to-13 emplacement bucket boundary.** Same confound: an emplacement count is a property of what the policy built, so bucketing on it re-selects populations exactly as brownout status did.

**That browned-out winners finish with 9.6 lives against clean winners' 5.7.** That figure is real, and it is `brutal` only — 58 browned-out winners against 55 clean ones. Paired within anchor it collapses to **+0.6, −1.4 and +0.5 lives**, better on **6 of 11**, **2 of 8** and **3 of 7** anchors that have winners of both kinds. The unpaired gap is act-3 anchors carrying larger life pools: act 1 ships 10 to 24 lives per anchor, act 3 ships 18 to 48, and act-3 anchors are where the overdrawing boards are winning.

body.text: One claim from the previous entry is left standing and should not be — it was not re-measured here and the same confound applies to it. That entry closes its backwards section with "at the derived ranges the trend inverts again, the gap going −11.9 to −22.2 and widening, so range interacts with it". That is a raw split of a second campaign, computed the same uncontrolled way. It is not withdrawn, because nothing has measured it either way; it is simply not evidence of anything until it is paired within policy.
A guard clause that was dead when it was written

`campaign_discipline()` needs each report's per-run records, and `sim/run.py --json` **drops** them unless `--detail` is also passed — an API trap worth writing down on its own, because anything computing a per-run statistic out of that JSON silently gets nothing rather than an error. The function returns an empty dictionary rather than raising, behind a two-part guard: no `runs` key at all, or `runs` present but trimmed of the field. The `grade verdict` selftest grew two cases for it, taking it to **14**, and one of those two exists only because the second half of that guard was **dead when written** — deleting it on purpose left the selftest green.

That was re-checked for this entry rather than taken on trust, by patching three separate breaks into an in-memory copy of `sim/run.py` and running the selftest against each. All three go red as the file ships. Remove the trimmed-runs case, and one of the three goes quiet:

=== selftest as it ships (14 cases) ===
  A drop `not runs` half of the guard: RED (IndexError: list index out of range)
  B drop `brownout_fraction not in` half: RED (KeyError: 'brownout_fraction')
  C pool instead of pair (within := raw): RED (AssertionError: ...)
=== with the trimmed-runs assertion removed ===
  A drop `not runs` half of the guard: RED (IndexError: list index out of range)
  B drop `brownout_fraction not in` half: GREEN
  C pool instead of pair (within := raw): RED (AssertionError: ...)
body.caption: Break-mode check, run from the scratchpad against an in-memory copy so the tracked file was never modified. Case C is the one that matters most: it makes the function pool instead of pair, which is the exact mistake this whole entry is about, and the selftest fixture is built so the raw column says +50% while the within-policy column says 0%. `grade verdict` runs the whole selftest at tier 1 in **203 ms**, with no Godot and no content load — 6 cases where the verdict must fire, 4 where it must stay silent, 4 structural.

body.text: The general lesson, and it is the same one twice in one day
A campaign-wide split of runs by an outcome property is a comparison between whatever populations that property selects.

It happened twice in the same session. Decision 086 spent hours looking for a constant that separates two campaigns which differ only in **level** and not in shape, and the honest move there was to weaken the claim until it needed no constant. Here the number looked like a statement about a game mechanic and was a statement about a population. Both times the fix was the same: find out what the number is actually a statement **about** before deciding what it means.

It is also worth saying plainly that a `high` design bug was filed in the morning and closed the same afternoon by its own follow-up measurement, and that this is a good outcome rather than an embarrassing one. The alternative was a re-priced constant, shipped on a number nobody had controlled, against a mechanic that turns out not to have been broken. The ticket stays in the backlog closed rather than deleted, carrying both the raw figure and the two controls, because the raw figure will be re-derived by somebody eventually and it needs to be findable with its refutation attached.

The commit records a tier-4 gate across the change: **43 passed, 0 failed, 426,674 ms**, with both parity legs reporting a cached skip — no rules file was touched, since the slope sweep never modified `sim/engine.py` on disk. A cached skip is not a pass, which is why the tally is 43 against a registry of 45. That gate was not re-run for this entry. What was re-run: the full campaign grade, the three slope rows, the three break modes, and `.venv/bin/python -m sim.run --selftest` at 14 cases.
No screenshot. There is no visual surface to any of this — it is a grading instrument and a constant that did not move, and the tables are the whole of what there is to look at.

entries.title: Third and last of the day — the largest balance workstream's acceptance criteria had never been run against the campaign they were written to describe, and one of them was impossible
entries.summary: `LF-255`, `LF-257`, `LF-054` and decision 088, closing an arc begun in `the-bound-was-not-there` and continued in `the-policies-that-overdraw-are-the-strong-ones`. `BAL-04` is the campaign re-grade, the largest remaining balance workstream. Measured against the shipped campaign its own acceptance criteria describe: the robustness bullet fails on **8 of 24** anchors, the mixed-weapon bullet fails on **7 of 24** and is **impossible by construction** on two of them, the composition bullet was failed by **all three acts** on the day it was written — 10.1 / 29.4 / 33.8% — and a fifth bullet had been satisfied three sessions earlier by decision 067. No code changed. Every bullet now carries the measured baseline it is judged against and the one-liner that reproduces it.

commits.subject: docs(balance): four of BAL-04's nine acceptance bullets were failed by the baseline they describe

body.text: Third and last of the day's three instrument entries, and the one that closes the arc. `the-bound-was-not-there` (decision 086) found that the grade table could not see a difficulty dissolve; `the-policies-that-overdraw-are-the-strong-ones` (decision 087) found that the discipline gap measured a population and not an effect. Both are linked at the foot of this page. This one is decision 088, and the sentence that holds the three together is its closing paragraph: **all three were found by pointing the instrument at the campaign and reading what came back — none by auditing the instrument.**
The defect

`BAL-04` is the campaign re-grade: density targets for the larger board, the leak budget, the capacity ladder, the composition check and the re-grade itself. It is the largest remaining balance workstream — fifteen tasks in `docs/issues/BAL-04-regrade-the-campaign.md` after this commit, fourteen before it, twelve of them still open. Its acceptance criteria were written before anything was measured against them. Measured now, against the shipped 18×15 campaign as of `54c666b`:

rows: ≥1 winning build with more than one weapon id
no act above 10% of spawn entries at `count: 1`

body.text: None of that is a statement about the content. It is a statement about the bar: a workstream held to these would have had to argue its way out of them at the end, which is the worst possible moment to discover a criterion was never met. **Every bullet now carries its measured baseline and the one-liner that reproduces it, and the bar is "no anchor gets worse" rather than an absolute invented in advance.**
Three failures, or four

The old section had **eight** bullets, one of which is compound — a robustness floor and a mixed-weapon requirement in the same sentence — which is how eight bullets are nine criteria. The table above has eight rows because the ninth criterion, `wave density` with rebased per-act figures recorded in `docs/STATE.md`, is not a baseline that can pass or fail today: it passes as it stands (act 1 32 units on screen, act 2 27 at 85%, act 3 21 at 66%) and the rebase it asks for is this workstream's own output.

Which leaves a discrepancy worth recording, in an entry about counts that were never checked. The commit subject, decision 088's opening line, the rewritten section's preamble and `LF-255`'s closing note all say **four of nine bullets failed**. The table each of them publishes enumerates **three** — the robustness floor, the mixed-weapon requirement, the composition bound — plus `PRESSURE_FLOOR`, which is the already-satisfied one. This journal is append-only and so is the decision log, so nothing is corrected there; it is written down here instead. Every underlying figure reproduces exactly, and they were all re-derived for this entry rather than taken from the commit body.
`ROBUST_ENOUGH = 8`, now read four ways

Decision 044 introduced the digit inside a **scorer**. `tools/sweep.py`'s `cell_score()` computes it over `standard_wins + brutal_wins` and 044's own words are that build count "pays up to `ROBUST_ENOUGH` and stops" — a point of diminishing returns for a search, so that a sweep cannot buy a green cell with an endless supply of marginal builds. It is a saturation cap on a **benefit**. It has since been read as a bar four separate times:

items: **044, as written:** a cap on the benefit of extra builds inside the sweep's scorer, over the two tiers summed.
**`BAL-04`'s acceptance bullet:** a per-anchor floor over the same sum — under which 8 of the 24 anchors fail today.

**`docs/STATE.md`'s priority list:** per anchor **per tier**. No anchor in the shipped campaign reaches 8 distinct winning builds on the top difficulty; the highest is anchor-14 at 7, so every anchor in the game fails that reading.
**The candidate metric decision 086 rejected:** a per-tier ceiling built on the same misreading, rejected there for the same reason.

body.text: Read as a per-anchor floor over `standard + brutal`, here is what the shipped campaign actually has on the eight anchors that miss it:

So the bullet is now **no anchor gets worse**, per anchor, against those eight numbers and the sixteen above them. That is a bar the campaign can be held to on the day it is written, which is the whole of the repair.
The bullet that could not be met

"At least one winning build on each anchor contains more than one weapon id" is **impossible on anchor-01 and anchor-02**, which unlock exactly one weapon between them. Five emplacements in `data/towers.json` deal damage — the pulse turret, the arc node, the ion lance, the flak array and the mortar — and the first of them unlocks at anchor-01, the second at anchor-03. What unlocks at anchor-02 is the scan relay, which does no damage and is therefore not a weapon id. Two anchors were permanently red against a criterion no content change could ever satisfy.

Conditioned on "two or more weapon ids unlocked", **17 of the 24 anchors meet it today**. Seven miss; two of those seven are the impossible ones, so the achievable score is 17 of 22 and there are **five real misses**: anchor-03, 04 and 05 with two weapons unlocked, and anchor-07 and 08 with three — while anchor-06, on the same three, does meet it. All five are Act I. Those five stop being a defect in the criterion and become content findings for the workstream, which is a strictly more useful thing for a bar to produce.
The composition bound becomes a regression bound
"No act has more than 10% of its spawn entries at `count: 1`" was failed by all three acts on the day it was written:

The intent behind it is sound and is unchanged. It was written after a transform free to cut the wave table took **251 of 252** Act III spawn entries to `count: 1` and reduced every wave to "N shards and one of each" — a content loss that no verdict in the grade table can see, because a flattened wave still grades fine. The repair keeps the intent exactly and drops the invented number: each act is pinned to **its own measured share** and forbidden to rise. Relaxing the bullet to a figure the acts pass — somewhere near 35% — was rejected, because it asserts nothing, while the regression form has no free parameter at all and is strictly stronger against the failure it was written for.

One check worth doing before trusting a baseline drawn out of the content: `count` is a **required** key in `data/schema/anchor.schema.json` under `waves[].spawns[]`, and all **829** spawn entries in the campaign carry it explicitly. The share is a property of the authored content, not an artefact of a default in the counting script.
Two backlog items closed, and a figure from yesterday's entry retired

`LF-257`. Decision 086 recorded that at decision 082's derived ranges the power-discipline gap "inverts again and widens", −11.9 → −22.2 points. Decision 087 then showed the shipped version of that same statistic is an artefact of **which policies overdraw**. Paired within policy, using the function 087 shipped, the derived-range campaign comes back flat — and so the sentence in 086 is retired by a later measurement rather than edited:

**There is no range–power interaction in that number.** The detail worth landing is in the top two rows: the uncontrolled statistic does not merely change magnitude between the two campaigns, it **reverses its ordering across the difficulties** — falling 21.8 → 15.6 in one and rising 11.9 → 22.2 in the other — while the controlled one stays within seven points of zero in both. That is the clearest single demonstration in the tree of why the raw split is not an instrument. It cost one script run against an already-cached grade, exactly as the backlog item predicted.

A note for anyone reading these three pages in sequence, because the arithmetic looks inconsistent otherwise: the backlog and decision 086 write these gaps **negative** (clean minus browned-out), and decision 088's table writes them **positive** (browned-out minus clean), which is the convention `sim/run.py` prints. Same magnitudes, opposite sign. The previous entry made the same note for the same reason.

`LF-054` — `PRESSURE_FLOOR` — closed as **already done**. Decision 067 **deleted** it rather than raising it, because a threshold picked to make today's data fail is fitted to that data. Nothing under `sim/` or `tools/` computes it any more; only a tombstone comment remains, and that comment names the replacement worth building. The item survived as open for three sessions purely because `BAL-04`'s task list and its acceptance criteria both still carried a bar for it. Both are corrected in this commit — a backlog item kept alive by two stale sentences in a spec nobody had re-read.
Two mistakes made on the way here, and they belong in the record

The first: `LF-255`, the backlog item that started this whole pass, was filed **this same morning** and named **five** anchors under `ROBUST_ENOUGH` when there are **eight**. It listed anchor-01, 02, 03, 04 and 08 with the right numbers and missed anchor-05, 07 and 23 entirely, because it was written from a partial scan and not re-derived before filing. That is an incomplete count inside an item whose entire point was that a number had not been checked against the thing it described. The closing note now carries the measured list and says which one it is.

The second was nearly a spectacular finding. The first attempt at the mixed-weapon baseline reported **0 of 24** anchors having a winning build with more than one weapon id — every anchor in the game, at every difficulty, apparently solved by a single emplacement type. It was wrong. A `built` entry in the grade JSON is not a tower id, it is `"<tower-id>@<x>,<y>"` with the position carried at four decimal places (`pulse-turret@0.0000,4.0000`, and free placement is why the coordinates are floats at all), so a filter matching bare tower ids matched nothing on every anchor and the aggregate came back a clean, uniform, entirely false zero. It was caught by printing the actual build lists instead of trusting the total — the same move that produced every real finding today.
What was measured

No code changed in this commit: `docs/DECISIONS.md`, `docs/issues/BAL-04-regrade-the-campaign.md`, `docs/BACKLOG.md` and `backlog.json`, four files. The gate on it was **tier 2 — 28 passed, 0 failed, 30,982 ms**, over its own 28,000 ms budget, which is `LF-240` and unrelated to this change: the tier-2 breach is a known regression in `sim determinism` with a measured fix already written up. Tier 2 is 19 tier-1 checks plus 9 tier-2 ones, which is where the 28 comes from.

Re-derived independently for this entry rather than copied out of the commit body: a fresh `.venv/bin/python -m sim.run --jobs 8 --json --detail` over the whole campaign (61 s wall, 6 m 15 s CPU) reproduces **24/24 `ok`**, the same eight anchors under 8 with the same per-tier counts, and the same 17 of 24 on mixed weapons with the same seven misses. The composition shares were recomputed straight from `data/anchors/*.json` and give 15/148, 106/361 and 108/320 to the decimal. `validate_data.py` reports `ok — 0 warning(s)` across 58 documents. Tier 1 is 19 passed, 0 failed, 7,221 ms.
No screenshot. There is no visual surface to any of this — it is a specification measured against a data set, and the tables are the whole of what there is to look at.
The lesson, three times in one day
Run the criterion against the baseline the day you write it.

Decision 086: the grade table could not see a difficulty dissolve. Decision 087: the discipline gap measured a population, not an effect. Decision 088: the acceptance criteria were never checked against the thing they describe. Three instruments, three defects, one day — and every one of them surfaced by running the instrument over the real campaign and reading the output, not by reading the instrument's code. A bar nobody can clear, sitting in a spec, is worse than no bar: it gets quietly reinterpreted at the end by whoever is tired, which is precisely how one digit acquired four meanings.

entries.title: Fourth and last of the day — the grader had never once bought an upgrade, and when it learned to, upgrading turned out to be a beginner strategy that dies before the top difficulty
entries.summary: `LF-245` and decision 089. The three entries before this one changed how the campaign is **judged**; this one changes what the grader can **do**, and it immediately finds something about the game. Across the shipped campaign **55–62% of every fund the player earns is never spent** — and that is not a dead economy, because costing the upgrade of every emplacement on the built board absorbs most of it and takes two anchors negative. The surplus was an artefact of the grader's repertoire: `Sim._dispatch_one()` has accepted `upgrade` since BAL-01 and no policy had ever scheduled one. `upgrade-ladder` is the 21st policy, a byte-identical clone of `cheap-mass` that also upgrades. It wins **11 of 24** anchors on standard against `cheap-mass`'s 9, **5 against 9** on hard, and **zero against 5** on brutal — a net negative campaign-wide that still opens nine cells nothing else can reach.

commits.subject: feat(balance): the grader learns to upgrade, and upgrading turns out to be a standard-difficulty strategy

body.text: Three entries today were about the instrument: `the-bound-was-not-there` (decision 086) found that the grade table could not see a difficulty dissolve, `the-policies-that-overdraw-are-the-strong-ones` (decision 087) found that the discipline gap measured a population rather than an effect, and `the-criteria-were-never-measured` (decision 088) found that the largest balance workstream's acceptance bar had never been run against the campaign it describes. All three are linked at the foot of this page. Every one of them changed how the campaign is **judged** and changed nothing about what the grader can **do**. This one is the other kind, and it is the payoff: it gives the grader a verb it never had, and the first thing that comes back is a statement about the design. One correction owed up front, and it is not a correction to anything — the previous entry is titled "third and last of the day" and this is the fourth. It was the last of the three that measured the instrument; it was not the last of the day. The journal is append-only, so that title stands and this sentence is the record.
The money nobody spent

Graded across the shipped campaign, **55–62% of every fund the player earns is never spent**. Read on its own that looks like a dead economy — money with nothing to buy. It is not. Cost the upgrade of every emplacement standing on the board at the end of each run, subtract it from what is left over, and most of the surplus disappears; on two anchors it goes past zero.

rows: unspent at the end of the run
still unspent after costing every upgrade

body.text: anchor-24 finishes holding **4,358**. anchor-10 and anchor-11 go **negative** on the second row — the board they build cannot afford to upgrade itself. So the money is not idle because there is nothing to buy; it is idle because nothing in the harness was buying.

Those figures were re-derived independently for this entry rather than copied out of the commit, and the re-derivation is worth recording because it pins down a method the commit does not state. They are **standard difficulty only**, averaged over the twenty policies that existed before this change: on that basis anchor-24's mean closing balance is **4,358** to the unit. The per-act shares reproduce to within a point or two depending on whether the share is pooled across runs (60.2 / 55.3 / 62.5) or averaged per run (57.7 / 53.9 / 62.6), and the same ambiguity accounts for the second row (24.9 / 15.9 / 29.7 pooled, 20.1 / 13.2 / 29.9 per run) against the published 22 / 16 / 28. The band **55–62%** holds under both readings, and anchor-10 and anchor-11 are the only two anchors in the campaign that go negative under either.
The hole was the repertoire, not the content

`Sim._dispatch_one()` has accepted an `upgrade` verb since BAL-01. No policy in `standard_policies()` had ever scheduled one. Every grade this project has taken, every sweep, every acceptance figure quoted in the three entries above, was taken by a grader that could not press the upgrade button — so the unspent money was a property of the instrument that measured it and not of the game it was pointed at.

That is the same shape `LF-244` found earlier this month, recorded in `never-pressed-the-sell-button` and closed by a fixture: `data/schema/fixtures/scheduled-verbs.json` names `target_mode`, `sell`, `upgrade`, `set_online`, `build` and the shutter ability as six verbs no policy ever schedules, so every one of that day's 1,440 parity runs exercised the absent branch for all six. `upgrade` was one of those six. This change is the first of them to be scheduled by a real policy rather than probed by a fixture.
The 21st policy, and why it is a clone

`upgrade-ladder` joins `standard_policies()` as policy 21: **twelve passes at t = 40 + 40p, each walking `upgrade` over indices 0–13 in order**. Its preference list is **byte-identical to `cheap-mass`** — `rest(has("pulse-turret"))`, the same expression, deliberately — so every difference between the two rows in the grade table is attributable to upgrading and to nothing else. It is mirrored 1:1 in `scripts/test/parity.gd`, which is what makes it a rules change and not a tooling one.

UPGRADE_LADDER_FIRST_S  = 40.0    # after wave 1 has paid out; cheapest upgrade is 70
UPGRADE_LADDER_GAP_S    = 40.0
UPGRADE_LADDER_PASSES   = 12      # t = 40..480, against a measured 410-460 s full run
UPGRADE_LADDER_MAX_INDEX = 14     # one past max_emplacements 13, the largest board authored
body.caption: Every constant is derived rather than picked, which is what decision 067 asks for. Walking off the end of the board is free and deliberate — an upgrade on an absent, unaffordable or already-upgraded index is a no-op — so the schedule needs no per-anchor knowledge and stays a constant `parity.gd` can mirror as a constant.

body.text: It **departs from `LF-245`'s prototype**, which used three passes ending at t = 84 — the first fifth of a run measured at 410–460 sim seconds. An upgrade the board could not afford at 84 s is exactly the one kills are meant to pay for later, so a schedule that stops there measures the opening and calls it the fight.
The answer came back the wrong way round

**Upgrading is a net negative campaign-wide, and it is still worth having.** It wins seven fewer cells than the policy it is a clone of. It also opens **nine cells `cheap-mass` cannot reach at all**, and it adds a distinct winning build to **10 of 72** anchor-by-difficulty cells — reproducing `LF-245`'s headline count from a completely different schedule. **No cell lost a winning build**, which is structurally guaranteed by adding rather than replacing a policy but worth confirming anyway, and the campaign holds at **24/24 `ok`**.

The entire table above was re-derived for this entry from a fresh `sim/run.py --jobs 8 --json --detail` over all 24 anchors, and every figure in it reproduces to the digit — 9/9/5 against 11/5/0, 23 and 16 of 72, mean spend 1046.7 and 1871.2, mean emplacements 10.54 and 10.38, nine cells opened, ten winning builds added, zero lost, 24 of 24 `ok`.
Depth is bought with width — and that is the mechanism of the losses, not of the wins
One row shows it. anchor-04 on standard, the two policies with identical preferences:

rows: seven pulse turrets, one scan relay
six pulse turrets, two scan relays

body.text: Upgrade depth is bought with board width. And the harder the tier, the more it wants width: brutal multiplies enemy hit points by **1.55** while cutting bounty to **0.80**, so the tier that most needs more guns is the tier where you can least afford to make the existing ones better. Hence 0 of 24 on brutal.

One thing worth adding that the commit does not say, found while checking it: **width explains where the ladder loses, and explains nothing about where it wins.** In all nine cells `cheap-mass` cannot reach, the ladder builds exactly as many emplacements as `cheap-mass` does — eleven against eleven on anchor-14 (standard and hard) and anchor-15, twelve against twelve on anchor-17, 18, 19, 20, 22 and 24. The boards are the same size and the upgrades are free of any width cost there, which is precisely why upgrading pays. So the trade is real but it is one-sided: on the boards where a smaller board is affordable, upgrading is a gain; on the boards where it costs an emplacement, it is a loss.

The counter-example is anchor-01, and it needs stating more carefully than the commit states it. There, the ladder wins on a **four**-emplacement upgraded board where `cheap-mass` needs five — depth substituting for width, on the one anchor small enough for it. But `cheap-mass` **also wins** anchor-01 on hard, with its five turrets and a spend of 500 against the ladder's 760, so nothing is beaten there; the four-emplacement board simply is a winning build that nothing else in the policy set had found. That is why anchor-01 hard is the tenth cell in the "adds a winning build" count while being absent from the nine-cells-opened list. The same 5 → 4 narrowing holds on standard, where it added nothing because another policy had already found that board; on brutal the four-emplacement board loses.
Two things I got wrong on the way here, both caught by measuring

**The draw hypothesis, and it is measurably wrong.** The first explanation for the collapse on brutal was the obvious one: an upgrade raises an emplacement's draw, power is the scarce resource, so upgrading must be starving the bus. Measured against `data/towers.json`, the pulse turret goes 12 → 18 MW on upgrade and 9 → 14 damage, so damage **per megawatt improves**, 0.75 → 0.78. Where it loses is money: 190 buys one upgraded turret for 14 damage, while 200 buys two plain ones for 18. Money is the abundant resource here and power the scarce one, so on that arithmetic upgrading should be attractive and it is not — which points at build **sequencing** rather than a draw penalty. `LF-259` now carries that as a hypothesis and says in as many words that it is not a measurement.

**A phantom hole, nearly filed.** A policy is authored in two places that must move together — `standard_policies()` in `sim/engine.py` and `_policies()` in `scripts/test/parity.gd` — and it looked like a divergence between them would pass parity in silence, which would have been a serious finding in a project whose whole rules-safety argument rests on that comparison. It is not true. `_two_way_diffs()` reports "present in python, absent from godot" and `_three_way_diffs()` reports "present in (sides) only", so a missing or extra policy fails and is **named**. The only cost is wall clock: you learn it after 1,512 simulations and about fifteen minutes per platform leg, where a name comparison would answer in milliseconds. Filed as `LF-260`, a tooling item, not a correctness one.
The reported set moved, which is the argument for reporting it

Decision 086 asserts that win share falls strictly from `standard` to `brutal` on the top tier only, and **reports** rather than asserts the middle tier, because a check that is red on arrival gets disabled instead of fixed. Adding one policy moved the reported list:

So `hard` no longer fails to bite on anchor-08 and anchor-15; it fails to bite on anchor-04 and anchor-08. One anchor was repaired by giving the grader a strategy, and one newly appeared for the same reason. **The reported set moves with the grader's repertoire and not only with the content** — which is the strongest argument yet for leaving it reported until the policy set settles, rather than promoting it to an assertion.
