Campaign win share moved to **42.4 / 30.6 / 24.0%** from 40.6 / 30.0 / 24.2, still falling strictly; both figures were re-derived here as 142/335, 102/333 and 80/334.
A run count in prose that had been wrong for some time

`tools/test_parity.py`'s docstring described the suite as "1152 simulations (24 anchors x 16 policies x 3 difficulties)". The policy set had been **20** for some time, making the real figure 1,440, and this change takes it to **1,512** — 24 × 21 × 3. The docstring now states the product rather than a literal and no run count survives anywhere in that file's prose. It is a small thing and it is the same failure the tier table in `CLAUDE.md` has had twice: a number written into prose rots within a day, and the only durable fix is to write the expression that produces it.
What was verified

**Parity: 1,512 runs identical on both platforms.** The Windows leg — the build the owner actually plays, and the reason decision 078 exists — ran fresh inside the gate at **936,361 ms** and came back identical. The Linux leg is worth describing precisely rather than summarising, because the gate tally does not read the way the claim does: the fresh 1,512-run Linux comparison was recorded at 21:26:46 UTC against digest `0b1a41338aef` with the change present in the working tree, and the gate run that follows it therefore reports `rules parity` as a **cached skip** — that skip is the "1 skipped" in the tally below. So both legs were freshly verified; only one of them was freshly verified **inside** the run whose numbers are quoted.

[ skip ] rules parity            626ms  parity cached — skipping 1512 runs (digest 0b1a41338aef, ...)
[  ok  ] rules parity (windows) 936361ms  1512 runs identical (gdscript vs python) [windows]

tier 4 — 44 passed · 0 failed · 1 skipped · 1368446ms
body.caption: The gate at tier 4, from `docs/STATE.md`. A cached skip is never a pass and the tally names it, which is exactly why the distinction above can be made at all.

body.text: Independently for this entry: a fresh full grade (24 anchors, 21 policies, 3 difficulties, `--jobs 8`) reproduces the headline table to the digit, the nine opened cells by name, the ten added winning builds by name, zero lost, 24/24 `ok`, the campaign win share to one decimal, the three anchors in the reported table, and the anchor-04 and anchor-01 build rows. The unspent-funds figures were re-derived from a separate run reading each simulation's closing balance, with the method caveat recorded above. `data/towers.json` confirms the upgrade arithmetic and the 70-credit cheapest upgrade; `data/anchors/anchor-11.json` confirms `max_emplacements` 13; `sim/engine.py`'s `DIFFICULTIES` confirms 1.55 / 0.80 on brutal and 1.35 / 0.90 on hard. `docs/STATE.md`'s grade table and both reported tables were regenerated in the commit.

**No screenshot.** There is no visual surface to any of this — it is a policy added to a headless grader, and the tables are the whole of what there is to look at. The one image that would have helped does not exist and was never captured: nobody has ever seen the ladder's four-turret anchor-01 board in the running game, because the grader has no renderer and the game has no autoplay that upgrades.
The lesson, and it is the day's fourth variation on one theme
A gate that runs the whole game proves nothing about a branch the shipped data never enters.

That line was written about a rule no shipped tower row exercised. It turns out to have a sibling one level up: **a grader that runs every policy proves nothing about a verb no policy schedules.** Three entries today found instruments that measured the wrong thing; this one found an instrument that could not reach part of the game at all, and the moment it could, it said something nobody had predicted — that upgrading is a strategy for the difficulty the player starts on, and stops working by the one they finish on. Whether that is the intended shape of the economy is a design question, and it is deliberately left open.

entries.title: The brief was eight anchors; the defect was one row of `data/towers.json`
entries.summary: `LF-254` and decision 090 — `BAL-04`'s first content slice. The dispatch was "do an Act I balance pass", because three separate `BAL-04` findings all pointed at the same eight anchors. They were not five anchors. They were one tower's stat: the arc node was paying a heavy weapon's power price for a light weapon's profile, **0.577 damage per megawatt against the pulse turret's 1.000** and **0.192** against flat armour 4, and it appeared in **zero winning builds on all six Act I anchors where it is unlocked**. Three numbers moved. Multi-weapon went **17/22 → 22/22** achievable anchors with **zero** per-anchor regressions, and no `capacity_mw`, wave table, `lives` or dialog line moved at all.

commits.subject: fix(balance): the arc node was priced as a heavy weapon and Act I's five multi-weapon misses were that one row

body.text: The brief dispatched this morning was **do an Act I balance pass**. Three separate `BAL-04` findings pointed at the same eight anchors, so a balance-analyst went at the **anchors**: retune wave tables, capacity and lives across anchor-01 through anchor-08. Yesterday's `the-criteria-were-never-measured` (decision 088) had rebased `BAL-04`'s acceptance criteria against measurement for the first time and found five achievable multi-weapon misses — anchor-03, 04, 05, 07, 08 — and called them, in its own words, "real content findings for this workstream rather than defects in the criterion".
They were not five anchors. They were **one row of `data/towers.json`**, and no anchor lever could have reached it.
Nine rows and one division
The measurement that found this was not a sweep over the anchors. It was dividing damage by megawatts for the nine rows of `data/towers.json` and noticing that one row was in the wrong band.

The arc node sat in the ion-lance power band and bought nothing for sitting there: no range — 3.8, the **shortest in the game**, against the turret's 4.0 — no splash, no shield targeting, and the worst armour penetration on the board. Against `warden-heavy`'s **flat** armour 4 it fell to **0.192** damage per megawatt against the pulse turret's 0.556, because 6 damage a shot minus armour 4 is 2 net.

The grade table agreed without being asked. The arc node appeared in **0 winning builds on all six Act I anchors where it is unlocked**, and in **54** instances campaign-wide against the pulse turret's **2,492**. Its own note in the data file had been making a claim about it for the whole time:
Chains. Draw is high enough that two of them force a real decision.
The decision it forced was to never build one.
Why no wave table could have fixed it

Act I capacity per emplacement slot is **9.2–11.0 MW against a 12 MW turret**, so on every Act I board **power binds strictly and slots never do**. Under a strictly power-bound board, damage per megawatt is the **only** figure of merit — and a 1.73:1 ratio does not move for a wave table, a lives count or a slot layout. Five anchors were carrying a criterion failure for a tower they could not have fixed.
Derived, not swept

The draw was not searched for. The rule stated first: **the arc node must stay strictly less power-efficient than the pulse turret against every enemy in the game**, measured in kills per second per megawatt **with overkill counted** — integer shots to kill, not raw damage per second, because a 6-damage weapon wastes less on a 22 hp target than a 9-damage one. `warden-mote` has 22 hit points: four arc shots deliver 24, three pulse shots deliver 27. Solving that equality per enemy gives the draw at which the two weapons are exactly as efficient:

The binding threshold is 16.88, so draw ≥ 17 — and every draw in `data/towers.json` is an even number of megawatts, so **18**. The same derivation on the upgrade gives 25.0 and 22.5, so **26**. Re-derived independently while writing this entry: at 18 MW the arc node is 0.833 damage per megawatt against the turret's 1.000 unarmoured, and 0.278 against 0.556 into flat armour 4 — still exactly half the turret against weight, which is the shape the rule was written to preserve. Decision 074's sentence about it drawing 2.2× for its chain is 1.5× now, and that decision is superseded by reference rather than edited.

The band was graded anyway, because a derivation that lands on a cliff edge is a guess with arithmetic in front of it. **15–18 MW is a plateau**: 24/24 `ok` and zero regressions at all four values, multi-weapon 20–21 of 22. 19 MW and above regresses anchor-12 or anchor-10. The one-anchor wobble inside the plateau is quantisation noise — `LF-264`, filed in this pass — and is not claimed as signal.
Three numbers

data/towers.json          arc-node.draw_mw          26 -> 18
data/towers.json          arc-node.upgrade.draw_mw  38 -> 26
data/anchors/anchor-04    starting_funds           620 -> 590
body.caption: The entire content diff. No wave table, no `capacity_mw`, no `lives` and no dialog line moved anywhere in the campaign.

body.text: That last sentence is load-bearing rather than decorative: it is why the `count: 1` composition share, `wave density` and `dialog capacity` below are **provably identical** rather than re-measured. One prose field moved with the numbers — the arc node's own note, which now says what the weapon is for:
Chains. Fast and shallow — more damage per emplacement than a turret, less per megawatt, and 6 a shot barely scratches armour. The answer to numbers, never to weight.

The win share still falls strictly across the three difficulties, which is the property that makes it a difficulty ladder rather than three labels. The only second-order movement is the `PLC-05` saturation denominator: lowering the maximum draw shrinks it on anchors 03/04/05 from 380 to 260, moving Act I's saturation share 29% → 31%, far below the 80% warn. **Nothing was bought with reactor megawatts** — no `capacity_mw` moved anywhere in this change, and the next section is why that was a refusal and not an oversight.
One of the three numbers is not derived, and it says so

anchor-04 needed a second, separate number and it was money: `starting_funds` 620 → 590. The **mechanism** is derived. At 620 credits the `rapid` policy affords a third 100-credit turret before the 80-credit scan relay, reaching 90 of the anchor's 94 MW and leaving **4 MW — less than the relay's 8**. So it plays the entire anchor blind to air and dies on wave 4. 94 MW is the only capacity in [88, 106] that leaves less than a relay after a weapon-first fill.

The **value** is not derived, and the analyst said so plainly instead of dressing it up. 584–596 is one verified plateau — every value `ok` at all three difficulties, carrying a multi-weapon winner, with `hard` biting, at standard+brutal 9–10 — and **590 is its midpoint**. The campaign's own funds ramp (starting funds as a fraction of the reference board: 60.0 / 67.6 / 71.8 / **79.5** / 87.2 / 93.2 / 106.8 / 102.3% across Act I) puts anchor-04 exactly on the 03↔05 interpolation and does **not** pick 590. It is recorded that way here because how a number was reached is worth more than how tidy it looks, and a plateau midpoint honestly labelled is a better artefact than a derivation invented after the fact.
Robustness, with the weakest closure named

Nine perturbations per anchor — capacity ±2, drone ±1, mote ±1, heavy +1, lives −1. `ok` holds 7–9 of 9 on every Act I anchor. The multi-weapon result holds **9/9 on anchor-06**, 7–8/9 on 03/04/07/08, and **4 of 9 on anchor-05**. anchor-05 is the weakest closure in the pass and is flagged rather than rounded up into the 22/22 headline. The single perturbation that breaks it is `heavy+1`, every time — exactly what the armour arithmetic at the top of this entry predicts, since the heavy is the unit the arc node is worst against.
Refused: buying the closure with reactor capacity

Per-anchor capacity was the obvious lever and it was tried before it was refused, with numbers. It **works on anchor-03**: 104 MW takes standard+brutal from 6 to 9 and is robust to 8 of 8 perturbations. It works nowhere else. The monotone ladder then forces every later Act I anchor up, and anchor-07 cannot take it — 116 MW gives standard+brutal 9 with **no** multi-weapon build, while 112 and 124 give multi-weapon but flatten all three difficulty tiers to identical win shares and drop standard+brutal below its baseline of 7. anchor-04 at 112 and anchor-05 at 120 each lose their multi-weapon build under a ±1 change to a single spawn entry.

So the offer was **+12 to +30 MW spread across six anchors** to buy one robust closure and two knife edges. That is the trap `CLAUDE.md` names in a single line — **density must never be paid for with reactor capacity** — and this project has already sprung it once.
Refused: `LF-218`'s rise in hit points per unit

Graded at three drone→heavy substitution depths on all six anchors, with unit counts falling so screen presence does not rise. Every depth that moved hit points per unit meaningfully took `brutal` to `unwinnable` or `single-solution`, or destroyed the multi-weapon result, on **every** anchor. The reason is the same armour arithmetic again: Act I's only unit with mass carries armour 4, which is **flat**, so raising the armoured share raises brutal difficulty superlinearly (hp ×1.55) and deletes the second weapon class at the same time. `LF-218` needs a **new Act I enemy** — armour 0, roughly 90–130 hit points, ground — which is content, not a knob. Filed as `LF-261`.
Act I is a reveal gate, and that is why `hard` could not bite

The sharpest finding of the pass, and it was not what the pass went looking for. Across anchors 02–08, a build containing a scan relay won **136 of 246** runs. A build without one won **0 of 195** — dying on wave 3 or 4 at every difficulty, because `warden-mote` is `kind: air` and nothing else in the Act I roster can see it.

That is why `hard` was failing to bite on anchor-04 and anchor-08 in the first place: **multiplying enemy hit points by 1.35 cannot move an outcome decided by whether a unit can be shot at all.** The relay costs 8 MW of a 92–110 MW bus, so it is a **tax rather than a trade** — you do not choose it, you pay it. Whether that is the right shape for Act I is a design question, not a tuning one, so it is filed as `LF-262` and left alone.
A bug that was not one, and a real one standing next to it

The analyst reported that the shield wall's upgrade makes the shield wall **worse**: base `slow` 0.28, upgraded `slow` 0.20, read as a downgrade. It is not a bug. `slow` is a speed **multiplier** — `speed = kind.speed * slow` — so lower is stronger, and the upgrade is a genuine improvement.

But checking the claim surfaced a real defect standing right next to it. `_covered_by()` takes `max()` over that value, and for a multiplier `max()` returns the **weakest** field covering the point — so an upgraded shield wall overlapping a base one has its stronger slow **silently discarded**. Both engines do the identical thing, so `rules parity` is perfectly clean and this is a shared design defect rather than a divergence: exactly the class of fault a parity harness is structurally blind to. Filed as `LF-263`.

This is the **third session running** in which briefing an agent to check its own brief, or checking the agent's report rather than filing it, caught something real. It is recorded here as method rather than as a scolding: the report was wrong about the bug, right that something was worth looking at, and the check cost about five minutes.
What the verification cost

`rules parity` had to run **fresh on both platforms** for a three-number data change, because the parity digest covers all **79 tracked data files** and not just the two rule implementations — a tower's draw invalidates the cache exactly as a rules edit would. **1,512 runs identical on Linux** (15 m 35 s, one run) and **1,512 identical on Windows across 8 shards**, sharded because the full Windows leg does not fit the tooling's 10-minute command ceiling. 1,512 is 24 anchors × 21 policies × 3 difficulties — the 21st policy is yesterday's `upgrade-ladder`, from `depth-is-bought-with-width`.

Gate at tier 3: **42 passed, 0 failed**, with `anchor grades` reporting 24 anchors `ok` at every difficulty. `music loudness` (tier 4) was not run, because no audio file changed. `tools/parity_costs.json` also moved in the commit and is not a content change — it is the Linux run's own per-anchor timing recalibration, written by the run that verified everything above.
Found while writing this entry, and not fixed here

The shield wall's note in `data/towers.json` still reads that it "ties the arc node as the biggest draw in Act I". After this change it does not tie — 26 MW against 18 — and it was not strictly true before either, since the ion lance unlocks at anchor-06 at 34 MW. It is a prose field with no validator behind it, which is why nothing went red. Recorded here because it is true and it is the kind of thing that rots quietly; not fixed in this change, because a chronicle entry does not get to edit the data it is reporting on.
The lesson, which is yesterday's from the other side

Decision 088 found that the acceptance criteria for the largest balance workstream had never been run against the campaign they describe. This one is the same shape one level down. **Before tuning the level, check whether the piece placed on it is priced.** The instrument that found a defect five anchors deep was one division over nine rows of a data file — cheaper than any sweep, and the sweep could not have found it at all, because the sweep only ever varied the anchors.

There is no screenshot on this page and that is deliberate. Three numbers changed in two data files and no pixel moved; a frame of the board would show the same board it showed yesterday, and an image taken to fill a slot is worth less than the sentence saying why there isn't one.

entries.title: Act I did not need more weight. It needed the same weight in fewer bodies
entries.summary: `LF-261` and decision 091 — the second content slice of `BAL-04`, and the direct payoff of the refusal this journal recorded at 09:40 this morning. This morning's entry ended by declining to raise Act I's hit points per unit, because Act I's only unit with mass carries flat armour 4, so "heavier" and "more armoured" were the same operation and the second one breaks the act. The fix was a unit, not a knob: `warden-hauler`, **120 hp = 3 × 40** and **bounty 36 = 3 × 12**, paid for with exactly three drones per hauler — so every Act I wave's total hit points and total bounty are byte-identical to baseline. hp per unit **46.9 → 58.2** against act 2's 61.6, on-screen presence **falls** 32.0 → 26.2, `hp/w` does not move at all, and the per-anchor grade is identical on all 24 anchors. anchor-02 refused outright; anchor-05 nearly did, and finding out why is what produced the design.

commits.subject: feat(balance): Act I gets the unarmoured body its roster never had, and hp per unit rises with no anchor moving

body.text: The previous entry, `the-piece-was-mispriced-not-the-board`, ended in a refusal. `LF-218` wants Act I's hit points per unit raised — acts 1 and 2 attrit the wave in the first fifth of the lane and act 3 does not — and decision 090 tried to do it inside the roster that already existed. It graded three `warden-drone` to `warden-heavy` substitution depths on all six Act I anchors and refused with numbers: every depth that moved hp per unit meaningfully took brutal to `unwinnable` or `single-solution`, or destroyed the anchor's multi-weapon winning build.

The reason was arithmetic rather than tuning. Act I's only unit with mass, `warden-heavy`, carries **flat armour 4**, which cuts the pulse turret 9 → 5 and the arc node 6 → 2. So "make Act I heavier" and "make Act I more armoured" were the same operation, and the second one raises brutal difficulty superlinearly while deleting the second weapon class at the same time. Decision 090 wrote down what it would take instead — a new Act I enemy, armour 0, roughly 90 to 130 hit points, ground — and filed `LF-261`.
This entry is that refusal being paid off, the same day.
The hole was already visible in the roster's own pattern
The unit was not invented to fit a target. Every act in this game has a tough **unarmoured** body — something with mass that you can simply shoot — except Act I:

Act I was light, light, and plated, with nothing in between — the only act on the board with an empty middle column. **It had no way to express "heavy but shootable"**, so every attempt to make it heavier made it armoured instead. That is the whole of decision 090's blocker stated as a gap in the content rather than as a failed sweep.
The derivation is one sentence

**A hauler is three drones fused into one body.** hp 120 = 3 × 40, bounty 36 = 3 × 12, and the wave rule pays for each hauler with exactly three drones. Everything else follows from that single choice.

data/enemies.json   + warden-hauler
                      hp      120     = 3 x warden-drone's 40
                      bounty   36     = 3 x warden-drone's 12
                      speed   0.9
                      kind    ground
                      armour  ABSENT  <- the point of the whole unit
                      leak_cost ABSENT -> decision 047 gives max(1, round(120/130)) = 1
body.caption: The entire new row. The absent keys are load-bearing: no `armour` is what the act was missing, and `leak_cost` is omitted because decision 047's rule already returns the default for 120 hit points.

body.text: The consequence is the part worth keeping. **Every Act I wave's total hit points and total bounty are byte-identical to baseline** — `hp/w` stays at 950 and the money the player can earn does not move by a credit. The only things that change are how many bodies carry that weight, how fast they walk, and that the mass is unplated. `LF-218` said the lever was hit points per unit; this says the act's problem was never **how much** weight it fields but **how that weight is distributed**, and proves it by holding the weight fixed.
What makes it read as mass: one turret cannot, two can

A pulse turret does 9 damage per 0.75 s over a 7.75-tile chord at range 4.0. That is twelve shots, **108 damage in one pass**. 108 is less than 120, and 2 × 108 = 216 is more than 186, which is a hauler at brutal. So **one turret cannot finish a hauler in a single pass and two can, at every difficulty** — where a drone (40 hit points, 62 at brutal) dies to one turret with room to spare. That is the distinction the roster was missing, expressed as arithmetic rather than as feel.
The wave rule is one integer expression, and integer on purpose

for every wave of anchors 03-08:

    h = drone_count // 4,  clamped to (drone_count - 2) // 3,  written only if h >= 2
    drone_count -= 3 * h

anchor-03, wave 2:   8 // 4 = 2,  (8 - 2) // 3 = 2   ->  h = 2
                     drone 8 -> 2,  + warden-hauler count 2
                     total hp before  8 x 40                    = 320
                     total hp after   2 x 40 + 2 x 120          = 320
body.caption: No per-anchor parameters and no seeded pacing. The rule alone puts the hauler's debut on anchor-03 wave 2, one wave before `warden-heavy` arrives on wave 3 — so the player's first encounter with mass is the unarmoured one.

body.text: **Integer and not a percentage, deliberately.** `round()` is banker's rounding and `10 * 0.15` is `1.4999999999999998`, so a rule written as "15% of the drones" silently means 10% on every wave of ten — a content rule that does not do what its own name says, with nothing red anywhere. Integer division has no such gap between the statement and the behaviour. The `h >= 2` clause exists for a second reason: it adds **zero** `count: 1` spawn entries, because a lone heavy body is what `warden-heavy` is already for. Act I's `count: 1` share actually falls, 10.1% → 7.9%.
What moved, and what deliberately did not

hp per unit closes **80% of the gap to act 2** while on-screen presence **falls** and hit points per wave do not move at all. Alongside that: 24/24 anchors `ok` at all three difficulties, per-anchor `standard / hard / brutal` **identical on all 24 anchors — not one cell moved in either direction**, multi-weapon stays 22/22 achievable, campaign win share 44.6/31.2/25.1 → 44.8/31.2/25.1 and still falling strictly, `validate_data.py` at 0 warnings. No `capacity_mw`, `starting_funds` or `lives` moved on any anchor, so no dialog line moved either.
It is not a no-op, and that was checked specifically

A change whose headline is "nothing regressed" is one bad step away from a change that did nothing at all, so the opposite was measured too. Every Act I anchor's peak bus load and brownout fraction move — anchor-04 standard peak **1.55 → 1.75** of capacity, anchor-08 standard **1.73 → 1.84** — and anchor-03 brutal's `distinct_builds_tried` goes 10 → 11. **Acts II and III move by exactly nothing, which is the control.**

`LF-218`'s own metric moves the right way as well. Presence in the last quarter of the lane rises on all six carrying anchors, and anchors 07 and 08 cross a whole 5% bucket. **Anchors 01 and 02, which did not get the unit, are unchanged to three decimal places** — the control that measurement needed. The instrument was `sim/coverage.py`'s existing 200-bucket profile regrouped read-only; nothing new was built inside a content pass.
anchor-02 refused, and it is the campaign's most build-starved anchor

Baseline `s/h/b` on anchor-02 is 5/3/2, which means brutal carries **two** distinct winning builds and any added body takes it to one — a single-solution level. It was tested at five substitution depths, three introduction waves, a single hauler on a single wave, and both the 2:1 and the hit-point-neutral 3:1 exchange. The one cell where it holds is speed 0.85, whose neighbours 0.80 and 0.90 both fail. **That is a cell, not a plateau**, which is exactly what `LF-264` says not to ship. anchor-02 does not get the unit; `LF-268` records why.
anchor-05 nearly refused, and that refusal is what produced the design

This is the most interesting thing in the workstream after the derivation. The first shape tried was a 2:1 exchange — two drones traded for one hauler, which **adds** hit points to the wave. Under it, anchor-05 lost a standard-difficulty winning build in **11 of 12 cells** swept, the one survivor again being an isolated speed value.

Under the hit-point-neutral 3:1 exchange, the same anchor is `+0` in **all 18 cells**. **Its problem was the added hit points, not the new unit.** That is what redirected the work from "trade drones for a tougher body" to "redistribute the same weight into fewer bodies" — which is the design that shipped, and the sentence at the top of this entry. The refusal did not stop the work; it changed what the work was.
One shipped number sits on the edge of its plateau, and is stated as such

Per `LF-264`, every stat was graded as a band rather than a point. hp 120 is clean from 95 through 125 with a cliff between 125 and 130. speed 0.9 is clean 0.85 to 1.00 and fails at 0.80 and 1.05, and 0.9 is the slower interior value of that band because freight ought to be slower than a drone — it is also exactly `hollow-vessel`'s speed, three acts later. The divisor 4 is clean at 4, 5 and 6 and fails at 3. **bounty 36 is the exception:** clean at 36, 39 and 42, failing at 33, so it sits at the **lower edge of a one-sided plateau** rather than in the middle of a two-sided one. It was kept because it is the derived money-neutral value — 3 × 12 — and moving it off the edge would break the property the whole design rests on. Decision 090's honesty about `starting_funds = 590` is the precedent for saying that plainly instead of smoothing it over.
A gate check quietly changed which act it measures against

`wave density` compares each act's peak on-screen presence against the busiest act. Act 1's peak fell below act 2's, so **act 2 is now the busiest act** and the reference rebased underneath the check: it reads act 1 26 (97%) · act 2 27 (100%) · act 3 21 (78%) against a 0.55 floor, where act 3 previously sat at 66% of act 1's 32. The acts are **more** comparable after than before, which is the check's stated purpose — but a check silently changing which act it measures against is a real semantic event, and it is recorded here rather than glossed. `BAL-04`'s task list already anticipated rebasing it.
The robustness comparison that matters is the one that did not change

Fourteen perturbations × six anchors, run on `HEAD` **and** on the post-change tree, so the comparison is like for like. `heavy+1` fails on anchors 03/04/05 and `cap-2` on 05/06 — **identically on both sides**. The hauler's own axes are the most robust in the battery: `hauler_hp ±10`, `hauler_speed ±0.05`, `hauler_bounty ±3` and `hauler_count +1` all hold `ok` on all six anchors, and in two places the after-state is better, with anchor-05's multi-weapon build surviving `mote+1` and `lives-1` where it did not before.

The honest reading of that battery is not "the change is safe". It is that **Act I's fragile axis is its armour share, not its unit count** — decision 090's flat-armour arithmetic confirmed a second time by an independent instrument. `LF-272` says to grade Act I against `heavy+1` specifically from now on.
A trap this project has been telling agents for sessions is inverted

Every brief written here says that a missing sprite renders as flat placeholder grey. It does not. Measured with the `--dump-placeholder` hook, an ordinal unit with no sprite falls back to a **filled amber disc**, `rgb(0.80, 0.58, 0.22)`, about `#cc9438`, radius roughly 8 px.

The consequence is worse than a wrong colour in a note. An agent sampling a capture for grey finds none, concludes the sprite loaded, and moves on — which is the **exact inversion** of the misdiagnosis the note exists to prevent. `LF-267`.
The art half could not photograph its own work

There is no hook to spawn an arbitrary enemy id — there is one for emplacements, `--build`, but nothing for units — so the sprite was literally unphotographable in the running game until the data row landed. Art verification is coupled to data by an accident of the tooling. `LF-265`.

So the sprite-smith verified the four yaws by **projecting the eye through the calibrated camera instead of looking at it**: predicted screen position of the eye at world (0, 0.72, 0.54) using the manifest's calibrated `ortho_scale` of 91.946 px per unit, against the glow pass's brightest pixel. **Within 4 px at every yaw, on a sphere of 7.8 px screen radius.** That is a stronger verification than a screenshot would have been, and it exists because the easy route was blocked. `calibrate()` reported tile 128×64, ratio 2.0000, elevation 30.0000, pivot (127.5, 171.5); four distinct sha256s across the yaws; every atlas cell byte-identical to its loose PNG.

body.caption: The three Warden ground units at all four yaws, composited on the board colour sampled from a real capture, with the tile diamond drawn from the measured pivot rather than from `CELL//2`. The question this sheet had to answer was two-sided: does the new unit read as the same family, and does it read as a different thing. Top row `warden-drone`, middle `warden-hauler`, bottom `warden-heavy`.

body.text: The silhouette numbers are the falsifiable form of "unarmoured". Bounding box and fill: drone 65×56 at 63.5%, hauler **117×102 at 49.7%**, heavy 110×113 at 63.4%. **The hauler is longer, lower and 25% less filled than the heavy** — open, framed freight where the heavy is a solid plated block. Colour is deliberately not the discriminator: the hauler's eye is 255,169,100 and the heavy's is 255,171,102, because a player should read mass from shape at gameplay zoom, not from hue.

body.caption: The same three at 1:1 (top) and at the 0.75 scale a self-screenshot actually shows (bottom). The bottom row is the row that matters — the project renders a 1920×1080 logical viewport into a 1440×810 window, so this is the size the silhouette has to survive at.

body.text: And then it walked

Once the data row landed, the unit could finally be photographed where it belongs. anchor-05, frame 4600: `warden_hauler` at yaw 135, on the lane, beside a `warden_heavy`. Hottest pixel (255,168,98) against the rendered (255,169,100), and 1,224 distinct colours in the crop — which is the real sprite and not the amber fallback disc, checked rather than assumed, for the reason two sections up.

body.caption: anchor-05, frame 4600. `warden-hauler` centre, walking the lane; `warden-heavy` above it and to the left. The comparison the family sheet argued in the abstract is settled here: the plated block is solid and compact, the freight is long, low and open, and the two do not read as the same body even at this size.

body.text: Found, filed, not fixed

items: `LF-265` — no hook to spawn an arbitrary enemy id, so art verification is coupled to data landing first.
`LF-266` — adding an `ASSETS` key invalidates all 27 render hashes.
`LF-267` — the missing-sprite fallback is an amber disc, not flat grey. Every brief in this repository says otherwise.
`LF-268` — anchor-02 cannot absorb any new content while brutal carries only two builds.
`LF-269` — anchor-05 is a knife edge on the economy axis, and that is pre-existing rather than caused here.
`LF-270` — `BAL-04`'s acceptance criteria have now been hand-rolled four separate times.
`LF-271` — `LF-218`'s quoted bucket figures no longer reproduce: 5/4/7, not 3/4/9.
`LF-272` — Act I's fragile axis is armour share, not unit count. Grade against `heavy+1`.

body.text: One more thing rode along, found by this workstream's `--import` rather than by looking for it: `scripts/test/verb_parity.gd.uid` was untracked while all 157 of its sibling `.uid` files are tracked — a gap dating from when `verb_parity.gd` landed.
The lesson, and it is this morning's from the other side of the board

Decision 090 said: before tuning the level, check whether the piece placed on it is priced. Decision 091 is the same move on the other side. **Before tuning the wave, check whether the roster has the shape the wave needs.** Act I had no way to say "heavy but shootable", so every attempt to make it heavier made it armoured instead — and six anchors' worth of sweeping could not have found that, because the answer was not in the sweep's search space at all.

Gate at tier 3: 42 passed, 0 failed. `rules parity` 1512 runs identical on Linux, digest `932ba387f3f5`, freshly verified, and 1512 identical across 8 shards on Windows. `music loudness` at tier 4 was not run, because no audio file changed.

entries.title: Both mechanical ways to catch a stale number in prose are wrong, so the line declares which number it quotes
entries.summary: Decision 092. I went looking for one thing and found another. `LF-262` says Act I is a reveal gate — across anchors 02–08 a build containing a scan relay won **136 of 246** runs and a build without one won **0 of 195** — and my framing of that in the backlog was "the first hour of the game has one real decision and the player is not told". The second half was wrong, and checking it first is what turned up a different defect: anchor-04's brief tells the player the shield wall costs "forty of those ninety-four" megawatts. **It draws 26**, and has since `LF-032` lowered it. The interesting part is what happened next: both obvious mechanical checks for this class of error were tried against the real dialog corpus and **both fail, in opposite directions**, so the fix is that a line now declares which data figure it reads aloud.

commits.subject: fix(dialog): the shield wall costs 26 MW and the brief said forty, so prose that quotes a number now declares which one

body.text: The previous entry, `the-same-weight-in-fewer-bodies`, closed out a content slice of `BAL-04`. This one is much smaller and started as a question rather than a task: `LF-262` had just recorded that Act I is decided by one binary — across anchors 02–08, a build containing a scan relay won **136 of 246** runs and a build without one won **0 of 195**, because the Warden's air unit cannot be targeted at all until something reveals it. The backlog item's justification line read "the first hour of the game has one real decision in it and the player is not told".

**The second half of that was wrong, and it was checked before anything was built on it.** anchor-02's brief has Okonkwo say "Motes. They run cold and they don't reflect — your guns will not see them without a relay lit", at exactly the anchor where the scan relay unlocks, and Vasquez answers it with the price. The gate is taught, by the right character, at the right moment. What remains open in `LF-262` is purely the design question the item already states — whether a mandatory 8 MW relay should be a tax or a trade — and nothing about it needed writing.
The sweep that settled it found a different defect

anchor-04's brief tells the player: "Shield wall's signed off — forty of those ninety-four if you raise it", and Vasquez answers "Forty. For a screen that doesn't shoot." **The shield wall draws 26.** It drew 40 until `LF-032` lowered it as overpriced, and the prose was never updated — a figure the player is read before the level, wrong by **14 MW**, for the whole life of the project.

`dialog capacity` is a check that exists precisely because tuning moves numbers that prose quotes, and it did not catch this, because it asks exactly one question: does the brief state its own `capacity_mw`. It does. Ninety-four is correct.
Both obvious checks are wrong, in opposite directions
This is what the entry is actually about. Two mechanical designs were tried against the real dialog corpus before either was implemented, and **both fail**:

items: **A regex over "<number> megawatts" misses this exact bug.** "forty" carries no unit word at all — the unit is implied by the "ninety-four" it is compared against. The existing `_spoken_numbers()` helper, which anchors on the unit word, returns `{94}` for that line and never sees the 40.

**"Every spoken number must be a live data figure" false-positives immediately.** anchor-06 says the ion lance "reaches across four lanes". anchor-08 says "the ring is drawing about nine megawatts that isn't going anywhere I can find", and anchor-17 says "the bus reading falls about six megawatts a wave and I cannot find where it goes".

body.text: Those last two are **deliberately unexplained**. They are the act's mystery. A check that demands they resolve to a data figure is a check that demands the story stop being a story — and that is the argument against inferring the dependency at all, not a tuning problem in the regex.
So the line declares what it quotes

A dialog line may now carry `quotes`, a list of dotted paths into `data/towers.json` or `data/enemies.json` — `shield-wall.draw_mw`, `restorer.effect.value`, `reach-sapper.drains_mw`. The new tier-1 check `dialog figures` resolves each path and asserts the live value is among the numbers the line actually says, spelled or in digits. **Ten figures are declared across seven anchors' dialog files** today. The writer names the dependency; the check does the arithmetic.

data/dialog/anchor-04.json

-     { "trigger": "brief", "speaker": "control",
-       "text": "... Shield wall's signed off — forty of those ninety-four if you raise it." },
+     { "trigger": "brief", "speaker": "control",
+       "quotes": ["shield-wall.draw_mw"],
+       "text": "... Shield wall's signed off — twenty-six of those ninety-four if you raise it." },

data/towers.json      shield-wall.draw_mw = 26
tools/check.py        dialog figures: 10 quoted figure(s) match the data they name
body.caption: The whole shape of the fix in one line of data. The declaration is what makes the dependency greppable as well as checkable: someone re-pricing an emplacement can now find who talks about it.

body.text: **The limitation, stated here rather than discovered later: it is opt-in, so it cannot prove a line should have been annotated.** A future brief that quotes a draw without declaring it is invisible to this check exactly as anchor-04 was. What it does guarantee is that a **declared** figure can never be silently invalidated by a tuning change — which is the failure that actually happened, twice now if you count decision 090's stale note on the same emplacement.
Proved red four ways before being trusted green

headers: why it is in the list
rows: a tuning change moves the value, 26 → 28
a path landing on an object, not a number
a silently-unresolvable path is a silently-absent check
a full rewording that keeps the figure
the design claim, not a formality

body.text: The last row is the one that matters. The check has to survive a writer moving the figure anywhere in the sentence, or the next narrative pass will start working around it — rewriting the line to "Raising it costs twenty-six" stays green. The tree was asserted byte-identical after all four injections.

**One real bug in the checker, found by running it.** The first `_all_spoken_numbers()` accumulated across sentence boundaries: "Anchor fourteen. Ninety-four megawatts" came back as **108**, because splitting on non-letters made "fourteen" and "ninety" adjacent tokens in one run. It now chunks on anything that is not a letter, a space or an ASCII hyphen, so a full stop or an em dash ends a number and a hyphen does not. Covered afterwards by "a hundred and ninety" → 190, "two hundred and ninety" → 290, and "forty-four megawatts back for ten drawn" → 44 and 10.
A diff-discipline failure worth recording

The first pass at annotating the seven dialog files wrote them back with `json.dumps(indent=2)` and produced **858 insertions** of pure formatting churn against this project's compact house style, for eleven lines of actual content. Rebuilt from `git show HEAD:` with surgical inserts instead: **11 insertions, 2 deletions**. Same content, a diff 78 times smaller — and the difference between a change a reader can check at a glance and one nobody will read.

**The prose fix keeps the beat.** "forty of those ninety-four" became "twenty-six of those ninety-four", and Vasquez's echo "Forty." became "Twenty-six." 26 of 94 is still over a quarter of the bus for a screen that does not shoot, which is the objection the exchange exists to make, so the correction cost the scene nothing.

**And the cost of shipping it, filed as `LF-273`.** This is a data change under `data/`, so the parity digest forced a full **1,512-run** comparison on **both** platforms — for seven dialog files and a schema that neither rule engine reads. The digest hashes 52 such files (25 dialog, 21 schema, 6 scenario) against 27 genuine rules inputs. That is roughly a 35-minute tax on changing one word of a mission brief, and it is filed rather than fixed here.

Gate at tier 3: 43 passed, 0 failed. `rules parity` 1512 runs identical on Linux, digest `234f711c8e46`, freshly verified, and 1512 identical across 8 shards on Windows. `music loudness` at tier 4 was not run, because no audio file changed. The check counts in `check.py`'s own docstring moved with it — tier 1 from 19 to 20, tier 2 to 29, tier 3 to 43, tier 4 to 46 — and `tier counts` asserts them against the registry, so they cannot drift quietly.
